docs.title: Dependency Profiles
docs.text: Starting with v3.1.0, duckdb, duckdb-engine, pandas, and pyarrow (~300 MiB) are removed from core and moved to an optional [sql] extra. dapr, temporalio, and orjson are promoted to core (they were already eagerly imported by every app).

docs.title: Deprecated extras (removed in v4.0.0)
docs.text:
These extras install nothing that core or [sql] does not already provide. Each is deprecated and removed in v4.0.0:

Extra Why it is redundant Do this [workflows] temporalio, orjson are core since v3.1 Remove it [storage] rocksdict is core Remove it [iam_auth] / [iam-auth] boto3 is core since v3.14 Remove it [azure] azure-identity is core since v3.14 Remove it [sqlalchemy] A subset of [sql] Use [sql] [pandas] A subset of [sql] Use [sql] [daft] An alias for [sql] (see below) Use [sql]

For example, atlan-application-sdk[iam-auth,pandas,sql,workflows] becomes atlan-application-sdk[sql]. Then run uv lock and review the diff. Every package the shim installed stays installed. Dropping a core shim changes only the lock's metadata, but replacing [pandas] or [sqlalchemy] with [sql] can add packages: [pandas] alone gains sqlalchemy and duckdb.

Do this before you move to v4. uv ignores an extra that no longer exists, so after the removal an app on [pandas] or [sqlalchemy] loses those packages without an error at install time. The D017 conformance rule warns on each of these extras now.

[incremental] is not deprecated. It is an alias for [sql] and stays supported.

docs.title: The [daft] extra
docs.text:
[daft] is deprecated and will be removed in v4.0.0. Move to [sql] (or [incremental] if you use the incremental analytics stack).

It is an alias for [sql], so a pin on atlan-application-sdk[daft] resolves the same packages it did before v3.22 and nothing breaks while you migrate.

If you are on v3.22 through v3.27, upgrade: over that range the extra resolved to nothing. That is a silent break rather than a loud one — imports still succeed and mocked unit tests still pass, so the first symptom is ImportError: duckdb is required for DuckDBConnectionManager on the first real transform, end-to-end. A version bump is the whole fix; no per-repo change is needed. The D010 conformance rule covers the residual case of an app on plain atlan-application-sdk with no extras at all.

docs.title: Packages the SDK no longer declares
docs.text:
The SDK declares only what it imports (a unit test holds this). These were declared but never imported, and are gone:

Package Was in Still arrives via aiohttp core the [harness] extra (kubernetes) only uvloop core uvicorn[standard] opentelemetry-exporter-otlp core — (the SDK now declares opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-grpc) duckdb-engine [sql], [incremental] — azure-storage-blob, azure-storage-file-datalake [azure] (deprecated) — pytest-order [tests] — numpy [scale_data_generator] pandas, where installed fastapi[standard]: fastapi-cli (and typer, rich, sentry-sdk), email-validator, pydantic-settings, pydantic-extra-types, opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http core (the extra) — (the SDK now declares fastapi, uvicorn[standard] and python-multipart)

If your app imports one of these, declare it in your own pyproject.toml; it was never a promise of the SDK's. The usual cases: aiohttp in app code, create_engine("duckdb:///...") (needs duckdb-engine), the Azure Storage SDK used directly, @pytest.mark.order in tests, pydantic's EmailStr (needs email-validator), pydantic_settings.BaseSettings, and the fastapi CLI (fastapi run / fastapi dev; use uvicorn). The SDK's own HTTP client is httpx.

docs.title: pandas 3 and pyarrow 26
docs.text:
The [sql] and [incremental] extras (and the deprecated [pandas]) accept pandas>=2.2.3,<4 and pyarrow>=23.0.1,<27. The SDK is tested against both pandas 2 and pandas 3. An app that pins pandas<3 keeps resolving and needs no change.

When your app's lock moves to pandas 3, two pandas changes reach code that reads SDK DataFrames (for example ParquetFileReader.read() and read_batches()):

  • Text columns use pandas' str dtype, and a missing value in one is NaN, not None. Test for a missing value with pd.isna(value), not value is None.
  • Copy-on-write is always on. Assigning through a chained index such as df["col"][mask] = value no longer changes df. Use df.loc[mask, "col"] = value.

ParquetFileWriter, the JSON-to-Parquet file converter and the scale data generator keep the same Parquet schema under either pandas version: text columns are written as Arrow string, as they were under pandas 2, rather than the large_string pandas 3 converts to by default. Two exceptions:

  • A text column holding more than 2 GiB of text in one chunk does not fit Arrow's string type, so it is written as large_string. The SDK's readers merge string and large_string shards.
  • A flush_fn you pass to RollingFileWriter serializes the data itself, so its schema is yours. DataFrame.to_parquet under pandas 3 writes text as large_string.

from application_sdk.workflows.metadata_extraction.sql import BaseSQLMetadataExtractionWorkflow

@workflow.defn
class MyMetadataWorkflow(BaseSQLMetadataExtractionWorkflow):

docs.title: v3
docs.text:
SqlMetadataExtractor is deprecated (removal in v4.0.0); subclass SqlApp (reference: atlan-mysql-app).

from application_sdk.templates import SqlApp

class MyMetadataExtractor(SqlApp):
    sql_client_class = MySQLClient

    fetch_database_sql = "SELECT ..."
    fetch_schema_sql = "SELECT ..."
    fetch_table_sql = "SELECT ..."
    fetch_column_sql = "SELECT ..."

    def map_database(self, record, connection_qn):
        from pyatlan_v9.model.assets import Database
        return Database.creator(name=record["database_name"], connection_qualified_name=connection_qn)

    # map_schema / map_table / map_column likewise. All four are required for
    # the default run(): the base ones raise Map*UnimplementedError.

Key changes: - Single class instead of workflow + activities split - Typed Input/Output Pydantic models instead of Dict[str, Any] - @task decorator instead of @activity.defn + manual execute_activity_method - Override run() to customize orchestration (default: parallel extract of all metadata types, then transform through the map_* functions)

docs.title: v2
docs.text:
from application_sdk.workflows.query_extraction.sql import SQLQueryExtractionWorkflow
from application_sdk.activities.query_extraction.sql import SQLQueryExtractionActivities

@workflow.defn
class MyQueryWorkflow(SQLQueryExtractionWorkflow):
    activities_cls = MyQueryActivities

docs.title: v3
docs.text:
SqlQueryExtractor is deprecated (removal in v4.0.0), but it is still the target for query-log connectors: SqlApp has no query-log capability yet (FND-4313). Migrate onto it as below; when SqlApp gains that capability, this step and the import rewriter move to it.

from application_sdk.templates import SqlQueryExtractor
from application_sdk.templates.contracts import (
    QueryBatchInput, QueryBatchOutput,
    QueryFetchInput, QueryFetchOutput,
)
from application_sdk.app import task

class MyQueryExtractor(SqlQueryExtractor):
    @task(timeout_seconds=600)
    async def get_query_batches(self, input: QueryBatchInput) -> QueryBatchOutput:
        ...

    @task(timeout_seconds=3600)
    async def fetch_queries(self, input: QueryFetchInput) -> QueryFetchOutput:
        ...

docs.title: v3
docs.text:
IncrementalSqlMetadataExtractor is deprecated (removal in v4.0.0). Subclass SqlApp as in Step 1 and override run() for the incremental orchestration:

from application_sdk.templates import SqlApp
from application_sdk.templates.contracts.sql_metadata import ExtractionInput, ExtractionOutput

class MyIncrementalExtractor(SqlApp):
    sql_client_class = MyClient

    async def run(self, input: ExtractionInput) -> ExtractionOutput:
        ...

SqlApp does not provide the v2 4-phase sequence (marker → fetch → diff → finalize). Write the phases the connector needs as @task methods and call them from run(). With SDK ≥ 3.60.0, build each entity's tasks on extract_entity / transform_entity (older SDKs name them _extract_entity / _transform_entity), and end the run() in finalize_extraction (SDK ≥ 3.33.2), which verifies the transformed tree before publish reads it (conformance rule P068 flags a run() that calls neither it nor super().run()).

docs.title: Step 3b: Upgrade REST/API Extraction (Asset-Mapper Pattern)
docs.text:
If your connector talks to a REST/API backend (rather than a SQL engine), v3 replaces the v2 TransformerInterface + Daft + YAML-query pipeline with a simpler pattern: typed records → pure mapper functions → pyatlan Asset instances. Reference implementations: atlan-openapi-app, atlan-azure-event-hub-app.

Note: The examples below import from the legacy pyatlan package (consistent with the built-in AtlasTransformer transformers, which still depend on pyatlan). If you are building a new connector that uses the pyatlan_v9 client elsewhere, prefer from pyatlan_v9.model.assets import ... and use the v9 serialisation API instead of .dict().

docs.title: When to use this pattern
docs.text:
Use the asset-mapper pattern when:

  • Your source is a REST API, SaaS service, or any non-SQL backend.
  • You don't have SQL queries to templatize in YAML.
  • You want typed intermediate records instead of untyped DataFrames.

SQL connectors use SqlApp (Step 1) and the templated-query pattern.

docs.title: v2
docs.text:
# app/transformer.py
from application_sdk.transformers.atlas import AtlasTransformer

class MyConnectorTransformer(AtlasTransformer):
    # YAML query files under app/sql/ define the per-entity shape
    # Daft DataFrames flow through transform → atlas entity emission
    ...

docs.title: v3
docs.text:
Two files replace the transformer subclass:

# app/api_types.py — typed intermediate records
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TopicRecord:
    name: str
    partition_count: int
    retention_ms: int

# app/asset_mapper.py — pure functions, one per entity type
from pyatlan.model.assets import KafkaTopic
from app.api_types import TopicRecord

def map_topic(
    record: TopicRecord,
    connection_qn: str,
    connection_name: str,
) -> KafkaTopic:
    """Pure function: no I/O, no side effects, deterministic."""
    return KafkaTopic(
        qualified_name=f"{connection_qn}/topic/{record.name}",
        name=record.name,
        connection_qualified_name=connection_qn,
        connection_name=connection_name,
        kafka_partitions=record.partition_count,
        kafka_topic_retention_time_ms=record.retention_ms,
    )

Wire them into extract/transform tasks on your App subclass:

# app/app.py
from application_sdk.app import App, task
from application_sdk.contracts import Input, Output, FileReference, UploadInput
from app.api_types import TopicRecord
from app.asset_mapper import map_topic

class FetchOutput(Output):
    file: FileReference

class TransformInput(Input):
    file: FileReference

class TransformOutput(Output):
    file: FileReference

class MyConnector(App):
    @task
    async def extract_topics(self, input: MyInput) -> FetchOutput:
        records = [TopicRecord(**row) async for row in self.client.list_topics()]
        local_path = "/tmp/topics.jsonl"
        write_jsonl(local_path, records)  # your serialisation helper
        return FetchOutput(file=FileReference.from_local(local_path))  # framework auto-uploads

    @task
    async def transform_topics(self, input: TransformInput) -> TransformOutput:
        # framework auto-downloads input.file before this task runs; input.file.local_path is set
        records = read_jsonl(input.file.local_path, TopicRecord)  # your parse helper
        assets = [map_topic(r, self.connection_qn, self.connection_name) for r in records]
        local_path = "/tmp/topics_assets.jsonl"
        write_jsonl(local_path, assets)  # your serialisation helper
        return TransformOutput(file=FileReference.from_local(local_path))  # framework auto-uploads

    async def run(self, input: MyInput) -> MyOutput:
        fetch_out = await self.extract_topics(input)
        transform_out = await self.transform_topics(TransformInput(file=fetch_out.file))

        # Required explicit hand-off: routes through atlan-objectstore (Atlan-owned) in SDR
        # so the publish app can read it. The activity interceptor only writes FileReferences
        # to the customer-owned objectstore (infra.storage). Omitting this call produces a
        # silent failure in SDR — the DAG succeeds but nothing is published. See ADR-0014.
        await self.upload(UploadInput(local_path=transform_out.file.local_path))
        return MyOutput(...)

Two-store rule: FileReference + the activity interceptor = task-to-task durability, customer-owned objectstore. App.upload() = app-to-app hand-off, Atlan-owned atlan-objectstore in SDR. These are two distinct stores. Forgetting App.upload() is a silent failure — all activities succeed but Atlan's publish app sees nothing. See ADR-0014 and file-reference.md.

docs.title: Rules for mapper functions
docs.text:
• Pure functions only — no I/O, no side effects, deterministic output for the same input. Temporal may replay these during retries.
  • One function per entity type — map_topic, map_consumer_group, map_process, etc.
  • Take a record + context, return an Asset — context (connection QN, tenant ID, workflow IDs) is passed as parameters, not read from globals.
  • Stamp sync metadata in a helper — a _apply_sync_metadata(asset, workflow_id, run_id, tenant_id) helper keeps sync-stamp logic in one place (see atlan-azure-event-hub-app/app/asset_mapper.py).

docs.title: What to remove from v2
docs.text:
• TransformerInterface subclasses (AtlasTransformer, QueryBasedTransformer)
  • Daft DataFrame pipelines for REST/API sources
  • app/sql/*.yaml query files (these are SQL-only)
  • Custom transform methods on Activities classes

The import rewriter (tools/migrate_v3/rewrite_imports.py) cannot auto-convert transformer code — it will leave # TODO(upgrade-v3) markers so you know where to apply this pattern manually.

docs.title: v2
docs.text:
from application_sdk.handlers import HandlerInterface

class MyHandler(HandlerInterface):
    async def load(self, *args, **kwargs) -> None: ...
    async def test_auth(self, *args, **kwargs) -> bool: ...
    async def preflight_check(self, *args, **kwargs): ...
    async def fetch_metadata(self, *args, **kwargs): ...

docs.title: v3
docs.text:
from application_sdk.handler import Handler
from application_sdk.handler.contracts import (
    AuthInput, AuthOutput, AuthStatus,
    PreflightInput, PreflightOutput, PreflightStatus,
    MetadataInput, MetadataOutput,
)

class MyHandler(Handler):
    async def test_auth(self, input: AuthInput) -> AuthOutput:
        # test connection
        return AuthOutput(status=AuthStatus.SUCCESS)

    async def preflight_check(self, input: PreflightInput) -> PreflightOutput:
        # run preflight checks
        return PreflightOutput(status=PreflightStatus.READY)

    async def fetch_metadata(self, input: MetadataInput) -> MetadataOutput:
        # return connector config
        return MetadataOutput(objects=[])

The load() method is removed — handler context (secrets, state) is injected automatically via self.context. Access credentials in handler methods with await self.context.get_secret(name).

docs.title: Connector-specific credential keys
docs.text:
Do not patch application_sdk.handler.service to change how requests are normalized. Rebinding service._CREDENTIAL_KEYS or service._normalize_credentials is deprecated (removal in v4.0.0), reaches only the worker, and is flagged by conformance rules B001 and B010.

When a v2 flat credential arrives (top-level host, authType, ...), the SDK lifts the shared keys into input.credentials and, on the worker and the API host alike, also every top-level field of your generated credential form (for example kerberos or an auth-type object such as basic). Declare the field in contract/app.pkl and regenerate; there is nothing to configure in code. A field the form declares never makes a body a credential on its own.

docs.title: Step 5: Upgrade the Application Entry Point
v2
docs.text:
from application_sdk.application.metadata_extraction.sql import (
    BaseSQLMetadataExtractionApplication,
)

app = BaseSQLMetadataExtractionApplication(
    name="my-connector",
    client_class=MyClient,
    handler_class=MyHandler,
)
await app.start()

docs.title: v3
docs.text:
ATLAN_APP_MODULE is mandatory in production. The base image entrypoint hard-fails at startup if it is not set. Set it in your app's Dockerfile — it should never be left to Helm values or runtime defaults.

The base image (registry.atlan.com/public/app-runtime-base:3) includes the application-sdk CLI, Dapr, and the entrypoint. You do not need a custom ENTRYPOINT or entrypoint.sh. The base image handles mode selection at runtime:

# Application-sdk v3 base image (Chainguard-based)
FROM registry.atlan.com/public/app-runtime-base:3

WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies first (better caching)
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser pyproject.toml uv.lock README.md ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/home/appuser/.cache/uv,uid=1000,gid=1000 \
    uv venv .venv && \
    uv sync --locked --no-install-project

# Copy application code
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser . .

# App-specific environment variables
ENV ATLAN_HANDLER_PORT=8000
ENV ATLAN_APP_MODULE=app.app:MyMetadataExtractor
ENV ATLAN_CONTRACT_GENERATED_DIR=app/generated

ATLAN_CONTRACT_GENERATED_DIR tells the SDK where to find the generated contract JSON files (configmaps, manifest). Place these files inside your repo's app/generated/ directory — the Pkl contract source (contract/app.pkl) outputs there, and COPY . . in your Dockerfile automatically includes it.

For local dev, pass the class directly — run_dev_combined derives the module path automatically:

from application_sdk.main import run_dev_combined

asyncio.run(run_dev_combined(MyMetadataExtractor))

run_dev_combined is the only place the SDK reads ./.env; importing application_sdk no longer loads it, so a container never does. Settings read at import (log level, OpenTelemetry exporters) miss a .env loaded that late: start with uv run --env-file .env python run_dev.py to apply the file to them too. See The .env file.

Three modes are available: - worker — Temporal worker only (production worker pods) - handler — HTTP handler only (production handler pods) - combined — both in one process (local dev, SDR)

docs.title: Step 5b: Multiple Workflows Per App
docs.text:
Skip this step if your v2 connector had only one workflow.

In v2 there was no first-class pattern for a connector that needed multiple workflows (e.g. metadata extraction + lineage + query mining). Teams worked around this with multiple WorkflowInterface/ActivitiesInterface pairs, separate entrypoint scripts, or other ad-hoc conventions.

In v3, one App subclass can expose multiple independently-triggerable workflows by decorating methods with @entrypoint. All entry points share @task methods, the HTTP handler, and AppContext — no code duplication.

docs.title: v2 — two separate workflow/activities pairs
docs.text:
# app/workflows/metadata_extraction.py
class MetadataExtractionWorkflow(WorkflowInterface):
    async def run(self, input):
        await execute_activity_method(self.activities.extract_tables, ...)
        await execute_activity_method(self.activities.transform, ...)

# app/activities/metadata_extraction.py
class MetadataExtractionActivities(ActivitiesInterface):
    async def extract_tables(self, input): ...
    async def transform(self, input): ...

# app/workflows/lineage.py
class LineageWorkflow(WorkflowInterface):
    async def run(self, input):
        await execute_activity_method(self.activities.fetch_lineage, ...)

# app/activities/lineage.py
class LineageActivities(ActivitiesInterface):
    async def fetch_lineage(self, input): ...

docs.title: v3 — one App, multiple @entrypoint methods
docs.text:
# app/connector.py
from application_sdk.app import App, entrypoint, task
from application_sdk.contracts import Input, Output
from typing import Any

class ExtractionInput(Input, allow_unbounded_fields=True):
    credential_guid: str = ""
    connection: dict[str, Any] = {}

class ExtractionOutput(Output):
    transformed_data_prefix: str = ""

class LineageInput(Input, allow_unbounded_fields=True):
    credential_guid: str = ""
    connection: dict[str, Any] = {}

class LineageOutput(Output):
    transformed_data_prefix: str = ""

class SnowflakeApp(App):
    # Shared task — callable from both entry points
    @task(timeout_seconds=3600)
    async def extract_tables(self, input: ExtractionInput) -> ExtractionOutput:
        ...

    @task(timeout_seconds=3600)
    async def fetch_lineage(self, input: LineageInput) -> LineageOutput:
        ...

    @entrypoint
    async def extract_metadata(self, input: ExtractionInput) -> ExtractionOutput:
        return await self.extract_tables(input)

    @entrypoint
    async def extract_lineage(self, input: LineageInput) -> LineageOutput:
        return await self.fetch_lineage(input)

docs.title: Workflow naming and HTTP dispatch
docs.text:
Entry point method Temporal workflow name HTTP trigger extract_metadata {app-name}:extract-metadata POST /workflows/v1/start?entrypoint=extract-metadata extract_lineage {app-name}:extract-lineage POST /workflows/v1/start?entrypoint=extract-lineage

For multi-entry-point apps the ?entrypoint= query parameter is required — omitting it returns 400.

docs.title: Dockerfile
docs.text:
One App = one ATLAN_APP_MODULE entry. No comma-separated list:

ENV ATLAN_APP_MODULE=app.connector:SnowflakeApp

docs.title: Manifest layout for multi-entry-point apps
docs.text:
For apps with multiple entry points, restructure ATLAN_CONTRACT_GENERATED_DIR into one subfolder per entry point (kebab-case):

app/generated/
  extract-metadata/
    manifest.json
  extract-lineage/
    manifest.json

Each manifest is served via GET /workflows/v1/manifest?entrypoint=<name> (returns 400 for invalid names, 404 if the folder is missing). Single-entry-point apps are unaffected — GET /workflows/v1/manifest (no query param) still works.

See docs/concepts/entry-points.md for the full @entrypoint and manifest reference.

docs.title: Step 6: Upgrade Worker Setup
docs.text: In v2, connecting to Temporal and registering workflow/activity classes was done explicitly. In v3, create_worker() auto-discovers all App subclasses and their @task methods — you don't register anything manually.

docs.title: v2
docs.text:
from application_sdk.worker import Worker
from application_sdk.clients.temporal import TemporalWorkflowClient

client = TemporalWorkflowClient(host=..., namespace=...)
await client.load()

worker = Worker(
    workflow_client=client,
    workflow_classes=[MyWorkflow],
    workflow_activities=[MyActivities()],
    passthrough_modules=["my_connector"],
)
await worker.run()

docs.title: v3
docs.text:
Worker setup is fully automatic when you use the CLI or run_dev_combined(). If you need a worker handle directly (e.g., in integration tests):

from application_sdk.execution import create_temporal_client, create_worker

client = await create_temporal_client(host="localhost:7233")  # pass host/namespace explicitly

# All registered App subclasses auto-discovered — no explicit list
worker = create_worker(client)
await worker.run()

Passthrough modules are declared on the App class itself as a ClassVar (a set, not a list), not as a class-kwarg:

class MyConnector(App):
    passthrough_modules = {"third_party_lib"}
    ...

Most apps need none. The worker passes through every library already imported when it starts, and re-imports only your app's own package in the sandbox, so Temporal checks your workflow code. Do not list your own package: that turns the check off. See Workflow Sandbox and Passthrough Modules.

docs.title: Concurrency defaults follow the pod's limits
docs.text:
The worker no longer defaults to 100 activity slots. Unless TEMPORAL_MAX_CONCURRENT_ACTIVITIES is set, it derives the slot count from the container: min(100, 32 × CPUs, memory limit ÷ 64 MiB), never below 16. The sdk-blocking- thread pool behind run_in_thread is min(32, max(16, CPUs + 4)) wide. In both, CPUs means the whole CPUs the process may use: the tighter of its CPU affinity and the pod's CFS quota (rounded down, never below 1), not the node's core count.

Small pods therefore allow fewer activities at once than before: a half-CPU pod under 1 GiB gets 16 slots and a 1-CPU, 2 GiB pod gets 32, instead of 100. Fleet usage peaks well below these, so most apps see no change in throughput. The startup log line Activity slots: N (...) shows the value and what it was derived from. If an app relied on the old width, set TEMPORAL_MAX_CONCURRENT_ACTIVITIES in its deployment, or raise the pod's limits.

docs.title: Step 7: Define Typed Contracts
docs.text:
v3 uses Input/Output Pydantic models for all task boundaries. The SDK validates these at import time.

from application_sdk.contracts import Input, Output, MaxItems
from typing import Annotated

class MyTaskInput(Input):
    workflow_id: str
    connection: str
    items: Annotated[list[str], MaxItems(1000)]  # bounded list required

class MyTaskOutput(Output):
    items_processed: int
    success: bool

Forbidden field types (raise PayloadSafetyError at class definition): - Any, bytes, bytearray - Unbounded list[T] or dict[K, V]

Safe alternatives: - Annotated[list[T], MaxItems(N)] for bounded lists - FileReference for large data (stored in object store, not in-memory) - allow_unbounded_fields=True escape hatch (use sparingly)

docs.title: ActivityStatistics / ActivityResult renamed
docs.text:
The v2 activity return types are renamed in v3:

v2 (application_sdk.activities.common.models) v3 (application_sdk.common.models) ActivityStatistics TaskStatistics ActivityResult TaskResult (deprecated in 3.58.0, removed in v4.0: nothing reads it; use TaskStatistics or your own TypedDict)

In v3 templates these are returned inside typed Output models, so you generally won't import them directly unless you are building a custom App from scratch.

docs.title: FileReference: passing large data between tasks
docs.text:
Temporal has a payload size limit (~2 MB). Use FileReference to store large data in object storage and pass only a lightweight reference through the workflow.

The framework handles upload and download automatically and transparently around every @task boundary:

  • After a task returns, any FileReference with local_path set (ephemeral) is uploaded to the object store and the reference is made durable before it enters the Temporal payload.
  • Before a task runs, any durable FileReference (with storage_path set) is downloaded to a local temp path so local_path is populated when your method is called.

You only need to declare FileReference fields in your contracts and use FileReference.from_local() when writing — no manual upload/download calls required:

from application_sdk.contracts import Input, Output, FileReference

class FetchOutput(Output):
    results: FileReference  # auto-uploaded by the framework after fetch() returns

class ProcessInput(Input):
    results: FileReference  # auto-downloaded by the framework before process() runs

# In the fetch task — write locally and return; the framework uploads automatically:
async def fetch(self, input: FetchInput) -> FetchOutput:
    local_path = "/tmp/results.parquet"
    write_parquet(data, local_path)
    return FetchOutput(results=FileReference.from_local(local_path))

# In the next task — local_path is already populated by the framework:
async def process(self, input: ProcessInput) -> ProcessOutput:
    data = read_parquet(input.results.local_path)
    ...

FileReference objects are tracked automatically and cleaned up by the framework's cleanup_files() / cleanup_storage() tasks.

docs.title: Step 8: Upgrade Infrastructure Access
docs.text: In v3, infrastructure services are created automatically at startup (by main.py) and injected into @task methods and handlers via self.context. You do not need to create DaprClient instances in your code.

docs.title: Infrastructure available in @task methods
docs.text: v2 v3 (self.context in @task methods) services.statestore.StateStore.get_state(...) await self.context.load_state(key) services.statestore.StateStore.save_state(...) await self.context.save_state(key, value) services.secretstore.SecretStore.get_credentials(...) await self.context.get_secret(name) services.objectstore.ObjectStore.get_content(key) await download_file(key, local_path, self.context.storage) services.objectstore.ObjectStore.upload_file(src, key) await upload_file(key, local_path, self.context.storage) services.eventstore.EventStore.publish_event(event) Automatic via interceptor

docs.title: Infrastructure available in handlers
docs.text: v2 v3 (self.context in handler methods) services.secretstore.SecretStore.get_credentials(...) await self.context.get_secret(name) /workflows/v1/config/{id} (503 error) Works automatically (object store wired) /workflows/v1/file (503 error) Works automatically (storage binding wired)

docs.title: Upgrading ObjectStore calls
docs.text:
# v2 — all calls went through the Dapr binding
from application_sdk.services.objectstore import ObjectStore  # v2

await ObjectStore.upload_file(source="/local/file.parquet", key="output/file.parquet")
data = await ObjectStore.get_content("config/settings.json")
files = await ObjectStore.list_files(prefix="output/")
await ObjectStore.delete_file("output/old.parquet")

# v3 — inside an @task method, use the storage module with self.context.storage:
from application_sdk.storage import upload_file, download_file
await upload_file("output/file.parquet", "/local/file.parquet", self.context.storage)
await download_file("config/settings.json", "/tmp/settings.json", self.context.storage)

# v3 — outside an App (standalone scripts, utilities): use the storage module directly
from application_sdk.storage import upload_file, download_file, list_keys, delete

await upload_file("output/file.parquet", local_path="/local/file.parquet")
await download_file("config/settings.json", local_path="/tmp/settings.json")
keys = await list_keys(prefix="output/")
await delete("output/old.parquet")

docs.title: Migrating AtlanStorage
docs.text:
# v2
from application_sdk.services.atlan_storage import AtlanStorage
summary = await AtlanStorage(store, atlan_store).migrate_from_objectstore_to_atlan(prefix)

# v3 — use the built-in App.upload() framework task, or compose storage calls directly
# Inside a workflow run():
await self.upload(UploadInput(local_path="output/"))

docs.title: Local development with credentials
docs.text:
For production-equivalent local testing, run the Dapr sidecar (uv run poe start-deps) and let the app pick it up automatically via DAPR_HTTP_PORT. For quick local runs without a sidecar, pass credentials directly — run_dev_combined auto-provisions them via the local vault:

from application_sdk.main import run_dev_combined

asyncio.run(run_dev_combined(
    MyApp,
    credentials={"host": "localhost", "authType": "basic",
                 "username": "dev", "password": "test-value"},
))

docs.title: Step 9: Upgrade to Typed Credentials
docs.text: v3 introduces a typed credential system that replaces bare credential_guid: str + Dict[str, Any] with a CredentialRef → typed Credential pipeline.

docs.title: Before (credential_guid pattern)
docs.text:
from application_sdk.contracts.base import Input

class ExtractionInput(Input, allow_unbounded_fields=True):
    credential_guid: str = ""

# In @task method:
from application_sdk.services.secretstore import SecretStore  # v2, deprecated

credentials = await SecretStore.get_credentials({"credential_guid": input.credential_guid})
await client.load(credentials)  # dict[str, Any]

docs.title: After (CredentialRef pattern)
docs.text:
from application_sdk.contracts import Input
from application_sdk.credentials import CredentialRef, api_key_ref, ApiKeyCredential

class ExtractionInput(Input, allow_unbounded_fields=True):
    credential_ref: CredentialRef | None = None

# In @task method:
cred = await self.context.resolve_credential(input.credential_ref)
assert isinstance(cred, ApiKeyCredential)
headers = cred.to_headers()  # {"X-API-Key": "secret"}

docs.title: credential_guid and credential_ref
docs.text:
Both credential_guid and credential_ref work on ExtractionInput and QueryExtractionInput. credential_guid is a supported route, not a legacy one: it is how the platform names the credential for a direct-mode run. When only credential_guid is provided, the SDK builds the GUID ref itself:

# These are both valid:
ExtractionInput(credential_guid="abc-123")       # GUID route (direct mode)
ExtractionInput(credential_ref=api_key_ref("prod-key"))  # pre-built typed ref

If your code calls legacy_credential_ref(guid), switch to CredentialRef.resolve(input). If it passes a credential_type, build the ref directly to keep typed resolution: CredentialRef(name=guid, credential_type="api_key", credential_guid=guid) (resolve() always uses credential_type="unknown", which resolves to RawCredential). The public constructor is deprecated and removed in v4.0; the GUID route it builds is not.

If you need to call a legacy client that expects a raw dict, use resolve_credential_raw():

raw = await self.context.resolve_credential_raw(ref)
await client.load(raw)  # dict[str, Any] — same as before

from application_sdk.credentials import register_credential_type

docs.title: v3
docs.text:
Only async clients are exposed. Use the credential system to supply the token:

from application_sdk.credentials import create_async_atlan_client, AtlanApiToken

cred = AtlanApiToken(token="my-token", base_url="https://my-tenant.atlan.com")
client = create_async_atlan_client(cred)

Inside an App, use the AtlanClientMixin to get a cached, per-run client:

from application_sdk.credentials import AtlanClientMixin, atlan_api_token_ref

class MyConnector(AtlanClientMixin, App):
    @task
    async def my_task(self, input: MyInput) -> MyOutput:
        ref = atlan_api_token_ref("atlan-token")  # name of your secret store entry
        client = await self.get_or_create_async_atlan_client(ref)
        # client is an AsyncAtlanClient; cached for the lifetime of this run

docs.text:
# v2
from application_sdk.clients.atlan_auth import AtlanAuthClient  # v2
auth = AtlanAuthClient()
headers = await auth.get_authenticated_headers()

# v3
from application_sdk.credentials import OAuthClientCredential, OAuthTokenService
cred = OAuthClientCredential(client_id="...", client_secret="...", token_url="...")
service = OAuthTokenService(cred)
headers = await service.get_headers()

docs.title: Step 11: Upgrade Heartbeating
docs.text: In v2, you applied @auto_heartbeater to activity methods to prevent Temporal from timing them out. In v3, heartbeating is built into @task — no decorator needed.

docs.title: v2
docs.text:
from application_sdk.activities.common.utils import auto_heartbeater

class MyActivities(ActivitiesInterface):
    @auto_heartbeater
    @activity.defn
    async def long_running_task(self, args: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        # heartbeats sent every 10 seconds automatically
        ...

docs.title: v3
docs.text:
from application_sdk.app import App, task

class MyConnector(App):
    # heartbeat_timeout_seconds: Temporal kills the task if no heartbeat is received
    # auto_heartbeat_seconds: framework sends a heartbeat every N seconds automatically
    @task(timeout_seconds=3600, heartbeat_timeout_seconds=60, auto_heartbeat_seconds=10)
    async def long_running_task(self, input: MyInput) -> MyOutput:
        # heartbeats are sent in a background loop — no decorator needed
        ...

docs.title: Manual heartbeats with progress data
docs.text:
Send a heartbeat with progress details so the task can resume from where it left off if Temporal restarts it:

from application_sdk.contracts import HeartbeatDetails

class MyProgress(HeartbeatDetails):
    last_processed_id: str
    records_done: int

@task(heartbeat_timeout_seconds=60)
async def process_batches(self, input: MyInput) -> MyOutput:
    # Resume after a retry
    prev = self.task_context.get_heartbeat_details(MyProgress)
    start_id = prev.last_processed_id if prev else None

    for batch in get_batches(start_from=start_id):
        process(batch)
        self.task_context.heartbeat(MyProgress(
            last_processed_id=batch.id,
            records_done=batch.count,
        ))

docs.title: Blocking sync operations
docs.text:
If you call blocking (non-async) code inside a task (e.g., a sync SDK or driver), use run_in_thread to avoid blocking the event loop and stalling heartbeats:

@task(heartbeat_timeout_seconds=60)
async def fetch(self, input: MyInput) -> MyOutput:
    result = await self.task_context.run_in_thread(my_sync_function, arg1, arg2)
    return MyOutput(data=result)

docs.title: Step 11b: The stall watchdog
docs.text:
What if you do nothing? The SDK now runs a stall watchdog inside every activity: it watches for observable forward progress, and reports when an attempt goes quiet for longer than max_no_progress_seconds (900s). At the same time timeout_seconds (start_to_close) becomes a 24h backstop you never tune, instead of a duration you guess.

There is no migration task here. This step exists to tell you that, precisely.

docs.title: On upgrade, no failure semantics change (the default timeout and telemetry do)
docs.text:
• You land in warn mode, which cannot fail an activity. It observes and reports.
  • heartbeat_timeout_seconds keeps its meaning and its 60s default. Crash, OOM and node-loss detection is unchanged.
  • No existing knob changes meaning, so there is no coupled default to bump.
  • The one thing that does change immediately is in your favour: with the backstop at 24h, a legitimately long run stops dying at a guessed ceiling.

What you gain is a report about your own code — the sites that go quiet, and the long opaque calls the SDK is currently vouching for unbounded. Reading it is optional and can wait; the app stays correct indefinitely without it.

docs.title: The added cost is telemetry
docs.text:
Two histograms and the occasional INFO log line. Warn-mode findings are deliberately never WARNING-level — a stall observation under a fleet-wide default is an expected observation, not an alert.

If you need most of that gone, ATLAN_PROGRESS_WATCHDOG=off — or progress_watchdog="off" on a single @task — is the kill-switch: no gap is reported and nothing is ever failed. It is not the normal state, and it also switches off the report you would otherwise use later. Note it is not completely inert — hold observations still record, since those are a work-list entry rather than a watchdog action — and it does not shorten a wedged attempt, which is bounded by timeout_seconds either way.

docs.title: One knob did change value: timeout_seconds
docs.text:
ATLAN_START_TO_CLOSE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS now defaults to 86400 (24 h) instead of 600. Nothing changes for a task that passes timeout_seconds= explicitly — which, if your app weight-classed its tasks, is most of them. Those explicit numbers are now the thing worth deleting: they are the guesses ADR-0018 exists to remove, and with the backstop in place a legitimately long attempt no longer needs one to survive. Delete them at your own pace; nothing forces it.

The one consequence to be aware of is on the other side of the trade: a wedged attempt is no longer killed by a small ceiling, so while your app is in warn its containment is the AtlanAppTaskStalled alert plus a human rather than an automatic kill. Detection improves — a wedge is now visible one budget in, where before it was only ever killed by luck. See ADR-0018 ("Migration & backward compatibility") for why that trade is the one being made.

SqlApp apps get the backstop without editing anything. SqlApp's twelve extract_* / transform_* tasks used to pin timeout_seconds=1800, heartbeat_timeout_seconds=120 and auto_heartbeat_seconds=30, which hid both the backstop and the env vars from every app built on it. They now declare nothing, so an attempt that ran longer than 30 minutes is no longer killed, and the heartbeat window is ATLAN_HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (default 60 s, beating every 10 s). If your app overrode those methods only to raise the 30-minute limit, the override can go. See Tasks → Which knob governs SqlApp.

docs.title: Declaring holds is an eventual optimisation, not an upgrade task
docs.text: Wrapping opaque calls in holding_progress() is work you take on when you want the stronger guarantee — a wedge caught in minutes rather than at the backstop — at a time of your choosing, guided by your own warn report. It is not a precondition for taking the version.

docs.title: Which code shapes eventually need action
docs.text:
Relevant only if and when you flip an app to enforce:

Your existing code In warn (today) In enforce Action Streaming through SDK writers / ObjectStore transfers / template page loops silent covered — hooks mark progress none Already calls self.heartbeat(...) silent covered — a beat marks progress none Opaque blocking call via run_in_thread reported as a long unbounded hold covered — unbounded auto-hold; the backstop is the only bound optional: declare an allowance to get a real bound A custom async loop doing its own I/O reported as a no-progress gap false-killed if any gap exceeds the budget add a beat or a hold An opaque single await against your source (your own async client) reported as a no-progress gap false-killed at the tail wrap in holding_progress() — expected in nearly every connector

The last two rows are why enforce is a per-app decision verified against a large-tenant profile, not a smoke test.

See Progress and Stalls for the three knobs, how to read your warn report, and how to size an allowance.

docs.title: Step 12: App Lifecycle Hooks
docs.text: v3 adds structured lifecycle hooks that replace ad-hoc cleanup logic that was previously scattered across activities or added as a final workflow step.

docs.title: on_complete
docs.text:
on_complete is called after run() finishes (whether successful or not):

class MyConnector(App):
    async def run(self, input: ExtractionInput) -> ExtractionOutput:
        ...

    async def on_complete(self) -> None:
        await self.notify_downstream()
        await super().on_complete()  # preserves built-in file/storage cleanup

docs.title: Built-in cleanup tasks
docs.text:
Two cleanup tasks are built into every App. Call them from run() or on_complete():

async def on_complete(self) -> None:
    await super().on_complete()  # runs built-in file/storage cleanup

cleanup_files() and cleanup_storage() are also available as individual workflow steps if you need to trigger cleanup mid-run (e.g., after a particularly large intermediate step).

docs.text:
# v2 — all of these are deprecated
import application_sdk.test_utils  # v2
from application_sdk.test_utils.credentials import MockCredentialStore  # v2
import application_sdk.test_utils.scale_data_generator  # v2

# v3
from application_sdk.testing import (
    MockStateStore,
    MockSecretStore,

    MockPubSub,
    MockCredentialStore,

)

docs.title: Using mock infrastructure in tests
docs.text:
In v3 you can test @task methods without any Dapr sidecar running:

import pytest
from application_sdk.testing import MockSecretStore, MockStateStore
from application_sdk.infrastructure import set_infrastructure, InfrastructureContext

@pytest.fixture
def infra():
    ctx = InfrastructureContext(
        secret_store=MockSecretStore({"api-key": "test-secret"}),
        state_store=MockStateStore(),
    )
    set_infrastructure(ctx)
    return ctx

async def test_my_task(infra):
    connector = MyConnector()
    output = await connector.my_task(MyInput(connection_id="test"))
    assert output.record_count > 0

docs.title: Pytest fixtures provided by the framework
docs.text:
# conftest.py — import to make the fixture available project-wide
from application_sdk.testing import clean_app_registry

# test_my_app.py — list it as a parameter on each test that needs isolation
async def test_something(clean_app_registry):
    ...

The clean_app_registry fixture resets AppRegistry and TaskRegistry between tests, preventing subclass registrations in one test from leaking into the next. It is not autouse — you must list it in the test's parameter list to activate it.

docs.title: MockCredentialStore
docs.text:
from application_sdk.testing import MockCredentialStore
from application_sdk.credentials import CredentialResolver

mock = MockCredentialStore()
ref = mock.add_api_key("test-key", api_key="test-secret")

resolver = CredentialResolver(mock.secret_store)
cred = await resolver.resolve(ref)
assert cred.api_key == "test-secret"

docs.title: MockHeartbeatController
docs.text:
For testing tasks that use self.task_context.heartbeat() without running inside Temporal:

from application_sdk.testing import MockHeartbeatController

controller = MockHeartbeatController()
# inject into task context or pass to the function under test
# controller.get_heartbeat_calls() returns the list of heartbeat calls

docs.title: Running locally with credentials
docs.text:
For quick local runs without a Dapr sidecar, pass credentials directly — run_dev_combined provisions them via the local vault, exactly as production does. For test isolation with typed mock infrastructure, use InfrastructureContext directly in pytest fixtures (see testing section above).

from application_sdk.main import run_dev_combined

asyncio.run(run_dev_combined(
    MyConnector,
    credentials={"host": "localhost", "authType": "basic",
                 "username": "dev", "password": "test-value"},
))

docs.text:
The SDK no longer reads these constants: the run mode comes from ATLAN_APP_MODE (or --mode), resolved at startup into AppConfig.mode. They are still importable and warn on access. Reading APPLICATION_MODE no longer fails for an unrecognised APPLICATION_MODE env value; it falls back to LOCAL. B001 flags each import.

docs.title: v2 FastAPI server models and utilities (deprecated, removed in v4.0.0)
docs.text:
application_sdk.server.fastapi.models and application_sdk.server.fastapi.utils are what is left of the v2 server, which v3 replaced with the handler service. Nothing in the SDK imports them any more. Every public name in both is deprecated and removed in v4.0.0, along with the v2 payload strategies in application_sdk.testing.hypothesis.strategies.server.fastapi. B001 flags each import.

Deprecated Replacement server.fastapi.models.FileUploadResponse application_sdk.handler.contracts.FileUploadResponse. Its attributes are snake_case (raw_name, not rawName); it serialises with the same camelCase aliases. server.fastapi.models.TestAuthRequest / TestAuthResponse handler.contracts.AuthInput / AuthOutput server.fastapi.models.PreflightCheckRequest / PreflightCheckResponse handler.contracts.PreflightInput / PreflightOutput server.fastapi.models.FetchMetadataRequest / FetchMetadataResponse, MetadataType handler.contracts.MetadataInput / MetadataOutput server.fastapi.models.Subscription handler.contracts.SubscriptionConfig server.fastapi.models.EventWorkflowRequest handler.contracts.CloudEventEnvelope server.fastapi.models.WorkflowRequest, WorkflowConfigRequest, WorkflowResponse, WorkflowData, EventWorkflowResponse, WorkflowConfigResponse, ConfigMapResponse none; the handler's /workflows/v1 and /events/v1 routes own these shapes, and the App's typed Input contract replaces the request dicts server.fastapi.utils.upload_file_to_object_store the handler's POST /workflows/v1/file, or application_sdk.storage.upload_bytes server.fastapi.utils.internal_server_error_handler none; the handler service installs its own sanitised 500 handling testing.hypothesis.strategies.server.fastapi.* none; build strategies from your app's own models in its tests

application_sdk.common.utils.download_file_from_upload_response now accepts the handler's FileUploadResponse. Before this change it raised ResponseTypeError: Unsupported response type: FileUploadResponse for it, because it only recognised the v2 class.

docs.title: Hypothesis strategies: orphaned modules and a duplicate (deprecated, removed in v4.0.0)
docs.text:
Three strategy modules had no importer anywhere in the SDK or its tests. Every public name in them is deprecated and removed in v4.0.0. strategies.sql_client duplicated strategies.clients.sql; its strategies moved there, and the old module serves them with a warning until v4.0.0. B001 flags each import.

Deprecated Replacement testing.hypothesis.strategies.sql_client.* the same name in testing.hypothesis.strategies.clients.sql testing.hypothesis.strategies.handlers.sql.sql_metadata.* none; build strategies from your app's own metadata rows in its tests testing.hypothesis.strategies.handlers.sql.sql_preflight.* none; build strategies from your app's typed preflight Input contract testing.hypothesis.strategies.outputs.statestore.* none; build strategies from your app's own credential and config models

Every integer the SQL client and logger strategies draw is now bounded; outputs.json_output still draws unbounded chunk_size and row counts until FND-4286 bounds them. sqlalchemy_connect_args_strategy, sql_engine_config_strategy and the logger strategies' attempt and timeouts draw no negative sizes, counts or timeouts (pool_recycle keeps SQLAlchemy's -1, "never recycle"), and every one has an upper bound. sql_data_strategy and sql_query_strategy draw within the 64-bit signed range. A property test that relied on drawing a negative timeout or an arbitrarily large integer from these strategies no longer sees one.

docs.title: Distributed locks (deprecated, removed in v4.0.0)
docs.text:
needs_lock has no effect in v3. create_worker registers neither the lock interceptor nor the acquire_distributed_lock / release_distributed_lock activities, and it takes no extra activities, so a task decorated with needs_lock runs with no concurrency limit. Setting IS_LOCKING_DISABLED=false does not change that. needs_lock now emits a DeprecationWarning, and create_worker logs a warning naming each decorated task.

The SDK's Redis clients still work, but they are deprecated too: the lock was their only use inside the SDK. B001 flags each import.

Deprecated Do this application_sdk.execution.needs_lock Remove the decorator. It never limited concurrency in v3. RedisLockInterceptor, RedisLockOutboundInterceptor, acquire_distributed_lock, release_distributed_lock, and the lock error leaves in execution._temporal._lock_errors Remove the import application_sdk.clients.RedisClient / RedisClientAsync (and clients.redis.BaseRedisClient, LockReleaseResult, the clients.redis_errors leaves) Use redis / redis.asyncio directly. RedisClientAsync still connects as before until v4.0.0. application_sdk.constants.REDIS_*, IS_LOCKING_DISABLED, LOCK_METADATA_KEY, LOCK_RETRY_INTERVAL_SECONDS Read the env vars in your app. The env vars still configure the deprecated clients until v4.0.0. The [distributed_lock] extra Depend on redis directly. The extra only installs it for the deprecated clients.

docs.title: Pub/sub subscribe and unimplemented binding shapes (deprecated, removed in v4.0.0)
docs.text:
DaprPubSub.subscribe() never delivered a message. It stored the handler, returned a handle whose is_active was True, and nothing ever called the handler. MockPubSub.subscribe() did deliver, so a test passed and the same code received nothing in production. Dapr delivers pub/sub messages to HTTP routes the app serves; the SDK builds those routes from SubscriptionConfig. Both subscribe() methods now emit a DeprecationWarning. publish() is unchanged. B001 flags each import.

Deprecated Replacement DaprPubSub.subscribe, PubSub.subscribe, MockPubSub.subscribe a SubscriptionConfig from application_sdk.handler.contracts, passed to create_app_handler_service(subscriptions=...). In tests, call its handler directly. infrastructure.Subscription, DaprSubscription none; a SubscriptionConfig has no handle to hold infrastructure.MessageHandler the handler field of SubscriptionConfig infrastructure.OutputBinding infrastructure.Binding (DaprBinding.invoke); the SDK never shipped an implementation infrastructure.InputBinding No input-binding replacement (the SDK never shipped an implementation). To receive messages, use SubscriptionConfig with create_app_handler_service(subscriptions=...) infrastructure.BindingRequest pass operation, data and metadata to Binding.invoke(); nothing accepted a BindingRequest

docs.title: Legacy AAF-* error codes (deprecated, removed in v4.0.0)
docs.text:
An SDK error class names its failure with one vocabulary, its code ClassVar (NOT_FOUND_CREDENTIAL, DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE_STORAGE, …). The older AAF-{COMP}-{ID} ErrorCode is no longer declared on any class. Each of these still works and warns. B001 flags each import, and E022 flags a class that binds DEFAULT_ERROR_CODE in this vocabulary. str() on a legacy-coded error keeps its [AAF-…] prefix until v4.0.0, so log text does not change.

Deprecated Replacement application_sdk.errors.ErrorCode and its 39 constants (APP_ERROR, STORAGE_CONFIG, CREDENTIAL_NOT_FOUND, …) the code (or qualified_code) of the error class Cls.DEFAULT_ERROR_CODE, err.error_code Cls.code, err.qualified_code the error_code= keyword of an SDK error constructor raise an AppError subclass whose code names the failure DEFAULT_ERROR_CODE = … on your own subclass of an SDK error delete it, and give the class its own code: ClassVar[str]

docs.text:
Every public SDK module now declares __all__, listing what it defines. A name a module only imported from elsewhere in the SDK is no longer part of that module's surface. Each name below was imported by connector apps from a module that only imported it. It still works and warns, and B001 flags each import. Import it from its home instead.

Every other name a module only imported still imports today, without a warning, but it is no longer surface and can go in any release. If you import one, import it from the module that defines it.

docs.title: retry_policy together with the @task retry scalars (warns now, an error in v4.0.0)
docs.text:
retry_policy replaces retry_max_attempts, retry_initial_interval_seconds and retry_max_interval_seconds. The task is dispatched with the policy as-is and the three scalars are never read, so @task(retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=2), retry_max_attempts=5) ran with 2 attempts and the 5 was dropped without a word. @task now emits a DeprecationWarning and logs a WARNING at decoration when retry_policy is passed together with any of the three, even when the value passed equals the default. From v4.0.0 it raises TaskDeclarationError. Retry behaviour is unchanged: the policy still wins.

Instead of Do this @task(retry_policy=policy, retry_max_attempts=5) @task(retry_policy=policy.with_max_attempts(5)) @task(retry_policy=policy, retry_initial_interval_seconds=5) @task(retry_policy=policy.with_initial_interval(timedelta(seconds=5))) @task(retry_policy=policy, retry_max_interval_seconds=60) RetryPolicy(..., max_interval=timedelta(seconds=60)) @task(retry_policy=RetryPolicy(), retry_max_attempts=1) @task(retry_policy=RetryPolicy()) to keep what runs today, or @task(retry_max_attempts=1) for what the scalar asked for
