The record is kept out of args, str() and repr(), so tracebacks, logs and Temporal failure text name only record_id, entity_type and reason. It is picklable, for mappers run in a process pool.
  • Not an AppError. A skip is a decision, not a failure: it has no category, owner or retry policy, and a generic except AppError must never treat it as one.
  • Uncaught fails visibly, once. A RecordSkipped that escapes the @task is an app bug and deterministic, so the activity boundary fails it as a non-retryable InternalError naming the ids, the reason and the fix, rather than burning the retry budget on the same outcome.

Rejected: a sync skip_record (needs thread-safety work for mappers run through run_in_thread, and a mapper with side effects is no longer pure), and an async helper that calls the mapper and records the skip (hides what the loop catches; the explicit try/except is four lines).

docs.title: Fetch failures: record_fetch_failure (FND-5294)
docs.text:
A failed per-item fetch is a different gap from a skip: the app never received a record, so there is nothing to keep but the id, and the cause is the source, not the data's shape. Filing it under a SkipReason would mislabel fleet-wide aggregates. It gets a sibling helper, record_fetch_failure(reason, *, entity_type, record_id, endpoint=None, http_status=None, detail=None) (application_sdk.outputs.fetch_failures), with its own closed FetchFailureReason (source_unavailable, not_found, forbidden, rate_limited), its own metrics (fetch-failures, fetch-failures-<reason>, -truncated, -unpersisted), its own artifact (fetch-failures) and its own framework task (merge_fetch_failures). The part layout, the merge, the cap, fail-open storage and the derived PARTIAL_SUCCESS are shared with skipped records (RunLogLayout / merge_run_log).

Two choices differ from skip_record, both because a line carries ids only:

  • Sync, not async. Parallel fetches run as gather tasks and as sync functions through run_in_thread; a sync function cannot await. The activity's lines are bounded by MAX_SKIPPED_RECORDS and hold no source data, so they stay in memory under a threading.Lock and are written once when the activity returns — no event-loop write per call is needed.
  • Metrics at activity end. OutputCollector is not thread-safe, so a worker thread never touches it. The sink counts; the output interceptor turns the counts into metrics on the event loop when the activity returns. An activity that raises records nothing, and its retry records its own.

The failure threshold stays with the app: an all-items failure is an outage and must raise, but only the app knows how many items it expected.

docs.title: Relationship to AssetValidationReport
docs.text: They answer different questions about different records. AssetValidationReport (ADR-0020) is the SDK checking assets an app did emit and reporting the ones that look wrong, warn-only; the app did not choose those failures. skip_record is the app declaring a record it chose not to emit, and why. They share the bounding rule and the summed-count-plus-capped-detail shape, not a report type: a skip is a decision, not a finding.

docs.title: Options Considered
docs.text:
• One artifact per activity (skipped-records-<activity_id>) — no merge task, but a fan-out of N activities lists N artifacts and the reviewer stitches them together. Rejected.
  • One artifact pointing at the parts prefix — no merge task, but every consumer of run artifacts would need to accept a prefix where today it reads a file. Rejected.
  • Fail the activity on upload failure — the review file is never silently incomplete, at the cost of re-running the activity body. Rejected in favour of fail-open with an explicit skipped-records-unpersisted count.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Apps get one call and no storage code; a sync mapper raises a RecordSkipped leaf for the loop to record. The migrate-asset-modeling creator-blank-guard default can become "skip via skip_record".
  • Runs that skip anything gain one short framework activity at the end.
  • The object-store layout and metric names are a cross-repo contract (docs/standards/cross-repo-contracts.md).

docs.title: ADR-0023: Consolidated API Host for Hosted Apps' Handlers
Status
docs.text: Accepted — supersedes in part ADR-0001. Records the architecture that shipped in application-sdk PR #4058; the mechanics live in The api distribution.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-0001 chose one handler service per app and rejected a shared "uber-handler" for five reasons: blast radius, coupled deployments, dependency conflicts, every app's credentials in one process, and no per-app scaling.

Since then the cost side of that trade-off grew. Every hosted app runs a handler service of its own, mostly idle, to answer a handful of short requests (auth, check, metadata, config, manifest) for the UI and Heracles. Each one carries the full worker SDK (Temporal, Dapr, the object store) though a handler uses none of it.

The consolidated API host serves those requests for many apps from one process. It installs atlan-application-sdk-api, the listed handler-side subset of application_sdk, plus one small generated package per app. That reverses ADR-0001 for the apps it serves, so the decision and its mitigations are recorded here.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Hosted apps' handler routes are served by one consolidated API host. ADR-0001 still holds for everything outside that scope.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• In: apps running on Atlan's hosted platform that opt in. An app opts in with a [tool.atlan-app-api] block in its pyproject.toml (see the api-server-consolidation-migration skill); once its routeToCommonAPIServer flag is set, every Heracles handler call for it lands on the host.
  • Out:
    • Apps that have not opted in. They keep their own handler service, as ADR-0001 describes.
    • Workers. Per-app workers (ADR-0002) and separate handler and worker deployments (ADR-0009) are unchanged. The worker still registers the same route modules, so an app answers alike on either surface.
    • Self-Deployed Runtime. Nothing in an SDR runtime on customer infrastructure moves onto the host. The one cross-over is the task queue the host stamps into a served manifest; Heracles re-stamps agent-side nodes with the SDR queue (see Cross-repo contracts).
  • Code ownership is still per app. Each app writes its own Handler subclass in its own repo, released on its own version. Only the process that serves it is shared.

docs.title: How ADR-0001's objections are answered
docs.text: ADR-0001 objection Position on the host Security: all credentials in one process Accepted as a trade-off, bounded by a rule: only trusted first-party apps are hosted. There is no secret isolation between hosted apps: every app's environment shares one os.environ. The host does not authenticate callers; a NetworkPolicy (owned by App Runtime) limits who can reach the pod to Heracles and the ingress. The SDK's own routes pass response-body text through redact_secrets, so a credential in exception text is not echoed back; an app's own routers (Handler.routers()) are mounted as written and get no such pass (see below). Config keys use the mounted app's name, never request input. Blast radius: one app's bug affects all Reduced, not removed. Each app gets its own run_in_thread / submit_in_thread pool (api-<app>-), so one app's hung blocking calls cannot take another app's thread slots (ADR-0010, FND-2973 addendum). Uploads land only under the app's own persistent-artifacts/apps/<app>/uploads/. The event loop, FastAPI's thread pool and the host's request concurrency limit stay shared: an app that blocks the event loop or leaks memory still affects every hosted app. Dependency conflicts One resolved environment, checked before it ships. All hosted apps share one atlan-application-sdk-api version and one version of every third-party package. Each app declares only its handler's own dependencies and api extras. The host pins each app by release tag plus commit SHA. Its lock fails in CI when the apps cannot be resolved together, and every staged app is probed in the locked environment before a pin moves. An app whose dependencies conflict cannot move to the new pin until the conflict is fixed. Coupled deployments Accepted. An app's handler change reaches the host only through a host pin bump (Renovate opens the PR), which rebuilds and redeploys the one host that serves every app. The SDK's release workflow does not push to the host. No per-app scaling Accepted. The host scales as one unit. Handler traffic is short, synchronous and low-volume, so per-app scaling bought little.

docs.title: Rules that keep hosted handlers safe to co-locate
docs.text:
• Handler code imports only the api distribution's listed modules; check_api_surface.py and gen_app_api.py check enforce this in CI.
  • Handler code does not log. It reports through its return value or a typed AppError; the shared routes log each outcome with the request id (conformance P060).
  • A handler reads its app's name from self.context.app_name, never from APPLICATION_NAME / ATLAN_APPLICATION_NAME. On the host those name the host itself.
  • An app's own routers (Handler.routers()) are served on the host too, mounted with include_router after the SDK's routes. The SDK does not redact their responses, so an app route sanitizes its own output: it never returns exception text, a DSN or a credential verbatim, and answers a failure with a fixed message.

docs.title: Option 1: Keep one handler service per app (ADR-0001)
docs.text: Rejected for hosted apps. It keeps the strongest isolation. The cost is an idle service per app carrying the full worker SDK.

docs.title: Option 2: Consolidated host with per-app packages (Chosen)
docs.text: One process, many apps, each mounted from its own generated package. The cost is the shared trust boundary and shared capacity described above. In exchange: one image and one environment for every opted-in app, with no worker runtime in it (the api-only core install is measured at 62 MB).

docs.title: Option 3: Consolidated host with per-app subprocesses
docs.text: Not chosen. Running each app's handler in its own process would restore secret and memory isolation. It would also bring back most of the per-app baseline cost the host exists to remove. It stays open if an untrusted or third-party app ever needs hosting; the trusted-first-party rule exists until then.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive: - One handler process and image for every opted-in app, not one per app. - Handler code is smaller and checked: no worker runtime, no logging, an import surface enforced in CI.

Negative: - Every hosted app can read every other hosted app's environment. Hosting a third-party or untrusted app requires a new decision. - A handler that blocks the event loop, leaks memory or crashes the process affects every hosted app. - All hosted apps move together on one dependency set. One app's dependency conflict blocks it from moving to a new host pin. - An app has two possible handler surfaces (host or its own service), and the routes must answer alike on both.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• The api distribution: build, routes, trust model, versions and release.
  • ADR-0001: the decision this supersedes in part.
  • ADR-0010: per-app thread pools on the host.
  • .claude/skills/api-server-consolidation-migration/SKILL.md: onboarding an app.

docs.title: Canonical apps
docs.text:
Three public repos are the reference implementations for apps built on this SDK. When you need to know how something should look in a consumer app — test layout, contract shape, entrypoint wiring, credential handling — read one of these rather than generalising from an arbitrary atlan-*-app. They are also the only apps a conformance rule's canonical_reference may name (alongside this SDK, for rules whose fix is an SDK seam). Every auto-fixable app-facing rule cites a file in one of them, except the few with no such site anywhere in the three — each listed with its reason in _SDK_ONLY_REFERENCE_EXEMPT in packages/conformance/tests/test_catalog.py.

Those references are checked nightly against the three apps' main by .github/workflows/canonical-reference-check.yaml (python -m conformance.tools.verify_canonical_references): every cited path, path:N line span and backticked symbol must still exist, and anything a reference names as absent (listed in NAMED_ABSENT) must still be absent. When a refactor here turns it red, re-point the citing rule's canonical_reference in packages/conformance/conformance/suite/rules/ and run gen-rule-docs.

Repo Why it's the reference atlan-openapi-app Non-SQL, public source — no credential config (hasCredentialConfig = false). Shows the shape when there is nothing to authenticate against. atlan-mysql-app SQL connector, real credentials. The fullest test suite: handler auth/preflight against a real MySQL including negative cases, credential resolution against fake secret stores, and a full-DAG e2e. atlan-metabase-app BI connector, real credentials, multi-entrypoint. Shows the non-SQL path on BaseE2ETest.

docs.title: Why this list matters
docs.text:
Most atlan-*-app repos are not safe to copy from. At any time some are mid-migration, some carry patterns the SDK has since deprecated, and some solved a problem locally that the SDK now solves centrally. A survey across arbitrary connector repos will therefore reproduce whatever the fleet's median staleness is — it cannot tell you what is correct.

Two authorities settle "what is correct": this repo's own tests, and the three apps above. Nothing else is evidence.

docs.title: What they establish about test layout
docs.text:
atlan-openapi-app, atlan-mysql-app and atlan-metabase-app each have exactly three test directories — unit/, integration/, e2e/.

None of the three has a tests/sdr/ or a tests/full_dag/, and none uses Scenario or BaseIntegrationTest. Concerns are placed like this:

Concern Where Example Handler functionality — auth, preflight called directly, negative cases included mysql tests/integration/test_mysql_handler.py (real MySQL); metabase tests/unit/test_handler.py (mocked client) Credential resolution proven once in this repo (tests/unit/credentials/); per-app, against fake secret stores mysql tests/integration/test_credential_resolution.py A full DAG, in either run mode tests/e2e/ via the generated app/generated/_e2e_base.py mysql tests/e2e/test_mysql_e2e.py

Tier 4 vs tier 5 is the mode ClassVar (RunMode.AGENT / RunMode.DIRECT) on one base class — not a different base class and not a separate test directory. See docs/standards/connector-ci-e2e.md.

docs.title: Coding Standards
docs.text:
• Primary coding standards live in docs/standards/coding.md (formatting, naming, docstrings for all functions/classes/modules).
  • Logging, exception, and performance guidance are in docs/standards/logging.md, docs/standards/exceptions.md, and docs/standards/performance.md.
  • Metric / Prometheus label cardinality rules are in docs/standards/metrics.md — read before adding a record_metric() call or a new OTel instrument.
  • Tooling enforcement is defined in .pre-commit-config.yaml (ruff for lint, format and import sorting; pyright).

docs.title: Key Rules Enforced by Pre-commit
docs.text:
1. No bare except: - Always use except Exception: or a specific exception type
  2. No useless f-strings - Don't use f"string" if there are no {placeholders}
  3. No Unicode in print statements - Windows CI fails on emojis (✓, ❌, ⚠️). Use ASCII: PASS, FAIL, WARNING
  4. Import sorting - Imports must be sorted (ruff I rules; uv run ruff check --fix sorts them)
  5. Type hints - Pyright enforces type checking. reportArgumentType, reportAttributeAccessIssue and reportFunctionMemberAccess are errors; findings that predate that are in pyright_baseline.json, which may only shrink
  6. Suppress with # pyright: ignore[<rule>], never # type: ignore - # type: ignore is switched off (enableTypeIgnoreComments = false), and a # pyright: ignore that no longer suppresses anything is an error (reportUnnecessaryTypeIgnoreComment)
  7. Conventional commits - Commit messages must follow conventional format (e.g., fix:, feat:, chore:)
  8. No customer names - Never reference customer names, tenant names, run IDs, or any customer-identifiable information in code, comments, docstrings, commit messages, or PR descriptions. Use generic language: "a production incident", "a prior RCA".

docs.title: Log Levels: WARNING Handled, ERROR Failed
docs.text: The customer-facing log view filters at ERROR, so an ERROR record reads as a failed run. Use ERROR only when the operation failed: the handler raises, exits, or returns a failure result. A failure the code caught and recovered from (a fallback, a best-effort close, a skipped item) is a WARNING with exc_info=True. Conformance L022 reports logger.error() in an except that does none of those. The full level table is in docs/standards/logging.md.

docs.title: Serialization & Type Systems
docs.text:
Use the right type system for each zone:

Zone Type System When to Use Example Temporal contracts pydantic.BaseModel Anything serialized through Temporal wire (workflow/activity I/O) Input, Output, FileReference, CredentialRef High-volume / low-level msgspec.Struct or plain dicts Performance-critical paths: pyatlan_v9 asset types, logging internals pyatlan_v9 types, log record construction

Rules: - All contracts (Input, Output, HeartbeatDetails, Record, FileReference, CredentialRef, credential types) MUST be frozen pydantic.BaseModel subclasses (typically via helpers in contracts/base.py or contracts/types.py; CredentialRef and credential types live in application_sdk.credentials). They are serialised through Temporal via pydantic_data_converter. - Define contracts as plain class bodies — no @dataclass decorator. Pydantic handles __init__, validation, and serialization automatically. - For frozen (immutable) contracts (e.g., FileReference, CredentialRef): use class Foo(BaseModel, frozen=True) or model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True). - Use Field(default_factory=...) for mutable defaults (lists, dicts, nested models). Do not use __post_init__ — that is a dataclass pattern. - Avoid Pydantic on high-volume paths (e.g., every log line). Use plain dicts instead — Pydantic validation overhead accumulates significantly. - Always use Pydantic v2 model_config = ConfigDict(...) style. Do not use the v1 inner class Config: pattern.

docs.title: Temporal Determinism (CRITICAL)
docs.text:
Code in run() and @entrypoint methods MUST be deterministic. Temporal replays workflows from history on worker restart — non-deterministic code corrupts the replay.

DO DON'T self.now() datetime.now(), datetime.utcnow() self.uuid() uuid.uuid4(), uuid.uuid1() await self.my_task(input) await http_client.get(url) Framework-provided random random.random(), random.choice()

All I/O, network calls, and non-deterministic operations go in @task methods.

docs.title: Preflight Gate (HYP-1883)
docs.text: Every extraction workflow runs a {app}:preflight Temporal activity as its first step. The activity resolves credentials, calls handler.preflight_check(PreflightInput), and aborts before extraction when the returned PreflightOutput.status is NOT_READY (READY proceeds; PARTIAL is deprecated and proceeds exactly like READY).

docs.title: What the gate does
docs.text:
• The workflow builds a PreflightGateInput — a secret-free envelope containing credential references and a raw model_dump() snapshot of the extraction input.
  • The activity resolves credentials, converts the snapshot into PreflightInput metadata, and calls the handler.
  • Field reads from the extraction input therefore happen inside the activity (not in the deterministic workflow context), which is required for Temporal replay safety.

docs.title: PreflightInput.metadata / connection_config on the gate path
docs.text:
The gate derives metadata and connection_config from extraction_snapshot via _config_from_snapshot() (runs in the activity frame). That helper:

  • Excludes credential-routing fields (extraction_method, credential_guid, etc.).
  • Produces both the original field name and its hyphenated variant so handlers that use either naming convention work on the gate path (e.g. include_filter and include-filter).
  • Drops credential-routing fields and genuinely empty values (None, empty string, empty container), but preserves False and 0 — a handler reading a bool/int config field off the gate sees the real value, not a silent default.

If no snapshot is present (gate inputs built without a model_dump-capable extraction input, e.g. manually constructed in tests), the activity falls back to input.metadata.

docs.title: Adopting the gate — two clauses
docs.text:
(i) The input must be gate-eligible. The gate only fires when the entrypoint's input is CredentialResolvable — it declares extraction_method, credential_guid, and agent_json as top-level fields. Declare them as real fields, not Pydantic extras or nested config: extras are not a portable way to satisfy the protocol (the isinstance check ignores them on Python 3.12+). A toolkit-generated AppInputContract(ExtractionInput) satisfies this automatically — ExtractionInput declares the fields and its _normalize_ae_payload lifts them out of the nested AE metadata. A hand-written input that omits them (or keeps them nested) is silently skipped — so the SDK warns at worker startup for any registered entrypoint whose input is not gate-eligible. The fix is to put the input on ExtractionInput (via the toolkit) rather than hand-rolling the lift.

(ii) Express the verdict by returning NOT_READY, not by raising. The handler reports readiness by returning PreflightOutput(status=NOT_READY, ...). Attach a typed error to each failed check — PreflightCheck(passed=False, error=AuthError(message=..., suggested_action=..., cause=exc)) — and the gate carries the primary failure's FailureDetails on the abort. Catch probe exceptions and turn them into checks; the returned status is what both surfaces render.

Raising is not a no-op, though, and the error's type decides what happens — see below.

docs.title: Fail-open semantics
docs.text:
Enforcement is scoped by who raised, not by the error's category and not by whether a verdict was reached.

  • Source-attributable (gate_classification="source_unverifiable") — a NOT_READY verdict, anything the handler raises (typed or not), a probe overrunning App.preflight_gate_timeout_seconds, a killed attempt whose earlier attempt left typed evidence, or a provably absent credential. Subject to preflight_gate_mode: soft reports would_block and proceeds; hard aborts the run only when the attributed failure's category is AUTH, PERMISSION, INVALID_INPUT, PRECONDITION, NOT_FOUND or (on the final attempt only) SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE or RATE_LIMITED, and otherwise reports would_block and proceeds — it never blocks on TIMEOUT or the deprecated fail-open categories. A verdict is reached on the attempt it happens on, except that a hard gate retries SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE and RATE_LIMITED until its final attempt.
  • Frame lost (gate_classification="frame_lost") — Temporal ended a running attempt and nothing survived: a probe that stalled the loop past the gate's cancel, or a worker that died under it. The chain cannot tell them apart, so this is its own value. Its evidence is a TIMEOUT, so hard mode reports it rather than blocking.
  • Gate plumbing (gate_classification="gate_broken") — the gate's own credential resolution failing (secret-store outage, a collapsed not-found wrapping a transport error), or no worker ever running the attempt. Always fails open, in both postures: a platform blip must never fail a healthy run.
  • Deprecated fail-open (gate_classification="deprecated_fail_open") — a typed leaf in DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED or CANCELLED raised from preflight_check. The pre-3.35 gate treated these as plumbing, and every hard-mode app that predates the origin rule raises them on purpose, so they keep failing open in both postures until 3.40.0 with a DeprecationWarning naming the app and the leaf. From 3.40.0 they are source-attributable like any other raise, and still never block a hard gate.

So a handler signals "ask me later" by returning READY with the failed check carrying a typed retryable error as an advisory row, never by raising one and never by returning NOT_READY: raising discards the other checks, and an untyped NOT_READY is attributed to PRECONDITION, which blocks a hard gate on a transient.

Every gated run emits a structured Preflight gate outcome event (outcome ∈ {proceeded, blocked, would_block, no_verdict, skipped}), plus a Preflight gate posture event per app at worker boot. An app that declares a warmup also stamps gate_tier and warmup_outcome on its rows (plus warmup_duration_ms / warmup_transitions once the wait has ended); every new row key must be added to _KNOWN_EXTRA_KEYS, or it is dropped before export and cannot be queried. tests/unit/observability/test_log_extra_allowlist.py scans every literal log field in application_sdk (keyword fields, literal extra={...} keys and _safe_log fields) and fails on one that is not allowlisted or prefixed.

docs.title: Logging contract
docs.text:
One record per gate event: the outcome row itself carries the level (FND-901 — the customer-facing log view filters at ERROR, so a block must be the ERROR record, not a WARN beside one). Each row stamps failure.audience (who must act) except proceeded/skipped.

  • Verdict blocks (PreflightFailed from a handler NOT_READY) — the outcome row at error, no stack trace, audience from the primary check's typed error (typically USER), plus failure.check / failure.message naming the check and why it failed. The block is an expected typed outcome, not a crash — but it aborted the customer's run.
  • No-verdict outcomes (budget overrun, handler crash — source_unverifiable; a killed frame — frame_lost) — the outcome row at error with exc_info, in both modes: the failure is real even when soft mode proceeds. There is a real exception behind these and it is the only diagnostic.
  • Gate plumbing failures (exception during dispatch — gate_broken) — the workflow's no_verdict row at error with exc_info=True, audience APP_OWNER, and failure.message from the envelope the plumbing error left at details[0] when it is readable.
  • Advisory failures (proceeded with any failed check — PARTIAL, or READY with a failed advisory row) — the outcome row at warning. F005 bans the handler from logging the warning itself, so the gate owns the one level that case is semantically for.
  • Clean proceeded / skipped / verdict would_block — info.
  • The interceptor's workflow.ended / activity.ended … BLOCKED (preflight gate) lifecycle records stay warning with no stack or frame, but carry the block's attributed sentence — the same details[0].message the outcome row's failure.message holds — so the reason is findable by a Body search and the two surfaces cannot disagree. A soft-mode would_block raises no block, so it has no such record and is reachable through failure.message only.
  • Interactive surfaces (the HTTP /workflows/v1/check endpoint and the SDR sdr:preflight_check activity) emit the sibling Preflight check outcome row via emit_preflight_check_outcome, with preflight_surface naming the surface. The level follows whether the log is the delivery channel: HTTP rows stay info (the verdict IS the response body rendered in the setup form); SDR failures surface through a workflow run log read at the default ERROR filter, so SDR rows mirror the gate — not_ready at error, advisory failure at warning, clean at info. Handler crashes stay error at each surface's boundary handler and additionally emit one outcome="crashed" row at error on every interactive surface (emit_preflight_crash_outcome), so the funnel sees the worst case; a typed client-input error that raises (wrong password, 4xx-class category) is counted as outcome="client_fault" instead — at info on HTTP where the response is the channel, at error on SDR where the row is — so it never pollutes the crash series and never drops from the denominator. The surface is the PreflightSurface enum, not a string, and its level policy is the _LOG_ROW_IS_ONLY_CHANNEL table — a new surface fails test_every_surface_has_a_level_policy until someone routes it.

docs.title: Contract Evolution
docs.text:
• NEVER remove or rename fields on Input/Output classes
  • NEVER change field types
  • Add new fields with defaults only (field: str = "")
  • Use Field(default_factory=list) for mutable defaults, never field: list = []

Breaking a contract silently corrupts in-flight Temporal workflows.

docs.title: Blocking Operations
docs.text:
Use an async-native library first (httpx not requests, asyncpg not psycopg2, aioboto3 not boto3), then an SDK async helper (self.context.storage, self.context.state). self.run_in_thread() is the last resort, for a blocking call with no async alternative. Never call blocking code directly on the loop:

# Wrong — blocks event loop, kills heartbeats
result = requests.get(url)

# Right — async-native
async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30) as client:
    result = await client.get(url)

# Last resort — no async driver exists; the call has its own timeout
rows = await self.run_in_thread(legacy_client.fetch, query, timeout=30)

Python cannot stop a thread from outside. When the task is cancelled, the awaiting coroutine returns but the thread runs on, holding its memory, connection and pool slot, while the worker starts its next activity. So:

  • Give the blocking call its own driver-level timeout (see below).
  • If the driver can cancel the call from another thread, register its cancel on current_cancel_handle() from inside the thread (or bind a CancelHandle), so a cancel stops the call itself. See Tasks → Cancelling a blocking call at the driver.
  • In blocking work that loops (batches, pages), check self.is_cancelled() between steps and return when it is True, or call raise_if_cancelled(). Code with no self imports both from application_sdk.execution.heartbeat.

Give the blocking call its own driver-level timeout (connect, socket, statement). An asyncio.wait_for / asyncio.timeout around run_in_thread cancels the call the same way a Temporal cancel does: it fires any registered driver cancel and makes is_cancelled() true inside the thread. A thread that neither registered a cancel nor checks keeps its pool slot until the driver returns, and is reported as stranded (a WARNING plus the offload.stranded_threads gauge, per app).

When ATLAN_OFFLOAD_MAX_THREADS_PER_APP is set, an app with that many calls in flight gets a retryable ResourceExhaustedError instead of queueing. See ADR-0010 → Addendum: containing stranded threads per app.

docs.title: Writing Files
docs.text:
Never write an artifact directly to its final name. Use application_sdk.common.atomic:

from application_sdk.common.atomic import atomic_write

# Wrong — a write that dies part-way leaves a truncated file at the real name.
# Nothing downstream can tell it from a correct one, so it gets carried forward
# and uploaded, and the failure surfaces in a consuming app's parser instead.
Path(out).write_text(payload)

# Right — the final path either does not exist or holds a complete file.
with atomic_write(out, operation="entity export") as handle:
    handle.write(payload.encode())

operation is a short phrase naming the step; it goes into the failure message and its evidence. Two companions:

  • atomic_path(path, operation=...) for writers that take a filename rather than a handle (pq.write_table, shutil.copy2), and atomic_copy(src, dst) for copies.
  • disk_full_guard(path, operation=...) for a write that genuinely cannot be atomic — an append across calls. It types the failure without the atomicity.

A full disk raises DiskFullError naming the path and the shortfall, which is the signal an operator reads to raise a deployment's ephemeral storage. Pass required_bytes= when the size is known up front and the check happens before the first byte moves. See docs/concepts/storage.md → Atomic artifact writes.

Every SDK writer already goes through this, so a Writer, FileReference, or the incremental helpers need nothing from you. This rule is for code that opens a file itself.

docs.title: Long-Running Tasks: Progress and Stalls
docs.text:
A task that goes quiet for longer than max_no_progress_seconds (900s) is reported as a stall — and failed, in an app that enforces. The SDK covers its own write, transfer and page loops, and auto-holds every run_in_thread offload; what it cannot see is a custom async loop or an opaque single await against the connector's own source client. Those need one line: self.heartbeat(...) in the loop, or async with self.holding_progress(label, timeout=...) around the opaque call.

timeout is how long you would let this one call run before you would rather it failed — not a prediction of its duration. Err generous; too tight false-kills a healthy run, and stall kills retry.

Read Progress and Stalls before writing a long-running task, and ADR-0018 if you need the design rationale.

docs.title: Large Payloads and FileReference
docs.text: Use FileReference for any data that cannot fit in Temporal's 2 MB payload limit. See docs/concepts/file-reference.md for the full guide: decision matrix, lifecycle, the Lazy() marker for selective materialization, dedup behaviour, and observability events.

docs.title: App-to-app hand-off (required for SDR deployments)
docs.text:
FileReference auto-durability writes to the customer-owned objectstore (infra.storage) — it is designed for task-to-task data passing within a single run.

Silent-failure rule: if a connector returns a FileReference from a @task but never calls App.upload() from run(), the DAG completes successfully but the publish app finds nothing in Atlan's bucket. This produces no error — the failure is invisible in the Temporal UI.

To hand off artifacts to Atlan system apps (publish, lineage, quality), call App.upload() explicitly from run() — it routes to the Atlan-owned atlan-objectstore (infra.upstream_storage) in SDR deployments:

from application_sdk.contracts import UploadInput

async def run(self, input: MyInput) -> MyOutput:
    fetch_out = await self.fetch_data(input)
    # Required: push artifact to Atlan's upstream store
    await self.upload(UploadInput(local_path=fetch_out.output_path))  # RETAINED is the default tier
    return fetch_out

Anti-pattern: calling App.upload() for task-to-task data. App.upload() routes to atlan-objectstore in SDR — using it for intermediate pipeline data (instead of FileReference) has three harms: pollutes Atlan's bucket with internal artifacts; bypasses SHA-256 dedup (every call is a full re-upload, even for identical files); and does not wire into cross-worker auto-materialization. Declare FileReference on task Input/Output contracts instead — the interceptor handles persistence and re-download automatically.

See file-reference.md § App-to-app hand-off and ADR-0014 for the full rationale.

docs.title: Replacing ParquetFileWriter / JsonFileWriter (v4.0 removal path)
docs.text: ParquetFileWriter, JsonFileWriter, ParquetFileReader, and JsonFileReader emit DeprecationWarning on construction and will be removed in v4.0. Migrate now — the replacement is fully supported and fully optimised (SHA-256 dedup + sidecars + parallel transfers via _run_bounded).

docs.title: Recommended: RollingFileWriter
docs.text:
application_sdk/storage/rolling.py provides a small format-agnostic helper that encapsulates the common pattern:

  • Owns a scoped output sub-directory (so the resulting FileReference covers only your chunks — never sibling content in base_path).
  • Buffers appended batches and rolls over to a new chunk file when any of the configured policies fire:
  • chunk_interval_seconds — wall clock (default 30s)
  • max_buffer_bytes — buffer ceiling in bytes (default 50 MB)
  • max_buffer_records — buffer ceiling in records (default None, opt-in)
  • Optional on_chunk_complete(chunk_index, chunk_path) callback for per-chunk checkpointing. Heartbeat with the SDK's self.heartbeat(...). A plain-function callback runs in the SDK's blocking pool, like flush_fn, so it never stalls the event loop. self.heartbeat works from there.
  • writer.file_reference returns an ephemeral FileReference for your typed Output; the activity interceptor uploads on task return.

Why the default policy bundle: the SDK runs in two extreme streaming regimes — slow JDBC streams (~200 rows/min) and fast msgspec transforms (~10 000 records/ms). A pure record-count threshold like chunk_size=10_000 either never trips (slow stream → one huge final file, blocks heartbeat) or trips every millisecond (fast stream → thousands of tiny files). A pure wall-clock interval handles the slow case but leaves no ceiling on memory when the stream is fast. The default bundle (time + bytes, plus opt-in records) gives:

  • Predictable checkpoint cadence regardless of upstream throughput.
  • Bounded peak memory: a runaway fast upstream hits the 50 MB ceiling long before it can OOM a typical pod.
  • An optional records-based escape hatch for callers who think in rows.

For advanced cases (e.g. fixed-size exports where only size matters), pass a custom rollover_policy= — see :class:TimePolicy, :class:SizePolicy, :class:CountPolicy, and :class:AnyOfPolicy exposed from application_sdk.storage.rolling.

docs.title: Parquet (pandas)
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

from application_sdk.contracts.types import FileReference
from application_sdk.storage.rolling import RollingFileWriter


def _flush_parquet(batches: list[pd.DataFrame], path: str) -> None:
    pd.concat(batches, ignore_index=True).to_parquet(path)


async def extract_users(self, inp: ExtractInput) -> ExtractOutput:
    async with RollingFileWriter[pd.DataFrame](
        base_path=inp.output_path,
        extension=".parquet",
        flush_fn=_flush_parquet,
        chunk_interval_seconds=60.0,
        # optional: per-chunk checkpoint, resumable via get_last_heartbeat_details()
        on_chunk_complete=lambda idx, path: self.heartbeat(f"wrote {path}"),
    ) as writer:
        async for df in self._stream_users():
            await writer.append(df)
    return ExtractOutput(data=writer.file_reference)

docs.title: JSON (line-delimited, orjson)
docs.text:
import orjson

from application_sdk.contracts.types import FileReference
from application_sdk.storage.rolling import RollingFileWriter


def _flush_jsonl(batches: list[list[dict]], path: str) -> None:
    with open(path, "wb") as f:
        for batch in batches:
            for record in batch:
                f.write(orjson.dumps(record))
                f.write(b"\n")


async def extract_events(self, inp: ExtractInput) -> ExtractOutput:
    async with RollingFileWriter[list[dict]](
        base_path=inp.output_path,
        extension=".json",
        flush_fn=_flush_jsonl,
        chunk_interval_seconds=60.0,
    ) as writer:
        async for records in self._stream_events():
            await writer.append(records)
    return ExtractOutput(data=writer.file_reference)

To support a new format, write a 3-line flush_fn and plug it in. CSV via pandas.to_csv, Arrow IPC via pyarrow.ipc, msgpack via msgpack.pack — all the same shape.

docs.title: Throughput vs the deprecated writers
docs.text:
Each run writes 200k rows (20 batches of 10k, 4 columns), with uploads excluded on both sides. RollingFileWriter uses the two examples above: DataFrame batches for Parquet, list[dict] + orjson for JSON.

Writer Parquet JSON ParquetFileWriter / JsonFileWriter, as shipped (per-slice gc.collect()) 0.77 s 0.80 s same, gc.collect() removed 0.11 s 0.19 s RollingFileWriter 0.07 s 0.07 s

Measured on arm64 macOS, Python 3.12, with the worker's imports loaded. The gc.collect() cost grows with the heap. With a production-sized heap the deprecated writers took 11.7 s (Parquet) and 15.5 s (JSON); without the GC they took 1.1 s and 1.4 s.

tests/unit/storage/test_rolling_throughput.py re-runs this comparison once per CI run, in the Unit Perf Tests job (it is marked perf). It fails if RollingFileWriter is slower than the deprecated writer it replaces.

docs.title: Alternative: bare copy-paste (no helper class)
docs.text:
If you want zero new dependencies, the loop the helper wraps is small enough to inline directly.

Parquet:

import os
import uuid
import pandas as pd
from application_sdk.contracts.types import FileReference


async def extract_users(self, inp: ExtractInput) -> ExtractOutput:
    output_dir = os.path.join(inp.output_path, f"users_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}")
    os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)
    chunk_index = 0
    async for df in self._stream_users():
        df.to_parquet(os.path.join(output_dir, f"chunk-{chunk_index}.parquet"))
        chunk_index += 1
    return ExtractOutput(data=FileReference.from_local(output_dir))

JSON (line-delimited):

import os
import uuid
import orjson
from application_sdk.contracts.types import FileReference


async def extract_events(self, inp: ExtractInput) -> ExtractOutput:
    output_dir = os.path.join(inp.output_path, f"events_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}")
    os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)
    chunk_index = 0
    async for records in self._stream_events():
        with open(os.path.join(output_dir, f"chunk-{chunk_index}.json"), "wb") as f:
            for record in records:
                f.write(orjson.dumps(record))
                f.write(b"\n")
        chunk_index += 1
    return ExtractOutput(data=FileReference.from_local(output_dir))

The bare pattern has no rollover or heartbeat awareness — each iteration of your stream loop produces one chunk file. Prefer RollingFileWriter when you want predictable checkpoint cadence on long-running activities.

docs.title: Reading a FileReference (replaces ParquetFileReader / JsonFileReader)
docs.text:
Declare the upstream artifact as a FileReference field on the consuming task's typed Input. The activity interceptor auto-materialises it to a local path before the task runs (with sidecar verification + parallel transfers). Read it directly with the library of your choice:

class TransformInput(Input):
    data: FileReference                              # auto-materialised

async def transform_users(self, inp: TransformInput) -> TransformOutput:
    df = pd.read_parquet(inp.data.local_path)
    ...

For JSON inputs, swap pd.read_parquet for an orjson.loads loop over the file lines. JsonFileReader coerced values through pandas: an int column with a missing key came back as float (3 → 3.0), the missing key as NaN. The orjson loop returns the values in the file, so fix the callers that relied on the coercion rather than rebuilding a DataFrame:

  • row[key] on an optional key raises KeyError — use row.get(key).
  • pd.isna / math.isnan checks for absence — use is None or key not in row.
  • A value formatted into a published key or qualified name changes ("3.0" → "3") — record it as an owner decision, don't paper over it.

No ParquetFileReader / JsonFileReader construction required — they exist only to bridge the legacy inline-upload contract and will be deleted in v4.0.

docs.title: Transitional opt-in on the legacy ParquetFileWriter
docs.text:
If you cannot migrate to the direct pattern immediately but want the SHA-256 + parallel-transfer benefits today, ParquetFileWriter accepts a defer_uploads=True flag. Default (False) preserves the pre-3.8 inline- upload behaviour so existing call sites are unaffected; True switches to the FileReference boundary. close() always returns a WriterResult that subclasses TaskStatistics (so result.total_record_count etc. continue to work via inheritance) and gains a result.files: FileReference | None field — None in default mode (no double-upload risk), ephemeral in opt-in mode.

async with ParquetFileWriter(
    path=base, typename="users", defer_uploads=True,
) as writer:
    await writer.write(df)
result = writer.last_result
return MyOutput(statistics=result, data=result.files)

The opt-in flag is a bridge for in-flight migrations only. New code should go straight to the direct copy-paste pattern above.

A writer's own files appear only after close(). Both legacy writers stage their chunks in a private directory (a hidden .sdk-writer-staging/ sibling of the output path) and move them into the output directory in one step at close(). Chunk filenames, object-store keys, and the statistics/ layout are exactly what they always were — only the moment the files land changes. Do not read a writer's output directory before its close() returns. Publishing only adds: anything already in a reused output directory stays there, and a deferred writer's FileReference covers it too.

The reason is cancellation. A cancelled activity leaves an orphaned worker thread that cannot be killed and is still writing to a path it resolved before the cancel; the chunk name it holds (chunk-<n>-part<m>) is identical to the one the retry will resolve. Staging means only a writer that reaches close() ever touches the output directory, so a retry can neither have its file overwritten by that orphan nor sweep the orphan's other files into its own FileReference (FND-315, FND-317).

docs.title: Before Every Commit
docs.text:
uv run pre-commit run --files <changed-files>

Or install hooks to run automatically: 

uv run pre-commit install

docs.title: Commits and PRs
docs.text:
• Commit message format is defined in docs/standards/commits.md (Conventional Commits).
  • PR size and review expectations live in CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Before Committing
docs.text:
Always run pre-commit checks before committing:

uv run pre-commit run --files <changed-files>

CI will fail if pre-commit checks fail. Common failures: - Linting errors (ruff) - Formatting issues (ruff-format) - Import order (ruff I) - Type errors (pyright)

docs.title: Commit Message Format
docs.text:
Conventional Commits, type(scope): description. The allowed types and scopes are listed once, in docs/standards/commits.md; read them there rather than from a copy.

Example: fix(io): align parquet writer row-group size with reader batch size

docs.title: DeepWiki MCP
docs.text: Use DeepWiki MCP to verify SDK implementation details before answering questions about atlanhq/application-sdk or atlanhq/atlan-python, even if local code is available.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• API usage, method signatures, parameters, and return types
  • Error debugging and implementation patterns
  • Usage examples from the repo

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
For most clients (e.g., Windsurf, Cursor), add this MCP server: 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "deepwiki": {
      "serverUrl": "https://mcp.deepwiki.com/sse"
    }
  }
}

For Claude Code: 

claude mcp add -s user -t http deepwiki https://mcp.deepwiki.com/mcp

docs.title: Usage Flow
docs.text:
1. ask_question for specific implementation questions.
  2. read_wiki_structure to see available docs.
  3. read_wiki_contents for deep dives.

If DeepWiki MCP is not available, recommend the setup above and proceed with the best local sources.

docs.title: Development Commands
docs.text:
• Setup and local run workflow: docs/guides/getting-started.md (uv sync, poe tasks, example run).
  • Task runner and common scripts live in pyproject.toml under [tool.poe.tasks].
  • Docs build configuration is in mkdocs.yml (install with uv sync --all-extras --all-groups, then uv run poe generate-apidocs). Check a docs change with uv run --group docs mkdocs build --strict: the SDK Gate's Docs area runs exactly that and fails on a page missing from nav, a broken link or anchor, or a relative link out of docs/.
  • Capability manifest: uv run poe regen-capabilities — refreshes docs/agents/sdk-capabilities.md from application_sdk/ HEAD. CI surfaces drift on every PR; comment /regen-manifest on a PR to have a bot regenerate and push. To check freshness: uv run poe regen-capabilities && git diff --exit-code -- docs/agents/sdk-capabilities.md.

docs.title: Pre-commit Checks
docs.text:
Always run pre-commit before committing code. CI will fail if pre-commit checks fail.

# Run on specific file(s)
uv run pre-commit run --files path/to/file.py

# Run on all files
uv run pre-commit run --all-files

# Install pre-commit hooks (runs automatically on git commit)
uv run pre-commit install

docs.title: What pre-commit checks:
docs.text:
• ruff: Linting (E722 bare except, F541 useless f-strings, etc.) and import sorting (I rules; the hook runs with --fix)
  • ruff-format: Code formatting (line length, spacing, etc.)

The dev group pins ruff to the hook's exact version, so uv run ruff check --fix and uv run ruff format give the same result as CI. - pyright: Type checking, held to pyright_baseline.json (errors only; see "pyright on the SDK tree" in docs/standards/ci.md). It fails on a new error per file and rule, and on a fixed one until you run uv run --frozen --all-extras --all-groups python .github/scripts/check_pyright_baseline.py --scope sdk --update and commit the lower baseline. - conventional-pre-commit: Commit message format (on commit-msg stage) - pre-commit-hooks: Merge conflicts, debug statements, trailing whitespace, BOM

docs.title: Common issues:
docs.text:
• E722: Use except Exception: instead of bare except:
  • F541: Remove f prefix from strings without placeholders
  • Unicode characters (emojis like ✓, ❌) fail on Windows - use ASCII alternatives

docs.title: Step 1: Install dependencies
docs.text: uv sync

docs.title: Step 2: Verify Dapr components are present
docs.text:
The components/*.yaml files are committed to the repo and do not need downloading. Confirm they exist:

ls components/

docs.title: Step 3 (optional): Start an external Dapr + Temporal
docs.text:
run_dev_combined() in Step 4 always starts its own embedded Dapr runtime and in-process Temporal server, so skip this step for it. You need it only for the manual application-sdk --mode combined approach below, which expects a standalone Temporal server and Dapr sidecar, as production has. It needs the Temporal CLI but not the Dapr CLI; see the Setup Overview.

uv run poe start-deps

To provision credentials into the local vault without running the full app (useful for standalone handler tests):

uv run poe provision-credentials

docs.title: Step 4: Run the app with run_dev_combined
docs.text:
Create a run_dev.py script (or add to your existing one):

import asyncio
from application_sdk.main import run_dev_combined
from app.my_app import MyApp

asyncio.run(
    run_dev_combined(
        MyApp,
        credentials={
            "host": "your-database-host.example.com",
            "port": "5432",
            "authType": "basic",
            "username": "myuser",
            "password": "mypassword",
            "extra": {"database": "mydb"},
        },
        example_input={
            "connection": {
                "connection_name": "test-connection",
                "connection_qualified_name": "default/my-app/1234",
            },
        },
    )
)

Then run:

uv run python run_dev.py

This does everything automatically: 1. Starts the handler + worker on port 8000 2. Provisions credentials (splits sensitive/non-sensitive, same as prod) 3. Starts the workflow with the provisioned credential_guid

docs.title: Manual curl approach
docs.text:
If you prefer to control each step, start Dapr + Temporal (Step 3), then start the app without credentials and use curl:

# Start the app
uv run application-sdk --mode combined --app app.connector:MyApp

# Provision credentials (app must be running)
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/workflows/v1/dev/local-vault \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"host": "localhost", "port": "5432", "authType": "basic",
       "username": "myuser", "password": "mypassword",
       "extra": {"database": "mydb"}}'
# Returns: {"data": {"credential_guid": "..."}, "success": true, "message": "Credentials provisioned successfully"}

# Start the workflow
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/workflows/v1/start \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"credential_guid": "<GUID_FROM_ABOVE>",
       "connection": {"connection_name": "test", "connection_qualified_name": "default/app/1234"}}'

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
This section is the one place the SDK's test commands are written down; other pages link here. Conventions for writing tests are in Testing and the testing standard.

# Unit tests, the way a CI matrix leg runs them: parallel under xdist.
# addopts in pyproject.toml already deselects integration, e2e, load and perf.
uv run pytest --import-mode=importlib -n auto tests/

# The same with coverage, as the one coverage leg runs it (85% floor).
uv run pytest --import-mode=importlib -n auto --cov=application_sdk --cov-report=term tests/

# One file, or tests matching a pattern, serially with output shown
uv run pytest tests/unit/storage/test_file_ref_sync.py -v -s
uv run pytest -k "test_name_pattern" -v

# Slow unit tests (@pytest.mark.perf), excluded from the command above
uv run pytest tests/unit -m perf

# Integration tests: embedded Temporal and Dapr, nothing to start first
uv run poe test-integration

# CI's own driver scripts (.github/scripts/tests, its own pytest.ini)
uv run pytest .github/scripts/tests

Measure coverage with --cov, not coverage run -m pytest: coverage run traces only the parent process, so the xdist workers' coverage is lost. Leave out --capture=no and --log-cli-level: xdist ignores the first in its workers, and live logging cost 42% of the wall time. The exact per-leg command CI builds (socket guard, timeouts, durations) is .github/scripts/unit_test_command.py.

docs.title: Documentation Updates
docs.text:
• When changing application_sdk modules, update the matching conceptual docs per docs/standards/documentation.md.
  • Conceptual docs live under docs/concepts/ (see the mapping in that rule file).
  • A new page under docs/ goes into nav in mkdocs.yml, and links to repo source use a full GitHub URL; CI's mkdocs build --strict fails otherwise (docs/standards/documentation.md).
  • Agent guidance goes in CLAUDE.md, never AGENTS.md: each AGENTS.md is a generated pointer at the CLAUDE.md beside it, and the check-agents-md-sync pre-commit hook fails any other content (.github/scripts/check_agents_md_sync.py --fix regenerates it). A command or prerequisite is written once: commands in docs/agents/dev-commands.md, prerequisites in docs/standards/setup.md; other pages link to them.
  • A new or changed env var gets a row in docs/configuration.md. tests/unit/test_env_var_docs_coverage.py fails until the name appears in a table row there (its own, or as a fallback in another row); a mention in prose does not count. See docs/standards/env-vars.md.

docs.title: Incremental state (application_sdk/common/incremental/**)
docs.text:
This package documents itself beside the code rather than under docs/concepts/. A change to it — in particular to state/store.py (CurrentStateStore, RunStateDirs), state/state_writer.py, state/incremental_diff.py, marker.py or helpers.py — updates:

  • application_sdk/common/incremental/README.md — the module's architecture, layout and deprecation table.
  • The skills under application_sdk/common/incremental/skills/ that describe the changed behaviour: implement-incremental-extraction/ (notably references/state-management.md), incremental-migrate/ (notably references/guardrails.md), and incremental-extraction.mdc. Every symbol they name must exist; mark deprecated ones as such.
  • docs/standards/cross-repo-contracts.md — the persistent-artifacts and current-state/incremental-diff entries, whenever the object-store layout, .sdk-manifest, run-stamped file names or metadata.json change. Other repos read these.
  • docs/agents/sdk-capabilities.md — regenerate with /capability-manifest when a public symbol changes.
  • CHANGELOG.md and the generated docs/changelog/v*.md archives — never: the release workflow writes them (see docs/changelog/index.md, which is maintained by hand).

The same applies to the template that drives the package, application_sdk/templates/incremental_sql_metadata_extractor.py, in addition to its docs/concepts/tasks.md mapping.

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text:
• application_sdk/ is the core SDK package (clients, handlers, activities, workflows).
  • contract-toolkit/ is the separately released Pkl package for authoring app contracts.
  • tests/ contains the test suite (currently organized under tests/unit/).
  • docs/ holds documentation sources (guides, concepts, setup).
  • components/ stores Dapr/Temporal configs used by local dev tasks.

For which docs to update when code changes, see docs/agents/docs-updates.md. For the generated public SDK surface inventory, see docs/agents/sdk-capabilities.md.

docs.title: Code Review
docs.text:
PRs to main are reviewed on request by lens, an AI reviewer that runs in .github/workflows/lens.yml. Comment /lens on a PR to start a review; a push never triggers one. Only OWNER, MEMBER, or COLLABORATOR comments can trigger it, and bot comments are refused. Maintainers can also start a review with workflow_dispatch from the Actions tab; that path has no bot check of its own, only the repo's Actions write permission.

Each run continues from the previous one on the same PR. lens posts a sticky summary comment and, when every finding is fixed or dismissed, an atlan-ci code-owner approval. /lens force bypasses the unchanged-head and round-cap rules; the per-PR cost cap still applies.

The old @sdk-review / @sdk-resolve (mothership) triggers are retired. A comment starting with either from a human OWNER, MEMBER, or COLLABORATOR is answered with a pointer to /lens; other comments get no reply.

docs.title: Where lens is configured
docs.text:
What Where Model, cost cap, round limits .github/lens/config.toml Which review cards apply to which paths .github/lens/rules.toml Review cards (what to check per area) .github/lens/cards/ Reviewer code .github/scripts/lens/

Config is read from the base branch only, so a PR cannot retune its own reviewer.

docs.title: Review checklist
docs.text: Use this when reviewing a PR by hand or with an agent.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text: ID Name Trigger G1 Security Blockers Any Critical security finding G2 Contract Safety Field removed/renamed/retyped on Input/Output (breaks Temporal replay) G3 Determinism Non-deterministic ops in run()/@entrypoint G4 Test Coverage New public API without tests G5 Secret Safety Hardcoded secrets or credentials in logs G6 Breaking API Public export removed without deprecation shim G7 CI Must Pass All required CI checks must be green G8 Branch Mergeable No unresolvable conflicts

docs.title: CI Cost
docs.text:
Applies to any change under .github/workflows/, a reusable workflow, or a bootstrap template. The rules and the reasoning behind them are in CI cost. Anything in a template or reusable runs in ~140 repos, so judge it by its fleet total.

  • New billed jobs — could the work be steps in an existing job?
  • "Nothing to do" filters sit on the job's if:, not on steps
  • No matrix whose legs finish in under a minute
  • Every PR-triggered workflow cancels superseded runs, or explains why not
  • Every upload-artifact sets retention-days
  • A new workflow_run trigger states its fan-in; a new cron justifies its frequency
  • No check re-runs on PR, merge queue and release with unchanged inputs

docs.title: Atlan Application SDK — Capability Manifest
docs.text:
Canonical inventory of every public symbol exposed by application_sdk, plus every typed Input/Output contract. Read this before reading SDK source. Generated by .claude/skills/capability-manifest.

To check if current: uv run poe regen-capabilities && git diff --exit-code -- docs/agents/sdk-capabilities.md

docs.title: Subpackage Index
docs.text: Subpackage Purpose Exports application_sdk.app Core developer abstractions — App, @task, @entrypoint, Input, Output, RetryPolicy, mcp_tool 75 application_sdk.clients Connection clients (SQL, Redis, Azure) and ClientInterface ABC 54 application_sdk.common Shared utilities — SQL filters, concurrency helpers, TaskStatistics, DataframeType 234 application_sdk.constants Import-time configuration read from env vars once at import — paths, Dapr component names, observability and validation settings (use AppConfig for anything read after startup) 146 application_sdk.contracts Typed Pydantic Input/Output base classes, payload safety, storage and type helpers 69 application_sdk.credentials Credential resolvers (Atlan, OAuth, Git, agent), registry, vault spec 81 application_sdk.dev Local-iteration helpers — embedded Dapr and Temporal daemons managed by the SDK, no host install needed 11 application_sdk.discovery Dynamic App and Handler loading from "module.path:ClassName" strings at container startup 4 application_sdk.errors Typed error hierarchy — AppError, the categorical leaves (AuthError, NotFoundError, …), FailureCategory and the FailureDetails wire envelope; each class's code ClassVar is the one error vocabulary 45 application_sdk.execution Task/workflow execution — retry, heartbeat, sandbox, AppWorker, Temporal client 69 application_sdk.handler HTTP handler framework — Handler ABC, DefaultHandler, preflight, auth, service factory 119 application_sdk.infrastructure Protocol-based infrastructure (StateStore, SecretStore, PubSub, Bindings, CapacityPool) 47 application_sdk.main Dev entry point — run_dev_combined() and AppConfig for local execution and container startup 2 application_sdk.main_errors Typed error leaves raised by the main entry point — app module resolution, run mode, Dapr detection 4 application_sdk.observability Logging context — ExecutionContext, CorrelationContext, request/correlation helpers 144 application_sdk.outputs Output collectors and record models for Automation Engine 44 application_sdk.pkl_version The Pkl toolchain pin — the one version CI renders contracts with, readable by an app's own tooling so a local render predicts the freshness gate 1 application_sdk.server FastAPI server, MCP integration, middleware, health endpoint 29 application_sdk.storage Object-store abstraction — factory, formats, batch, transfer, cloud bindings 128 application_sdk.templates SQL metadata extractor templates and their contracts 19 application_sdk.testing Test infrastructure — mocks, fixtures, hypothesis strategies, integration helpers 427 application_sdk.tools Developer command-line tools — provision-credentials for local development 1 application_sdk.transformers Legacy daft+YAML transformer stack (back-compat only — migrate to pyatlan record mappers; see upgrade-guide-v3.md). 27 application_sdk.validation Offline artifact & asset validation — format-agnostic wrapper (ADR-0020) plus pyatlan_v9 .validate() wrappers, no network call 95

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Test commands: docs/agents/dev-commands.md (Testing), the one place they are written down. Conventions: docs/standards/testing.md.
  • New code should target 85% coverage per docs/standards/review-checklist.md (the tooling threshold in pyproject.toml is 85% — CI fails below it). The same floor applies to each top-level application_sdk subpackage on its own, except those listed with a different floor in [tool.application-sdk.coverage.package-floors]; the coverage leg uploads coverage.xml and htmlcov/ as the sdk-unit-test-coverage artifact (14 days).
  • Current tests live in tests/unit/, which mirrors application_sdk/: application_sdk/a/b/c.py → tests/unit/a/b/test_c.py (so _runtime/ → tests/unit/_runtime/, execution/_temporal/interceptors/ → tests/unit/execution/_temporal/interceptors/). tests/unit/test_unit_tree_mirrors_package.py fails a test directory with no package counterpart; a deliberate exception goes in its _NOT_MIRRORED with what it tests instead.
  • Before writing a local double, look for a shared one. tests/unit/_doubles.py holds FakeClock (an injected monotonic clock with advance), StaticHandler (a Handler whose entry points succeed empty), SiblingProbe (fan-out first-failure), loaded_after_importing / loaded_after_running (fresh-interpreter import probes), record_connect_params (SQLAlchemy do_connect recorder) and the Temporal interceptor inputs; MockSecretStore records get_optional calls (get_get_optional_calls()), so a store that only records or answers from a dict is a MockSecretStore. Directory fixtures live in the nearest conftest.py: store in tests/unit/storage/ (memory) and tests/integration/ (local), mock_next in tests/unit/execution/_temporal/interceptors/, and the emulator guards require_minio / require_azurite / require_testbench in tests/integration/storage/ (opt in with pytestmark = pytest.mark.usefixtures("require_minio")). A double used by one module stays in it; move it to _doubles.py when a second module needs it.
  • Keep a test module under 1,500 lines. When one grows past that, split it by the area it covers and move shared handlers and factories into a support module beside it — tests/unit/handler/test_service_*.py share _service_support.py.
  • A unit test that takes ≥10s on its own (a throughput comparison, a 100k-key scale probe) gets @pytest.mark.perf. addopts excludes it from the 12-leg matrix; the Unit Perf Tests job runs it once, in one process, with uv run pytest tests/unit -m perf. Every other unit test runs under a 120s per-test --timeout in CI, and only the ubuntu 3.12 leg measures coverage.
  • An unconditional @pytest.mark.skip must name its ticket in the reason (reason="waits on FND-1234"); the hook in tests/conftest.py fails the test otherwise (FND-4286). Fix or delete a broken test instead of skipping it. skipif is not checked.
  • For how a consumer app's tests should be laid out, read docs/agents/canonical-apps.md and then the app itself — not an arbitrary atlan-*-app, which may be mid-migration or carry deprecated patterns.
  • When a fixture stands in for a generated artifact (app/generated/**, atlan.yaml, a served API envelope), build it from a real one and say in a comment which repo it was read from. A fixture with the shape inverted still passes — for a reason unrelated to its claim — and it flatters the code under test, which is APP-TESTS-001's self-certifying PR arriving through the fixture rather than the assertion. FND-1667 shipped one: a credential template written as {"id": ...} with no config, where the toolkit emits config and no id. Nothing caught it until someone ran the selector against a real tree.
  • When the generated artifact can be rendered here, render it instead of copying it. Each fixture listed in tests/regen_fixtures.py (today tests/unit/handler/fixtures/generated_bigquery_credentials/, rendered from fixtures/bigquery_contract/app.pkl) is toolkit output; tests/unit/test_rendered_fixtures.py renders each one again with the pinned pkl and fails when a copy is stale. To add one, write its contract and add an entry to FIXTURES. After changing a contract or contract-toolkit/src, run uv run poe regen-test-fixtures and review the diff. The Linux unit legs install pkl and set SDK_TESTS_REQUIRE_PKL, so the check cannot pass there by skipping. tests/unit/validation/resources/artifact_schemas.json is held to its toolkit example the same way, by test_fixture_is_the_generated_example.
  • addopts has --strict-markers: a mark not listed in [tool.pytest.ini_options].markers (or registered by a plugin) fails collection. Register a new mark there before using it.
  • No reruns and no flaky marker: CI runs each test once. Fix a flaky test in place.
  • The conformance package's own tests (packages/conformance/tests/) share helpers through tests/_helpers.py: ids / active_ids (all findings vs unsuppressed only — the runner gate's view), write_py, scan_files(scan_all, tmp_path, files), uv_lock, extract_node and sdk_root(). Import them (from tests._helpers import active_ids) instead of copying a helper from the nearest test file. Seven drift guards (test_contract_ledger_drift, test_dependency_audience, test_deprecations_manifest, test_public_errors_drift, test_removed_imports, test_sdk_type_aliases_drift, test_toolkit_baseline_drift) get the monorepo root from sdk_root(), which fails under CI and skips only locally: a miss in CI means the layout changed, which is when the guard is needed. Other drift tests (for example test_sdk_contract_fields_drift) do not use it yet; a new path-based drift guard should.
  • The CI script tests (.github/scripts/tests/) run under .github/scripts/pytest.ini, not the root config. Its pythonpath makes every script and every shared helper there (_workflows.py, _frozen_clock.py, _gha_expr.py, …) importable by name, so never add a sys.path.insert for either directory (test_pytest_ini.py fails one). Read workflow YAML through _workflows.py instead of a per-file _load / _job / _step. See docs/standards/ci.md ("Running the script tests").
  • For consumer apps built on this SDK, the conformance suite's T-series (packages/conformance/conformance/docs/rules/tests.md) enforces the agreed per-connector testing-tier architecture (unit + integration required, e2e recommended, UI optional except for top connectors) plus test-quality checks — assertion-free tests, uncollectable test files, disabled coverage gates, and more. Run it with /remediate or uv run atlan-application-sdk-conformance detect --series T.

docs.title: Shared Harness Doubles
docs.text:
The four harness seams each have one shared double under tests/unit/testing/: _atlas_fakes.py (pyatlan), _cluster_fakes.py (Kubernetes), _temporal_fakes.py (Temporal) and _ae_fakes.py (Automation Engine). Use them; do not write a per-file _FakeAE or a private _node / _succeeded / _result builder.

  • FakeAE implements every public AEClient method with the client's parameters, records each call's bound arguments (ae.calls_to(m), ae.args(m, *names), ae.methods), and serves scripted poll_native_status readings in order. test_ae_fakes.py fails when a client method is added or its signature changes, so update the fake in the same PR.
  • Build DAGRunResult / DAGNodeResult with node(), run_result(), succeeded(), failed(), stalled() and numbered() from the same module.
  • A test that needs failure behaviour the constructor cannot script (for example, a submit that reports a run id and then raises) uses a thin FakeAE subclass that calls super().

docs.title: Shared State Under xdist
docs.text:
An xdist worker runs many tests in one process, and threads from earlier tests (offloads, log flushes) are still running. Keep every test's changes local:

  • Never patch a stdlib function through an SDK module path. patch("application_sdk.X.time.monotonic") patches the one global time module, so the event loop and every thread see the fake. Use tests.unit.private_stdlib.private_stdlib(X, "time") and patch the copy it yields. tests/unit/test_no_global_stdlib_patches.py fails the global forms.
  • Never importlib.reload an SDK module. A reload makes new class and enum objects that earlier importers do not see. Put import-time env parsing in a _load_*() function and test that.
  • Use monkeypatch.setenv / delenv / chdir / syspath_prepend, not os.environ / os.chdir / sys.path directly.
  • tests/unit/conftest.py already resets, around every unit test: the App and Task registries, the infrastructure context, the sizing sink, psycopg2's encodings map, and os.environ. It also loads the hypothesis unit profile (deadline=None); do not call settings.load_profile in a test module.

docs.title: Timeouts a Passing Test Must Beat
docs.text:
A healthy test must never have to finish inside a timeout that exists to prove the failure path. On a loaded 4-vCPU runner — Windows especially, where Event.wait(0.001) rounds to ~15.6 ms and thread-pool spin-up is slow — the success path misses a short bar and reads as a TIMEOUT, an unverifiable source, or a hang.

  • Any timeout a passing test must beat is ≥5s; ≥30s when it covers subprocess or pool spin-up. This includes pytest.mark.timeout, the bound you give asyncio.wait_for, and every budget or deadline handed to the code under test.
  • Short timeouts are only for tests whose subject is the timeout, and only on the step that hangs: test_source_probes.py's _cut_off("tcp") keeps DNS and TLS generous while cutting TCP short.
  • pytest.mark.timeout counts fixture setup too, and on Windows its thread method calls os._exit, killing the whole xdist worker — a "worker crashed" red with no FAILED line. Use it only as a hang guard (timeout(30)).
  • Prove "did not wait" or "did not block the loop" structurally, not with a wall-clock upper bound: record the budget at the seam that would wait (test_restart_marker.py's idle fixture), or assert that a blocked call has not finished when the loop observes it (test_sql_client_cancellation.py). A lower bound (elapsed >= budget) is safe; an upper bound measures runner load.

docs.title: Never Assert on Elapsed Wall-Clock Time
docs.text:
assert elapsed < 1.0, assert lag < 0.1, assert ticks >= n measure the CI runner, not the code: a loaded 4-vCPU runner misses the bar with nothing wrong and one matrix leg goes red at random (FND-4233). Assert the property instead:

  • The event loop stayed free — route the blocking cost through tests/unit/loop_probe.py::LoopProbe.block() and call assert_loop_stayed_free.
  • A budget or remaining time — inject the clock (clock=, a module-local _monotonic seam) or freeze the one the code reads; assert the exact value.
  • It returned promptly / did not wait for a blocked call — have the blocked call set a flag only when it returns and assert the flag is unset once the caller has returned; or bound the wait with asyncio.wait_for / Event.wait at 5–30s, so the bound decides how long a regression takes to fail, never whether a healthy run passes.
  • A complexity guard (linear, not quadratic) — count the steps; failing that, size the input so the regression takes minutes and bound it at 30s. A ratio of two millisecond timings swings past any bar under load, even fastest-of-five.

tests/unit/test_no_wall_clock_asserts.py fails on any new ordered assertion over a clock delta or a value named elapsed/lag/ticks/gap(s)/took.

docs.title: Asserting a Preflight Gate Verdict
docs.text:
The gate emits one Preflight gate outcome row per invocation and picks the log level from the verdict (FND-901): error for a block or an unverifiable source, warning when it proceeded with a failed advisory check, info otherwise. Read the row through the shared capture rather than patching preflight_gate.logger by hand — a reader that watches info alone returns an empty list on exactly the runs it was written to pin, and keeps passing:

from application_sdk.testing import capture_preflight_outcomes  # in conftest.py


async def test_block_names_the_failing_check(capture_preflight_outcomes):
    ...
    assert capture_preflight_outcomes.level == "error"
    assert capture_preflight_outcomes.matrix[0]["name"] == "credentialScopes"

The capture patches nothing: it adds a loguru sink for the test and records the outcome rows the gate's real logger delivers to it. A passing assertion therefore proves the row reached a sink at that level with those bound fields, which a stand-in logger cannot — the adapter runs exactly as in production, so each row also carries the context it stamps (app_name, source, …).

Suites that patch the logger with a MagicMock themselves can use outcome_rows / outcome_level / single_outcome over the mock instead; prefer the fixture. Both paths assert exactly one row, because returning the first match hides a double emission.

Boundary: the capture covers rows the gate activity emits. The workflow wrapper's skipped / no_verdict rows go through Temporal's workflow.logger (app/base.py), which the capture does not read — pin those paths against workflow.logger directly.

docs.title: Asserting Other Log Lines
docs.text:
Assert a log line from the record a real sink received, not from a patched module logger. A MagicMock logger proves a method of that name was called; it cannot prove the record reached a sink at that level, rendered, with the bound fields that survive export. Two of these tests hid real export defects while they read a mock, and now pin them as strict xfails.

  • loguru_capture (tests/unit/conftest.py) yields every raw loguru record emitted during the test; filter on record["extra"]["logger_name"] and record["level"].name.
  • gate_records (tests/unit/execution/conftest.py) is that filter for the preflight gate's non-outcome lines: gate_records("WARNING").
  • To check what is exported, run the record's extra through _build_extra_dict — the allowlist the OTLP and NDJSON sinks apply. A key it drops is counted on log.extra_key.dropped; to assert on that counter, see the drop_state fixture in tests/unit/observability/test_log_extra_allowlist.py.

docs.title: Registry Isolation
docs.text:
AppRegistry / TaskRegistry resets have one definition: clean_app_registry and clean_task_registry in application_sdk.testing.fixtures. The unit and integration conftests apply them to every test through an autouse fixture, so a test needs no reset of its own. Request them by name only where ordering matters — a fixture that registers an app must run after the reset.

Do not add a setup_method / teardown_method, try/finally, or fixture whose job is AppRegistry.reset() or TaskRegistry.reset(). pytest runs the conftest autouse fixtures before a class's setup_method and tears them down after teardown_method, so each test already starts and ends with both registries empty.

clear_infrastructure() is different: only tests/unit/conftest.py clears the infrastructure context around every test. In tests/unit, do not add that cleanup either. In tests/integration, a test or fixture that calls set_infrastructure must still clear it in its own finalizer, or the next test on the worker inherits the context.

Call a reset inside a test only when the reset is the behaviour under test (an app that is no longer registered, a cleared context).

docs.title: What SDK Review Checks for Tests
docs.text:
The reviewer enforces these test rules (G4 guardrail):

  • New public API (class/method/module exported in __init__.py) -> MUST have tests
  • Bug fix PR -> MUST have a regression test
  • Security fix PR -> MUST have a regression test
  • Performance fix PR -> MUST have a behavior test
  • Code quality / docs / v2 cleanup -> existing tests passing is sufficient

docs.title: Test Patterns the Reviewer Flags
docs.text:
• @pytest.mark.asyncio or @pytest.mark.anyio (redundant with asyncio_mode="auto" — remove it; only a non-default argument such as loop_scope="session" needs the mark)
  • assert result or assert result is not None (too vague — assert specific values)
  • Missing clean_app_registry fixture when defining App subclasses in tests
  • Real external calls in unit tests (use MockStateStore, MockSecretStore, MockPubSub)
  • Missing MockHeartbeatController for heartbeat-enabled @task methods
  • Tests checking implementation details instead of behavior

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
The SDK's release notes live in CHANGELOG.md at the repository root. The release workflow generates it: never edit it by hand.

CHANGELOG.md holds only the current major version's releases. On the release that bumps the major, the workflow moves every section from an older major into docs/changelog/v<major>.md in this directory, unchanged and newest first, one file per major. Those archives aren't built into this site. Read them on GitHub.

docs.title: How a section is generated and checked
docs.text:
