This is an optimisation, not a bug A long bounded hold that stayed inside its allowance Nothing. Somebody already sized this site A lapsed hold on a site you believe is healthy Raise the allowance — this one will false-kill once you enforce A gap that only ever appears on one tenant, at one step Look at the step before you change a number. This is what a real wedge looks like

Read the report from a large tenant. A small tenant's fast steps hide the very gaps that only open at the tail — which is where the original failures came from.

docs.title: Metric reference
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels task_no_progress_gap_seconds histogram task_name, progress_last_label, watchdog_mode task_hold_duration_seconds histogram task_name, hold_label, hold_bounded, hold_lapsed

app_name is inlined onto every series, and the rest of the app identity (version, release channel, k8s topology) is reachable through target_info — see Monitoring.

docs.title: Modes: off, warn, enforce
docs.text:
Mode Behaviour off No gap is reported and nothing is ever failed. A kill-switch, not a normal state warn The watchdog runs and reports; it can never fail an activity. The default enforce Reports the gap, then fails the attempt

Two things off does not do, both worth knowing before you reach for it:

  • It is not fully inert. The gap metric and its log stop, but the hold telemetry does not — task_hold_duration_seconds still records once per released hold, i.e. once per run_in_thread offload, because a hold observation is a work-list entry rather than a watchdog action.
  • It does not shorten anything. A wedged attempt is bounded by timeout_seconds, which off does not touch — so it makes a wedge invisible without making it cheaper. If that is the problem you have, the lever is the backstop; see the stalled-task runbook.

Warn is the default fleet-wide because it cannot fail anything, which means nobody has to opt in and every app starts producing its own work-list on upgrade. See Setting them for the @task arguments and the env vars behind them.

docs.title: When a stall does fail an attempt
docs.text:
In enforce, the watchdog cancels the attempt and the SDK turns that into a TaskStalledError — a subtype of AppTimeoutError, code TIMEOUT_TASK_STALLED, carrying stalled_for_seconds and last_progress_label. It is retryable on purpose: the dominant cause is a transient source-side hang that self-heals on a fresh attempt, and a genuine wedge re-stalls at a cost of a few multiples of the budget rather than of the backstop.

Detection latency is the budget plus at most one heartbeat tick.

Effective kill times:

Situation Killed at Quiet step, no hold max_no_progress_seconds Wedged call inside a declared hold timeout + max_no_progress_seconds Wedged call inside an unbounded hold (including any run_in_thread) the 24h backstop Nothing beating at all (OOM, node loss, starved loop) heartbeat_timeout_seconds (60s), unchanged

Before flipping an app to enforce, verify against a large-tenant / tail profile — not a smoke test. A small run hides the tail gaps, and because stall kills retry, an under-instrumented app burns the same wasted work up to three times before failing.

docs.title: What if I do nothing?
docs.text: Nothing fails differently. See Upgrading: the stall watchdog for the full answer, including which code shapes do eventually need action and which never will.

docs.title: Server (Handler Service)
docs.text: In v3, the HTTP server is created by the create_app_handler_service() function. This replaces the v2 APIServer class and its register_workflow() / HttpWorkflowTrigger pattern.

docs.title: Creating the Handler Service
docs.text:
The handler service auto-wires routes from your Handler methods:

from application_sdk.handler import create_app_handler_service
from my_package.handlers import MyHandler

app = create_app_handler_service(handler=MyHandler())

When started (via the CLI --mode handler or --mode combined), this creates a FastAPI application with:

  • Routes for test_auth, preflight_check, and fetch_metadata derived from your Handler subclass
  • Health check endpoints
  • MCP server integration (if configured)

docs.title: Health Check Endpoints
docs.text:
Every handler service exposes health checks at two equivalent paths each:

Endpoint Method Purpose /health (alias: /server/health) GET Liveness probe /ready (alias: /server/ready) GET Readiness probe

These are registered automatically. No configuration is needed.

In combined mode, /ready returns the co-hosted worker's readiness. It sends the same body as the worker health port's /ready, and a 503 when the worker is not ready, so the two ports give the same answer about the pod. In handler-only mode it always returns 200 {"status": "ok"}.

docs.title: Worker liveness window
docs.text: In worker and combined mode the SDK also runs a WorkerHealthServer that exposes /health, /ready, and /live.

docs.title: Poll-loop checks (on by default)
docs.text:
/live returns 503 when the worker is alive but its Temporal poll loop is confirmed dead (FND-4641). Kubernetes then restarts the pod, which recovers a worker that the in-process restart supervisor and fatal-teardown watchdog could not. Two conditions trip it:

Condition Default Opt-out sdk-core's poller gauge reads a definitive zero for N consecutive observer readings N = 5 (about 5 minutes at the 60s interval) ATLAN_WORKER_LIVENESS_MAX_ZERO_POLLER_READINGS=0 A fatal poll error is followed by no polling reading within the bound 600 seconds ATLAN_WORKER_LIVENESS_FATAL_RECOVERY_SECONDS=0

The zero-poller check does not false-positive on an idle queue: an idle worker still reads its configured poller count. An unknown reading (gauge unreadable) resets the count rather than adding to it. The fatal check is cleared by the first polling reading after the fatal, which the supervisor produces when it rebuilds a worker that polls again. When the gauge cannot be read at all (Prometheus exporter or observer disabled), no recovery is visible, so a fatal restarts the pod after the bound even if the supervisor recovered in process. The 503 body carries the poller counts, fatal count and fatal_unrecovered_since for diagnosis.

docs.title: Import-wait check (on by default)
docs.text:
/live also returns 503 when a thread has waited longer than ATLAN_WORKER_LIVENESS_MAX_IMPORT_WAIT_SECONDS (default 300) on the same module import lock (FND-5531). Temporal's deadlock interrupt (TMPRL1101) can land inside Python's import system and leave a module's import lock unable to wake its next waiter. That thread then waits forever while holding the lock of the module it was importing, so every later import of that module hangs in every thread, activities included, while the poll loop keeps polling.

The check reads CPython's own record of which thread waits on which import lock (importlib._bootstrap._blocking_on). It starts no thread and imports nothing. A wait is timed from the first /live request that sees it. A healthy import, even a slow cold one, never waits this long. The 503 body names the module and the waiting thread, and the ERROR log adds where the stuck import chain was started (the outermost line that called into the import machinery) plus the thread's full stack. When that line is a function-local import in workflow code, the fix is to move it to module level; restarting the pod only stops the bleeding, and a cold, busy replacement can hit the same wedge. If a future Python changes that private table, the check logs one warning and stays healthy. Set the variable to 0 to disable it.

docs.title: Idle window (off by default)
docs.text:
Setting ATLAN_WORKER_LIVENESS_MAX_IDLE_SECONDS to a positive value makes /live fail once no worker activity (an activity execution or heartbeat) has been recorded within that window, so a Kubernetes livenessProbe can recycle a worker whose Temporal poll loop has silently parked while run() never returns or raises (BLDX-1552) — the one failure the in-process restart supervisor cannot see.

The window is disabled by default (0) because a positive value false-positives on legitimately idle queues, where no work arriving is normal rather than a stall. Enable it only for continuously-busy queues, and set it larger than the longest activity that runs without heartbeating so a slow but healthy activity is not mistaken for a parked poll loop. The probe never fails before the first activity is recorded, so it does not kill a worker during startup. See the env var in docs/concepts/common.md.

docs.title: Handler Method Routing
docs.text:
The service maps your Handler methods to HTTP endpoints:

Handler method HTTP endpoint Method test_auth() /workflows/v1/auth POST preflight_check() /workflows/v1/check POST fetch_metadata() /workflows/v1/metadata POST

The service layer injects self.context into the handler before each request and clears it after. Your handler methods receive typed Input objects and return typed Output objects.

docs.title: Full Endpoint Reference
docs.text:
All routes registered by create_app_handler_service():

Endpoint Method Description /workflows/v1/auth POST Test authentication credentials /workflows/v1/check POST Run preflight connectivity checks /workflows/v1/metadata POST Browse source metadata (schemas, tables) /workflows/v1/start POST Start a workflow run (use ?entrypoint=<name> for multi-entry-point apps) /workflows/v1/validate POST Validate a workflow configuration against the entry point's published input contract, without starting anything. Also served by the consolidated API host (see Validating a workflow configuration) /workflows/v1/stop/{workflow_id}/{run_id} POST Terminate a running workflow /workflows/v1/result/{workflow_id} GET Fetch the final result of a completed workflow /workflows/v1/status/{workflow_id}/{run_id} GET Poll workflow execution status /workflows/v1/config/{config_id} GET Retrieve a workflow config (configmap) /workflows/v1/config/{config_id} POST Update a workflow config /workflows/v1/file POST Upload a file to the handler /workflows/v1/configmap/{config_map_id} GET Retrieve a configmap by ID /workflows/v1/configmaps GET List all configmaps /workflows/v1/manifest GET Retrieve the app manifest (supports ?entrypoint=<name>) /manifest GET Alias for /workflows/v1/manifest (for backward compat) /workflows/v1/dev/local-vault POST Provision credentials in the local dev vault (local dev only — requires ATLAN_DEPLOYMENT_NAME=local; returns 403 otherwise) /dapr/subscribe GET Dapr pub/sub subscription list /events/v1/event/{event_id} POST Handle a Dapr event /events/v1/drop POST Return a Dapr DROP status, instructing the sidecar to drop the received event without retry or dead-lettering /health, /server/health GET Liveness probe /ready, /server/ready GET Readiness probe /metrics GET Prometheus metrics (always exposed; merges SDK custom metrics + HTTP server instrumentation + prometheus_client defaults, plus Temporal Rust-core families proxied from 127.0.0.1:9464 when enabled and reachable) / GET API root / service info

docs.title: Validating a workflow configuration
docs.text:
POST /workflows/v1/validate?entrypoint=<name> checks the body a workflow will be started with against the entry point's published input contract, then stops. That is the same model GET /workflows/v1/input-contract serves. Call it when a workflow is created, so a configuration the runtime cannot execute is rejected at submission instead of failing at engine time.

It lives with the metadata routes, so it ships in atlan-application-sdk-api. The consolidated API host serves it from the app's generated contract, and so does the worker, which resolves the same contract. It needs no Temporal connection and no running worker.

It goes further than the JSON Schema, because it also runs the contract's field_validators. For the SQL templates those reject:

  • SQL-unsafe filter values;
  • include/exclude/temp-table patterns that every engine the SQL templates target rejects (POSIX ERE, PostgreSQL, ICU, RE2, Java): an unterminated ( or [, a reversed character range, or a trailing backslash. Syntax that only some dialects accept (\p{L}, POSIX classes, a lone )) is left for the source to judge. The error names the field and position, never the pattern.

workflow_id / workflow_type and inline credentials (v2 or v3 shape) are taken out before the contract judges the body, as /start does: credentials are never part of a workflow's configuration. Instead, the route checks credentials for the fields the app's own generated forms mark required per auth type (required = true on each FieldSpec in credentials.pkl):

What the body carries Checked against 422 field Inline credentials, e.g. at credential creation The credential form, <credential-type>.json, for the selected authType (else the form's default), including its anyOf implications credentials.extra.atlan_oauth_id extraction_method: "agent" The workflow form's agent schema (agent-json → agentConfigs): every required field must map to a secret key agent_json.gcp-wif.extra.atlan_oauth_id, or agent_json when there is no populated spec A GUID-routed method (direct, …) The workflow form's credential slot: when it is required, the body must reference a credential (credential_guid, or any populated CredentialRef field) credential_guid

Each check runs only when the form that governs it ships in generated/. A required field with a non-empty declared default counts as provided. A vault credential's stored values can't be read here, so send the credential inline when it is created to have its fields checked. A declared-source (format 2) agent spec is left to its own validation. Each gap is a pydantic missing error naming the field. No credential value is returned or logged.

Outcome Status Body The body fits the contract 200 {"success": true, "data": {"entrypoint"}} The body does not fit the contract, or is not a JSON object 422 {"success": false, "message": "Invalid request: <fields>", "detail": [{"field", "message", "type"}]} Invalid ?entrypoint= name / several entry points and none named 400 Unknown ?entrypoint= 404

The 422 never includes pydantic's input, because the rejected value can be a credential. The SDK's own validators (SQL filters, regex structure, incremental markers, required credential fields) name the field and the problem, never the value. A custom validator in an app's contract is returned as written, so it must not put the value in its message either. /workflows/v1/start (worker only) answers the same 422 shape when its body does not fit the entry point's input type, before it touches Temporal.

docs.title: MCP Server Integration
docs.text: If your application exposes an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, the handler service can integrate it. MCP endpoints are wired alongside the standard handler routes.

docs.title: CLI Usage
docs.text:
In production, run the handler service as a separate pod:

application-sdk --mode handler --app my_package.apps:MyExtractor

For local development, --mode combined runs both the handler service and the Temporal worker in one process:

application-sdk --mode combined --app my_package.apps:MyExtractor

docs.title: Programmatic Usage
docs.text:
For integration tests or custom setups:

from application_sdk.main import run_dev_combined
from my_package.apps import MyExtractor

import asyncio
asyncio.run(run_dev_combined(MyExtractor))

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Handler methods signal errors by raising a typed AppError leaf from application_sdk.errors:

from application_sdk.errors import AuthError
from application_sdk.handler import Handler

class MyHandler(Handler):
    async def test_auth(self, input: AuthInput) -> AuthOutput:
        if not valid:
            raise AuthError(message="Invalid credentials")
        ...

The service answers with the HTTP status for the leaf's category (AuthError is 401; see Handlers for the table) and the redacted message as detail. HandlerError is deprecated (removal in v4.0).

docs.title: State, Secrets, Pub/Sub, and Bindings
docs.text:
The Application SDK abstracts four infrastructure capabilities behind Protocols: StateStore, SecretStore, PubSub, and Binding. In production, Dapr implements all four. In tests, lightweight mock implementations let you inject any behavior you need without Dapr running.

Access these through InfrastructureContext. See Infrastructure for how to set and retrieve the context.

docs.title: StateStore
docs.text:
Key-value storage scoped to a workflow run. Use it to persist intermediate results between tasks — for example, storing a checkpoint after each page of an API call so a retry can resume from where it left off.

Protocol:

class StateStore(Protocol):
    async def save(self, key: str, value: dict[str, Any]) -> None: ...
    async def load(self, key: str) -> dict[str, Any] | None: ...
    async def delete(self, key: str) -> bool: ...
    async def list_keys(self, prefix: str = "") -> list[str]: ...

Accessing in a task:

from application_sdk.infrastructure import get_infrastructure

@task(timeout_seconds=3600)
async def fetch_pages(self, input: FetchInput) -> FetchOutput:
    state = get_infrastructure().state_store
    if state is None:
        raise RuntimeError("StateStore not configured")

    checkpoint = await state.load(f"checkpoint:{input.workflow_id}")
    start_page = checkpoint["page"] if checkpoint else 1

    for page in range(start_page, total_pages + 1):
        # ... fetch page ...
        await state.save(f"checkpoint:{input.workflow_id}", {"page": page})

    return FetchOutput(...)

Dapr backend — in atlan.yaml, enable the state store:

dapr:
  statestore:
    enabled: true

The Dapr component name is statestore by default (read at module import time from STATE_STORE_NAME).

Testing without Dapr:

from application_sdk.testing import MockStateStore

mock_state = MockStateStore()
# Supports save/load/delete/list_keys and records all calls for assertions

docs.title: SecretStore
docs.text:
Provides access to secrets at runtime. The SDK uses this internally to resolve credential names / refs (legacy: credential GUIDs) — your app typically does not call SecretStore directly; use CredentialResolver instead (see Credentials).

Protocol:

class SecretStore(Protocol):
    async def get(self, name: str) -> str: ...
    async def get_optional(self, name: str) -> str | None: ...
    async def get_bulk(self, names: list[str]) -> dict[str, str]: ...
    async def list_names(self) -> list[str]: ...

Two built-in implementations:

Class Source Use case EnvironmentSecretStore os.environ Local dev, CI DaprSecretStore Dapr secret store sidecar Production

Injecting for tests:

import json
from application_sdk.testing import MockSecretStore

secret_store = MockSecretStore({
    "my-credential-name": json.dumps({
        "type": "basic",
        "username": "admin",
        "password": "secret",
        "host": "localhost",
    })
})

See Credentials for the full credential resolution flow, and Secret Stores for Dapr component configuration (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Kubernetes Secrets).

docs.title: PubSub
docs.text:
Topic-based messaging. Use PubSub to publish events — for example, notifying downstream apps when extraction completes. To receive them, declare a SubscriptionConfig (below).

Protocol:

class PubSub(Protocol):
    async def publish(
        self,
        topic: str,
        data: dict[str, Any],
        *,
        metadata: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    ) -> None: ...

subscribe() is deprecated — removal in v4.0.0

PubSub.subscribe(), Subscription and MessageHandler are deprecated. DaprPubSub.subscribe() never delivered a message: it stored the handler and nothing called it. MockPubSub.subscribe() did deliver, so a test could pass while production received nothing. Both now emit a DeprecationWarning.

To receive messages, declare a SubscriptionConfig and pass it to the handler service. The SDK lists it at /dapr/subscribe and mounts handler as a FastAPI POST route at /subscriptions/v1/{route}, where Dapr delivers each message:

from application_sdk.handler.contracts import SubscriptionConfig

async def on_extraction_complete(event: dict) -> None:
    ...

subscriptions = [
    SubscriptionConfig(
        component_name="pubsub",
        topic="extraction-complete",
        route="extraction-complete",
        handler=on_extraction_complete,
    )
]
# create_app_handler_service(..., subscriptions=subscriptions)

In a unit test, call on_extraction_complete directly.

Publishing a message:

PubSub is not part of InfrastructureContext. Use DaprPubSub from application_sdk.infrastructure — it implements the PubSub Protocol and handles serialisation and error wrapping:

from application_sdk.infrastructure import AsyncDaprClient, DaprPubSub

@task(timeout_seconds=60)
async def notify_complete(self, input: NotifyInput) -> NotifyOutput:
    async with AsyncDaprClient() as dapr:
        # Targets the Dapr pub/sub component named "pubsub" (components/pubsub.yaml).
        pubsub = DaprPubSub(dapr)
        await pubsub.publish(
            topic="extraction-complete",
            data={"workflow_id": input.workflow_id, "record_count": input.record_count},
        )
    return NotifyOutput()

Message dataclass:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Message:
    data: dict[str, Any]
    metadata: dict[str, str]   # default: {}
    id: str | None             # default: None
    topic: str | None          # default: None

Dapr backend — enable in atlan.yaml:

dapr:
  pubsub:
    enabled: true

DaprPubSub publishes to the component named pubsub unless you pass pubsub_name. Do not point it at EVENT_STORE_NAME (eventstore) by default: the SDK uses that component for its own lifecycle events through get_infrastructure().event_binding, and locally it is a binding (bindings.localstorage), not pub/sub. create_app_handler_service(event_triggers=...) does subscribe through EVENT_STORE_NAME, so in deployments where that component is pub/sub it receives Atlan events; publishing your own topics belongs on pubsub.

Testing without Dapr:

from application_sdk.testing import MockPubSub

mock_pubsub = MockPubSub()
# Records publish calls; use mock_pubsub.get_published(topic) to assert.
# Its subscribe() is deprecated (see above).

docs.title: Binding
docs.text:
Generic I/O bindings connect your app to external resources — object stores, queues, HTTP endpoints, email gateways — using Dapr's binding abstraction. For object storage (the most common use case), prefer the storage module's upload_file/download_file helpers (see Storage); bindings are for everything else.

Protocol:

class Binding(Protocol):
    @property
    def name(self) -> str: ...

    async def invoke(
        self,
        operation: str,
        data: bytes | None = None,
        metadata: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    ) -> BindingResponse: ...

Response type:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BindingResponse:
    data: bytes | None = None
    metadata: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

InputBinding, OutputBinding and BindingRequest are deprecated — removal in v4.0.0

The SDK never shipped an implementation of InputBinding or OutputBinding, and nothing accepts a BindingRequest. For outbound calls use Binding.invoke(operation, data, metadata), which DaprBinding implements. There is no input-binding replacement: to receive messages, use SubscriptionConfig with create_app_handler_service(subscriptions=...).

docs.title: CapacityPool (deprecated)
docs.text:
Deprecated — removal in v4.0.0

CapacityPool, LocalCapacityPool, RedisCapacityPool, configure_capacity_pool() and get_capacity_pool() are deprecated and emit a DeprecationWarning. The framework never configured a pool at startup — setting the REDIS_* env vars did not create one — and nothing in the SDK reads it, so get_capacity_pool() returned None unless the app called configure_capacity_pool() itself.

To cap parallel work inside a task, bound it in the app:

sem = asyncio.Semaphore(8)

async def fetch_one(item_id: str) -> dict:
    async with sem:
        return await self._fetch_item(item_id)

docs.title: Infrastructure Summary
docs.text:
Protocol Dapr Component Mock Access Purpose StateStore statestore (STATE_STORE_NAME) MockStateStore get_infrastructure().state_store Checkpoint / resume SecretStore Dapr secret store MockSecretStore get_infrastructure().secret_store Credential resolution Binding Dapr binding MockBinding get_infrastructure().event_binding External I/O PubSub pubsub MockPubSub DaprPubSub(AsyncDaprClient()) Event publishing (subscribe() deprecated) CapacityPool (deprecated) — LocalCapacityPool get_capacity_pool() Deprecated; removal in v4.0.0

StateStore, SecretStore, and Binding are held in InfrastructureContext and accessed via get_infrastructure(). PubSub is built from a Dapr client with DaprPubSub. CapacityPool is deprecated (see above). See Infrastructure for the test fixture pattern and set_infrastructure() / clear_infrastructure() usage.
