docs.title: Multi-App Coordination
docs.text: The Application SDK treats each App as an independent unit of execution — one Temporal workflow per app. When a connector needs multiple phases (metadata extraction → asset publishing, for example), those phases can run as separate apps coordinated by the Atlan platform.

docs.title: Pattern 1: Automation Engine DAG (recommended)
docs.text:
The Atlan Automation Engine (AE) reads app/generated/manifest.json and orchestrates apps as a directed acyclic graph. The SDK generates this manifest from your PKL contract.

AE reads manifest.json
  → starts App A (extract)
      ↓ on success
  → starts App B (publish) with App A's connection_qualified_name as input

This is the recommended pattern for production multi-phase connectors. It:

  • Decouples phase retries (a failed publish doesn't re-run extraction)
  • Shows each phase as a separate workflow in the Temporal UI
  • Lets you deploy phases at different scales or with different Temporal queues
  • Requires no SDK-level coordination code — the DAG lives in manifest.json

The manifest is generated from your contract/app.pkl by pkl eval (the make-contract skill walks you through writing one). See the PKL contracts guide for details on how to structure app.pkl and trigger manifest generation.

A two-phase manifest, as the toolkit generates it (abridged — publish carries more toggle args, and both nodes carry error_handling timeouts):

{
  "execution_mode": "automation-engine",
  "dag": {
    "extract": {
      "activity_name": "execute_workflow",
      "activity_display_name": "Extract My Connector Metadata",
      "app_name": "my-connector",
      "inputs": {
        "workflow_type": "my-connector",
        "app_name": "my-connector",
        "task_queue": "atlan-my-connector-{deployment_name}",
        "args": {
          "credential": "{{credential}}",
          "target": "{{target}}"
        }
      }
    },
    "publish": {
      "activity_name": "execute_workflow",
      "activity_display_name": "Publish to Atlas",
      "app_name": "publish",
      "inputs": {
        "workflow_type": "PublishWorkflow",
        "app_name": "publish",
        "task_queue": "atlan-publish-{deployment_name}",
        "args": {
          "connection_qualified_name": "$.extract.outputs.connection_qualified_name",
          "transformed_data_prefix": "$.extract.outputs.transformed_data_prefix",
          "publish_state_prefix": "$.extract.outputs.publish_state_prefix",
          "current_state_prefix": "$.extract.outputs.current_state_prefix",
          "connection_entity": "{{connection}}"
        }
      },
      "depends_on": { "node_id": "extract", "tag": "success" }
    }
  }
}

Deprecation note: The workflow_type body field is a deprecated fallback — the SDK logs a deprecation warning when it encounters it. The canonical form is POST /workflows/v1/start?entrypoint=<name>. AE manifests currently emit workflow_type for compatibility with older AE controllers; once your AE controller supports query parameters on start requests, migrate to ?entrypoint=<name>. New code outside of AE manifests should always use the query param.

The $.extract.outputs.* JSONPath references are resolved by AE at runtime against App A's run() return value, so that output must carry every key publish reads — build it on PublishInputMixin (see What Publish Reads from Extract).

docs.title: Pattern 2: Single App with Multiple Entry Points
docs.text:
If your phases must share in-flight state or run within the same Temporal workflow history, use a single App with multiple @entrypoint methods:

from application_sdk.app import App, entrypoint, task

class MyConnector(App):
    @entrypoint
    async def extract_metadata(self, input: ExtractionInput) -> ExtractionOutput:
        out = await self.fetch_schemas(FetchInput(connection_id=input.connection_id))
        return await self.transform(TransformInput(schemas=out.schemas))

    @entrypoint
    async def mine_queries(self, input: QueryInput) -> QueryOutput:
        return await self.fetch_queries(input)

Each @entrypoint is a separate Temporal workflow (my-connector:extract-metadata, my-connector:mine-queries). They can be triggered independently via POST /workflows/v1/start?entrypoint=extract-metadata.

This pattern works well when both entry points share the same credentials, handler, and configuration, but need to be triggered at different times or frequencies.

docs.title: Restarting the Same App (Incremental Processing)
docs.text:
For Apps that process data in pages or checkpoints and need to avoid Temporal history-size limits, App.continue_with(new_input) restarts the current App with a fresh workflow run while preserving correlation context. This is a within-app pattern — not cross-app coordination — but it is relevant when a single App drives a long multi-cycle extraction.

See Apps — continue_with() for usage details.

docs.title: Passing Data Between Apps
docs.text:
When apps coordinate via AE, the downstream app receives inputs via the args block in manifest.json. Use JSONPath references ($.upstream_node.outputs.field) to pass structured data.

For large intermediate files, use FileReference with StorageTier.RETAINED:

from application_sdk.contracts import FileReference, Output, StorageTier, UploadInput

class ExtractionOutput(Output):
    parquet_file: FileReference   # StorageTier.RETAINED — kept for downstream

class MyExtractor(App):
    @task
    async def transform(self, input: TransformInput) -> ExtractionOutput:
        path = "/tmp/output.parquet"
        write_parquet(path, records)
        up = await self.upload(UploadInput(local_path=path))
        return ExtractionOutput(parquet_file=up.ref)

The downstream app receives the FileReference.storage_path (object-store path) via the AE args substitution and downloads it before processing.

When atlan-objectstore is bound, App.upload() writes to Atlan's S3 so downstream AE nodes (publish, lineage) can read it. Without the explicit self.upload() call, downstream nodes see nothing — the DAG succeeds but the publish app finds no artifact in its bucket. See ADR-0014.

docs.title: Observability Across Apps
docs.text: Correlation IDs propagate automatically when AE starts child apps. All spans from a multi-app run share the same correlation_id in logs and traces, making it easy to trace a full extraction + publish cycle in Grafana/Loki.

docs.title: PKL Contracts
docs.text:
Every Atlan app ships a machine-readable contract — contract/app.pkl — that drives the entire deployment lifecycle: the setup form users fill in, the credential form, the Automation Engine DAG, the typed Python Input class your workflow receives, and the marketplace manifest.

One file, app.pkl, generates everything. This guide is the short path through it. The full authoring reference lives with the toolkit:

  • Toolkit README — quick start, outputs, widget table, curated examples
  • Field reference — every property, its default and what it renders

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Contracts amend the toolkit's App.pkl. One pkl eval, run from the app repo root, writes every output at its final path:

contract/app.pkl
    │
    └── pkl eval --project-dir contract -m . contract/app.pkl
            ├── atlan.yaml                                  (marketplace manifest, repo root)
            ├── app.yaml                                    (SDR CI shim, repo root)
            ├── app/generated/{name}.json                   (setup form)
            ├── app/generated/atlan-connectors-{name}.json  (credential form)
            ├── app/generated/manifest.json                 (AE DAG)
            └── app/generated/_input.py                     (typed Input class)

The SDK's handler auto-serves these files from app/generated/ (override with ATLAN_CONTRACT_GENERATED_DIR):

Generated File Served At {name}.json GET /workflows/v1/configmap/{name} atlan-connectors-{name}.json GET /workflows/v1/configmap/atlan-connectors-{name} manifest.json GET /workflows/v1/manifest

No handler overrides needed. Commit the generated files; do not edit them by hand.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Use the pinned pkl — the one CI renders contracts with — not whatever brew last shipped:

python -m application_sdk.dev.pkl print-version   # the version CI uses
PKL="$(python -m application_sdk.dev.pkl path)"   # download + cache that build
"$PKL" --version

The binary is cached under ~/.cache/atlan-sdk/pkl/<version>/. Each download attempt has a 60-second socket timeout. A 5xx response or a dropped connection is retried up to 2 times (3 attempts in total). A 404 means the pin has no asset for your platform, so it fails after the first attempt. A cached binary is used only if it runs and reports the pinned version. Otherwise it is downloaded again.

pkl is a language, not just a renderer, so versions disagree about what your contract means: backslash line-continuations inside a multi-line string are valid from 0.28 on and a hard Invalid character escape sequence before it. A clean render on a different version is therefore not evidence the Generated Artifact Freshness gate will pass — which is the whole reason that gate exists (FND-1864). The pin lives in one place, application_sdk/pkl_version.py.

Already have a pkl you like? Keep it, but check it:

python -m application_sdk.dev.pkl check   # exit 1 if it has drifted from CI

docs.title: Step 1 — Declare the Toolkit Dependency
docs.text:
Create contract/PklProject:

amends "pkl:Project"

dependencies {
  ["app-contract-toolkit"] {
    uri = "package://atlanhq.github.io/application-sdk/contracts/app-contract-toolkit@<LATEST_VERSION>"
  }
}

<LATEST_VERSION> is the version in contract-toolkit/src/PklProject on main (each release is also tagged contract-toolkit-v<version>).

Resolve and lock it from the repo root:

pkl project resolve contract
# Creates contract/PklProject.deps.json — commit this file

docs.title: Step 2 — Write app.pkl
docs.text:
This is the toolkit's own minimal example, contract-toolkit/examples/minimal/app.pkl, which toolkit CI evaluates on every change:

/// Minimal example — demonstrates the smallest possible App.pkl contract.
///
/// Every field not set here takes its documented default. No credentials,
/// no connector, opted-out of publish in the pipeline. Use this as the
/// starting point when scaffolding a new app contract.
amends "../../src/App.pkl"

name = "minimal"
displayName = "Minimal Example"
icon = "https://assets.atlan.com/assets/fullscreen-exit.svg"
hasCredentialConfig = false

pipeline {
  publish = null
}

uiConfig = new UIConfig {
  tasks {
    ["Configuration"] {
      inputs {
        ["target"] = new TextInput {
          title = "Target"
          helpText = "What to process."
          placeholderText = "my-target"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

In your app, replace the first amends line (a path inside the toolkit's source tree) with the package import:

amends "@app-contract-toolkit/App.pkl"

Everything else comes from the toolkit: set only what differs from the documented defaults. Do not import Config.pkl, Credential.pkl or NativeApp.pkl — they are legacy modules, and conformance flags contracts that use them. Widgets (TextInput, SqlTree, CredentialInput, SageV2, …) are re-exported from App.pkl and used unqualified.

For a connector with credentials and a schema filter, start from the README quick start, then pick the closest example.

docs.title: Step 3 — Add the Generate Task
docs.text:
The SDK does not ship a built-in generate poe task — you add it to your app's pyproject.toml. Use exactly this wiring; it is what the Generated Artifact Freshness gate runs, and any other command produces output the gate reports as stale:

[tool.poe.tasks]
generate.shell = """
  PKL="$(python -m application_sdk.dev.pkl path)"
  "$PKL" eval --project-dir contract -m . contract/app.pkl
  uvx ruff check --fix --quiet --force-exclude app/generated/*.py
  uvx ruff format --force-exclude app/generated/*.py
"""

Then run:

uv run poe generate

Run it from the repo root. --project-dir contract is required: pkl looks for PklProject in the current directory, not next to the module. Do not move _input.py out of app/generated/ afterwards.

docs.title: Generated Python Is Lint-Clean
docs.text: The toolkit lays out every generated .py file exactly as ruff does with default settings, and toolkit CI fails if ruff would change one. Do not exclude app/generated/_input.py from ruff, pyright or pre-commit — the generated input model is meant to be type-checked with the rest of your app.

docs.title: The DAG — How Extraction Flows
docs.text:
By default, manifest.json describes a two-node DAG:

extract → publish

The extract node runs your app's main workflow. The publish node runs the Publish App on the output of extract. Drop it with pipeline { publish = null } (as the minimal example does) when your app publishes nothing.

docs.title: What Publish Reads from Extract
docs.text:
The generated publish node reads these keys from the extract workflow's output, via $.extract.outputs.<key>:

  • connection_qualified_name
  • transformed_data_prefix
  • publish_state_prefix
  • current_state_prefix

Your workflow's output must carry every key the DAG references. Build it on PublishInputMixin, which derives the two state prefixes from connection_qualified_name:

from application_sdk.contracts import Output, PublishInputMixin


class MyExtractionOutput(Output, PublishInputMixin):
    pass


return MyExtractionOutput(
    connection_qualified_name=connection_qualified_name,
    transformed_data_prefix=transformed_data_prefix,
)

To publish from a different node, override publish in extraNodes and set its upstream, as below.

docs.title: Adding an Intermediate Node
docs.text:
extraNodes {
  ["lineage"] = new DAGNode {
    displayName = "Extract Lineage"
    workflowType = "LineageExtractionWorkflow"
    taskQueue = "atlan-my-connector-{deployment_name}"
    args {
      ["credential"] = "{{credential}}"
      ["connection"] = "{{connection}}"
    }
    dependsOn { "extract" }
  }
  ["publish"] = new PublishNode {
    upstream = "lineage"
  }
}

docs.title: Zero-Out Instead of Delete (Cross-Connection Enrichers)
docs.text:
If your app enriches assets another connector owns — writing its own namespaced attributes onto them rather than creating them — publish's default handling of an asset that falls out of a run is wrong for you. It issues a hard Atlas DELETE, destroying a still-live asset along with its downstream lineage and its user-curated tags and descriptions.

Declare a ZeroOutSpec so publish clears just your attributes instead:

pipeline {
  publish {
    zeroOutConfig = new ZeroOutSpec {
      // Types your app owns outright — these keep being hard-deleted.
      exclude { "Process"; "ColumnProcess" }
      // attribute -> zero value, written as-is inside entity.attributes.
      attrs {
        ["myConnectorNodeStatus"] = null
        ["myConnectorProjectId"] = null
      }
      // Same shape, for entity-root fields.
      rootAttrs { ["classifications"] = new Listing {} }
    }
  }
}

Also settable directly on PublishNode when you override the node via extraNodes["publish"]. Leave it unset and the arg is omitted, which is how zero-out stays off — do not build an empty spec to disable it.

Do not hand-write this as a raw JSON string in Pkl: a string is spliced unparsed, so a typo yields a broken manifest with no error at generation time, and it needs a post-generate merge script that CI's single hook may not run. The typed spec type-checks and needs no post-processing. See the toolkit reference for the full semantics, including why attrs is a value map rather than a list of names.

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text:
Widgets are declared under uiConfig.tasks[<step>].inputs. The README widget table lists each widget, the UI component it renders and the Python type it adds to _input.py; the field reference covers every widget property.

If your handler overrides Handler.warmup, set warmup = true on the SageV2 widget so the setup UI runs the warmup flow before the warmup-tier checks. Leave it unset otherwise; the flag must match the handler. See SageV2 warmup.

docs.title: Bumping the Toolkit Version
docs.text:
When a new toolkit version ships:

  1. Update the version in contract/PklProject
  2. Re-resolve: pkl project resolve contract
  3. Regenerate: uv run poe generate
  4. Diff the generated files — review changes before committing

Find the latest version in contract-toolkit/src/PklProject, or list the release tags:

git ls-remote --tags https://github.com/atlanhq/application-sdk 'contract-toolkit-v*'

Changes per version are in the toolkit CHANGELOG.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Before pushing, reproduce what the freshness gate checks:

python -m application_sdk.dev.pkl check   # local pkl matches CI's pin
uv run poe generate                        # regenerate from scratch
git status --porcelain                     # empty = generated files are fresh

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Every example under contract-toolkit/examples/ is an executable contract, evaluated by toolkit CI, with its generated output committed next to it. Start with:

  • minimal — smallest possible contract; all defaults
  • tree-filters — include/exclude filter tree pickers
  • full — every overridable feature: JDBC URL auth, all pipeline steps, diverse widgets, UI rules, extraNodes
  • fanin — multi-parent fan-in via dependsOn
  • publish-controls — publish toggles, errorHandling, zeroOutConfig

The README describes the rest.

docs.title: Building a REST API Connector
docs.text:
This guide builds a complete REST API connector from scratch — an app that calls an HTTP API, transforms the response into Atlan metadata, and uploads it. Use this when you're connecting to a SaaS tool, file-based source, or any non-SQL data source.

For SQL connectors, see Creating an SQL Application.

docs.title: What You're Building
docs.text:
A connector that:

  1. Authenticates with an API using an API key
  2. Fetches entities (e.g. tables, pipelines, dashboards)
  3. Writes JSONL output to object storage
  4. Uploads the output to Atlan via App.upload()

docs.title: Project Setup
docs.text:
uv init my-connector && cd my-connector
uv add "atlan-application-sdk"  # brings httpx, the SDK's HTTP client
mkdir -p app

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
Define input, output, and credential types in app/contracts.py:

from __future__ import annotations

from application_sdk.contracts import Input, Output


# --- Workflow contracts ---

class ExtractionInput(Input):
    credential_guid: str = ""
    output_path: str = ""
    days_back: int = 30


class ExtractionOutput(Output):
    output_path: str = ""
    record_count: int = 0


class FetchEntitiesInput(Input):
    credential_guid: str = ""
    output_path: str = ""
    days_back: int = 30


class FetchEntitiesOutput(Output):
    output_path: str = ""
    record_count: int = 0

Input and Output are Pydantic BaseModel subclasses — do not use @dataclass on them.

docs.title: HTTP Client
docs.text:
Put your HTTP client in app/clients.py:

from __future__ import annotations

import httpx

class MyApiClient:
    def __init__(self, api_token: str, base_url: str = "https://api.example.com") -> None:
        self._client = httpx.AsyncClient(
            base_url=base_url,
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_token}"},
            timeout=30,
        )

    async def get_entities(self, page: int = 1) -> list[dict]:
        response = await self._client.get("/v1/entities", params={"page": page})
        response.raise_for_status()
        return response.json()["data"]

    async def close(self) -> None:
        await self._client.aclose()

docs.title: Handler
docs.text:
The handler wires up test_auth and preflight_check:

from __future__ import annotations

from application_sdk.handler import Handler
from application_sdk.handler.contracts import (
    AuthInput, AuthOutput, AuthStatus,
    MetadataInput, ApiMetadataOutput,
    PreflightInput, PreflightOutput, PreflightStatus,
)

from app.clients import MyApiClient


class MyConnectorHandler(Handler):
    async def test_auth(self, input: AuthInput) -> AuthOutput:
        # Credentials arrive as a list of key/value pairs.
        api_token = next((c.value for c in input.credentials if c.key == "api_token"), "")
        base_url = next(
            (c.value for c in input.credentials if c.key == "base_url"),
            "https://api.example.com",
        )
        client = MyApiClient(api_token=api_token, base_url=base_url)
        try:
            entities = await client.get_entities(page=1)
            return AuthOutput(
                status=AuthStatus.SUCCESS,
                message=f"Connected: {len(entities)} entities found",
            )
        finally:
            await client.close()

    async def preflight_check(self, input: PreflightInput) -> PreflightOutput:
        return PreflightOutput(status=PreflightStatus.READY, message="OK")

    async def fetch_metadata(self, input: MetadataInput) -> ApiMetadataOutput:
        # Metadata extraction is driven by the App, not the handler.
        return ApiMetadataOutput()

docs.title: App (Connector)
docs.text:
The App subclasses App directly (REST connectors typically manage their own output pipeline):

# app/connector.py
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os

from application_sdk.app import App, task
from application_sdk.contracts import UploadInput, StorageTier
from application_sdk.credentials import CredentialResolver, api_key_ref
from application_sdk.infrastructure import get_infrastructure

from app.clients import MyApiClient
from app.contracts import (
    ExtractionInput,
    ExtractionOutput,
    FetchEntitiesInput,
    FetchEntitiesOutput,
)


class MyConnectorApp(App):

    async def run(self, input: ExtractionInput) -> ExtractionOutput:
        fetch_out = await self.fetch_entities(
            FetchEntitiesInput(
                credential_guid=input.credential_guid,
                output_path=input.output_path,
                days_back=input.days_back,
            )
        )
        # Explicit hand-off to Atlan: routes through atlan-objectstore (Atlan-owned)
        # in SDR deployments so the publish app can read it. The activity interceptor
        # only writes FileReferences to the customer-owned objectstore (infra.storage).
        # Omitting this call produces a silent failure in SDR — the DAG succeeds but
        # the publish app finds nothing. See ADR-0014.
        await self.upload(UploadInput(local_path=fetch_out.output_path))
        return ExtractionOutput(
            output_path=fetch_out.output_path,
            record_count=fetch_out.record_count,
        )

    @task(timeout_seconds=3600, auto_heartbeat_seconds=30)
    async def fetch_entities(
        self, input: FetchEntitiesInput
    ) -> FetchEntitiesOutput:
        infra = get_infrastructure()
        resolver = CredentialResolver(secret_store=infra.secret_store)
        ref = api_key_ref(input.credential_guid)
        raw = await resolver.resolve_raw(ref)
        client = MyApiClient(
            api_token=raw.get("api_token", ""),
            base_url=raw.get("base_url", "https://api.example.com"),
        )

        os.makedirs(input.output_path, exist_ok=True)
        output_file = os.path.join(input.output_path, "entities.jsonl")
        record_count = 0

        try:
            with open(output_file, "w") as f:
                page = 1
                while True:
                    entities = await client.get_entities(page=page)
                    if not entities:
                        break
                    for entity in entities:
                        atlan_entity = _transform_entity(entity)
                        f.write(json.dumps(atlan_entity) + "\n")
                        record_count += 1
                    page += 1
        finally:
            await client.close()

        return FetchEntitiesOutput(
            output_path=input.output_path,
            record_count=record_count,
        )


def _transform_entity(raw: dict) -> dict:
    return {
        "typeName": "Table",
        "attributes": {
            "name": raw["name"],
            "qualifiedName": raw["id"],
            "description": raw.get("description", ""),
        },
    }

Silent-failure rule: App.upload() in run() is required for any data that Atlan system apps (publish, QI, lineage) must consume. The activity interceptor only writes FileReference objects to the customer-owned objectstore (infra.storage). In SDR deployments, App.upload() routes through atlan-objectstore (infra.upstream_storage, Atlan-owned). Connectors that omit this call produce a silent failure — the DAG completes normally but the publish app finds nothing in Atlan's bucket. See ADR-0014.

docs.title: Local Development
docs.text:
Create run_dev.py:

import asyncio
from application_sdk.main import run_dev_combined
from app.connector import MyConnectorApp

asyncio.run(
    run_dev_combined(
        MyConnectorApp,
        credentials={
            "authType": "api_key",
            "api_token": "my-test-api-token",
            "base_url": "https://api.example.com",
        },
        example_input={
            "connection": {
                "connection_name": "test-connection",
                "connection_qualified_name": "default/my-connector/1234567890",
            },
            "days_back": 7,
        },
    )
)

Start dependencies and run:

# Terminal 1 — Temporal
temporal server start-dev --db-filename temporal.db

# Terminal 2 — Dapr (resolve the pinned daprd binary via the SDK; no Dapr CLI)
DAPRD=$(uv run python -c "from application_sdk.dev._dapr import _ensure_daprd_binary; print(_ensure_daprd_binary())")
"$DAPRD" \
  --app-id app \
  --app-port 8000 \
  --dapr-http-port 3500 \
  --dapr-grpc-port 50001 \
  --scheduler-host-address '' \
  --placement-host-address '' \
  --config components/configuration.yaml \
  --resources-path components &

# Terminal 3 — App
DAPR_HTTP_PORT=3500 DAPR_GRPC_PORT=50001 uv run python run_dev.py

Trigger the workflow:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/workflows/v1/start \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "credential_guid": "test-local-cred",
    "connection": {
      "qualifiedName": "default/my-connector/1234567890",
      "name": "my-test-connection"
    }
  }'

docs.title: Payload Safety
docs.text:
If any of your task inputs or outputs could be large, use FileReference instead of embedding data directly:

from application_sdk.contracts import Input, FileReference, StorageTier

class FetchEntitiesInput(Input):
    credential_guid: str = ""
    output_path: str = ""
    # Don't pass entity lists as task args — use FileReference instead

See Storage for the full pattern.

docs.title: Heartbeats in Long Tasks
docs.text:
For tasks that run more than a few minutes, use auto_heartbeat_seconds to let Temporal know the task is alive:

@task(timeout_seconds=7200, auto_heartbeat_seconds=30)
async def fetch_entities(self, input: FetchEntitiesInput) -> FetchEntitiesOutput:
    ...

For tasks where you want manual control (e.g. to include progress in the heartbeat), define a typed HeartbeatDetails subclass so that task_context.get_heartbeat_details(cls) can recover state on retry:

from application_sdk.contracts import HeartbeatDetails

class PageProgress(HeartbeatDetails):
    page: int = 0
    total: int = 0

@task(timeout_seconds=7200)
async def fetch_entities(self, input: FetchEntitiesInput) -> FetchEntitiesOutput:
    for page in range(total_pages):
        # process page...
        self.task_context.heartbeat(PageProgress(page=page, total=total_pages))

Never import from temporalio directly — use self.task_context.heartbeat() which wraps the Temporal primitive.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Raise a typed AppError leaf from application_sdk.errors. Whether Temporal retries the task follows from the leaf: AuthError, AppPermissionDeniedError, NotFoundError and InternalError fail it permanently, while SourceUnavailableError and RateLimitedError are retried. classify_http_exception picks the leaf for an httpx failure, so the connector keeps no status table of its own:

from application_sdk.errors import InternalError, classify_http_exception

@task(timeout_seconds=3600)
async def fetch_entities(self, input: FetchEntitiesInput) -> FetchEntitiesOutput:
    try:
        ...
    except httpx.HTTPError as e:
        # A 400 is unmapped by default; for this API it means the connector
        # built a bad request, so fail fast instead of retrying it.
        leaf = classify_http_exception(e, overrides={400: InternalError})
        if leaf is None:
            raise  # unmapped: Temporal retries it as an untyped failure
        raise leaf(message="API request failed", cause=e) from e

NonRetryableError from application_sdk.app is deprecated (removal in v4.0.0). See Map an HTTP failure to a leaf for overriding a status the source uses differently.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Use MockSecretStore to test without real credentials:

import json
import pytest
from application_sdk.infrastructure import set_infrastructure, clear_infrastructure, InfrastructureContext
from application_sdk.storage import create_memory_store
from application_sdk.testing import MockSecretStore

@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def infra(tmp_path):
    # MockSecretStore stores secrets as JSON strings (same as the real Dapr secret store).
    # create_memory_store() provides an in-process object store so upload_file() works without Dapr.
    set_infrastructure(
        InfrastructureContext(
            secret_store=MockSecretStore({
                "my-test-cred": json.dumps({
                    "type": "api_key",
                    "api_token": "test-token",
                    "base_url": "http://localhost",
                })
            }),
            storage=create_memory_store(),
        )
    )
    yield
    clear_infrastructure()


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_fetch_entities(httpx_mock, tmp_path):
    httpx_mock.add_response(
        url="http://localhost/v1/entities?page=1",
        json={"data": [{"id": "e1", "name": "Entity 1"}]},
    )
    httpx_mock.add_response(
        url="http://localhost/v1/entities?page=2",
        json={"data": []},
    )

    app = MyConnectorApp()
    result = await app.fetch_entities(
        FetchEntitiesInput(
            credential_guid="my-test-cred",
            output_path=str(tmp_path),
        )
    )
    assert result.record_count == 1

docs.title: Runtime Interactions — Cookbook
docs.text:
@signal, @query, and @update let external callers reach into a running App without killing or restarting it. The SDK lifts these decorators from your App subclass onto the generated run class, so the client API works transparently.

This page collects the patterns app authors actually need. Each example is paste-into-an-App-subclass and works against the SDK as of BLDX-1283.

TL;DR — when to reach for each decorator

Need Decorator Mutate state and return a value, with validation, exactly-once delivery @update Pure trigger — fire-and-forget, no payload, no return value @signal Read state without mutation, fast response @query

docs.title: Contracts enforced by the SDK
docs.text:
The SDK validates interaction signatures at class-definition time (when generate_workflow_class is called). Violations raise InvalidInputError immediately — not at runtime.

Decorator Parameter rule Return-type rule @signal No params besides self None (-> None) @query No params besides self Must be a subclass of Output @update Exactly one param besides self, must be a subclass of Input Must be a subclass of Output

Dynamic interactions (@update(dynamic=True) etc.) are exempt.

docs.title: 1. Pause / Resume / Graceful Cancel
docs.text:
A long extract that customers can pause mid-flight (maintenance window, source incident) without losing progress.

from application_sdk.app import App, update, wait_condition
from application_sdk.contracts.base import Input, Output


class ExtractInput(Input):
    source_url: str = ""


class ExtractOutput(Output):
    rows_extracted: int = 0
    final_state: str = ""


class PauseInput(Input):
    reason: str = ""


class StateMessageOutput(Output):
    message: str = ""


class ExtractApp(App):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.state: str = "running"
        self.rows_extracted: int = 0

    async def run(self, input: ExtractInput) -> ExtractOutput:
        for batch in self._batches(input.source_url):
            # Block here while paused — wait_condition is deterministic
            # and free when nothing is happening.
            await wait_condition(lambda: self.state != "paused")

            if self.state == "cancelled":
                break

            self.rows_extracted += await self._process(batch)

        return ExtractOutput(
            rows_extracted=self.rows_extracted, final_state=self.state
        )

    @update
    async def pause(self, input: PauseInput) -> StateMessageOutput:
        self.state = "paused"
        return StateMessageOutput(message=f"paused: {input.reason}")

    @update
    async def resume(self, input: PauseInput) -> StateMessageOutput:
        self.state = "running"
        return StateMessageOutput(message="resumed")

    @update
    async def graceful_cancel(self, input: PauseInput) -> StateMessageOutput:
        self.state = "cancelled"
        return StateMessageOutput(message=f"cancelling: {input.reason}")

Client side

handle = await client.start_workflow(
    ExtractApp.run, ExtractInput(source_url="..."),
    id="extract-1", task_queue="default",
)
await handle.execute_update("pause", PauseInput(reason="customer-maintenance-window"))
# ... later ...
await handle.execute_update("resume", PauseInput())

docs.title: 2. Live Progress / ETA Query
docs.text:
Operators see throughput without waiting for the run to finish. Useful for any long extractor.

from datetime import datetime

from application_sdk.app import now, query


class ProgressOutput(Output):
    tables_done: int = 0
    tables_total: int = 0
    elapsed_seconds: float = 0.0
    eta_seconds: float | None = None


class MetricsApp(App):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.tables_done: int = 0
        self.tables_total: int = 0
        self.started_at: datetime | None = None

    async def run(self, input: ExtractInput) -> ExtractOutput:
        self.started_at = now()
        tables = await self._list_tables(input.source_url)
        self.tables_total = len(tables)

        for t in tables:
            await self._extract_table(t)
            self.tables_done += 1

        return ExtractOutput(rows_extracted=self.tables_done)

    @query
    def progress(self) -> ProgressOutput:
        elapsed = (
            (now() - self.started_at).total_seconds()
            if self.started_at else 0.0
        )
        rate = self.tables_done / elapsed if elapsed > 0 else 0
        remaining = self.tables_total - self.tables_done
        return ProgressOutput(
            tables_done=self.tables_done,
            tables_total=self.tables_total,
            elapsed_seconds=elapsed,
            eta_seconds=remaining / rate if rate > 0 else None,
        )

Client side (status endpoint, oncall CLI, dashboard)

p = await handle.query("progress")
print(f"{p.tables_done}/{p.tables_total} — ETA {p.eta_seconds:.0f}s")

docs.title: 3. In-Flight Rate-Limit Adjustment
docs.text:
Source is hitting a quota. Back off without killing the run.

from datetime import timedelta

from application_sdk.app import update, wait_condition


class RateLimitInput(Input):
    rps: int = 100


class RateLimitOutput(Output):
    rps: int = 0


class RateLimitedApp(App):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.rps_limit: int = 100  # default

    async def run(self, input: ExtractInput) -> ExtractOutput:
        rows = 0
        async for batch in self._batches(input.source_url):
            # Re-read the live limit each batch; updates flip it mid-flight.
            await wait_condition(
                lambda: True, timeout=timedelta(seconds=1 / self.rps_limit)
            )
            rows += await self._process(batch)
        return ExtractOutput(rows_extracted=rows)

    @update
    async def set_rate_limit(self, input: RateLimitInput) -> RateLimitOutput:
        self.rps_limit = input.rps
        return RateLimitOutput(rps=self.rps_limit)

    @set_rate_limit.validator
    def _validate_rps(self, input: RateLimitInput) -> None:
        if input.rps < 1 or input.rps > 10_000:
            raise ValueError("rps must be in [1, 10_000]")

Client side (oncall during a source incident)

await handle.execute_update("set_rate_limit", RateLimitInput(rps=10))   # back off
# ... source recovers ...
await handle.execute_update("set_rate_limit", RateLimitInput(rps=200))  # ramp back up

The validator runs before the interaction body. If it raises, the client gets a WorkflowUpdateFailedError and no state mutation happens.

docs.title: 4. External Update Advances a Watermark
docs.text:
A webhook, cron, or sibling app notifies a long-running extractor that new data is ready.

from application_sdk.app import update, wait_condition


class WatermarkInput(Input):
    new_watermark: str = ""


class WatermarkOutput(Output):
    watermark: str = ""


class IncrementalApp(App):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.watermark: str = ""
        self.advance: bool = False

    async def run(self, input: ExtractInput) -> ExtractOutput:
        while True:
            await self._extract_since(self.watermark)
            # Block until an external system sends a new watermark.
            await wait_condition(lambda: self.advance)
            self.advance = False

    @update
    async def new_data_available(self, input: WatermarkInput) -> WatermarkOutput:
        self.watermark = input.new_watermark
        self.advance = True
        return WatermarkOutput(watermark=self.watermark)

Client side (a webhook handler in a different service)

await client.get_workflow_handle("incremental-extract-1").execute_update(
    "new_data_available", WatermarkInput(new_watermark="2026-05-21T08:00:00Z")
)

Use @update (not @signal) when the caller needs confirmation that the watermark was received, or when the new watermark value must be validated before the run acts on it.

docs.title: 5. Operator Probe for Incident Response
docs.text:
"Where did it stop?" during oncall, without reading logs.

from application_sdk.app import query


class CheckpointOutput(Output):
    partition: str | None = None
    offset: int = 0


class CheckpointedApp(App):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.checkpoint: CheckpointOutput = CheckpointOutput()

    async def run(self, input: ExtractInput) -> ExtractOutput:
        for partition in self._partitions():
            for batch in self._read(partition, offset=self.checkpoint.offset):
                await self._process(batch)
                self.checkpoint = CheckpointOutput(
                    partition=partition,
                    offset=batch.end_offset,
                )
        return ExtractOutput(rows_extracted=...)

    @query
    def get_checkpoint(self) -> CheckpointOutput:
        return self.checkpoint

Client side

$ temporal workflow query --workflow-id=extract-1 --type=get_checkpoint
{"partition": "shard-7", "offset": 1842394}

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
The same determinism rules that apply to run() apply to every runtime interaction — they all execute inside the run sandbox.

  • No I/O, no random, no time.time(). Use now() / uuid4() (from application_sdk.app). Network calls and DB queries belong in @task activities an interaction may invoke if needed.
  • Don't await long-running work in an interaction. Updates have a deadline (default 10s). Flip a flag in the interaction; let run() do the actual work.
  • Prefer wait_condition over polling. while not flag: await asyncio.sleep(0.1) works but is wasteful. wait_condition is the deterministic primitive and runs only when something changes.
  • Validators raise → update is rejected with WorkflowUpdateFailedError on the client. Use @<update_name>.validator for argument shape checks (non-empty strings, integer ranges). The interaction body should assume validated input.
  • Interaction state is per-run. The App instance lives for one execution; instance fields reset across runs. For cross-run state, use self.state.persistent / self.state.scratch (SDK state accessors).
  • Dynamic interactions (@update(dynamic=True) etc.) are supported — useful for catch-all routers. The interaction signature must be (self, name: str, args: Sequence[temporalio.common.RawValue]). Dynamic interactions are exempt from the Input/Output contract check.
  • Signals carry no payload. They are pure triggers. To pass data into a running workflow, use @update.
  • Interactions can arrive before run() starts. A signal sent with the start (signal-with-start) or an update-with-start is handled in the run's first activation, before run()'s first line. The SDK binds the App instance to the run when the run is created, so @task methods an interaction awaits still run as activities and self.context is set. Until run() starts, self.context.correlation_id is the run id; it switches to the caller's correlation id when run() begins.

docs.title: Secret Stores and Credentials
docs.text:
This guide covers the full credential lifecycle in the Application SDK: how credentials flow from Dapr secret stores into typed Python objects that your app code uses safely.

For the concise API reference, see Credentials.

docs.title: How Credentials Flow
docs.text:
External store           Dapr sidecar         SDK resolver          App code
(Vault, K8s, AWS SM) ──► DaprSecretStore ──► CredentialResolver ──► BasicCredential
                                                                      ApiKeyCredential
                                                                      ...
  1. Helm / Kubernetes provisions a Dapr secret-store component pointing at the external store.
  2. The SDK's DaprSecretStore calls the Dapr sidecar API to read the secret JSON.
  3. CredentialResolver deserialises the JSON into a typed Credential model.
  4. App code receives a strongly-typed object — no dict["password"] access patterns.

docs.title: Typed Credentials
docs.text:
All credential types are frozen Pydantic models available from application_sdk.credentials:

Type Fields Factory ref BasicCredential username, password basic_ref(name) ApiKeyCredential api_key, header_name, prefix api_key_ref(name) BearerTokenCredential token, expires_at bearer_token_ref(name) OAuthClientCredential client_id, client_secret, token_url, scopes, access_token oauth_client_ref(name) CertificateCredential cert_data, key_data, ca_data, passphrase certificate_ref(name) AtlanApiToken token, base_url atlan_api_token_ref(name) AtlanOAuthClient client_id, client_secret, base_url atlan_oauth_client_ref(name) GitSshCredential key_data, passphrase git_ssh_ref(name) GitTokenCredential token git_token_ref(name) RawCredential data (raw dict) CredentialRef.resolve(input) for a credential_guid input (legacy_credential_ref(guid) is deprecated, removed in v4.0)

docs.title: Using credentials in a task
docs.text:
from application_sdk.credentials import basic_ref, BasicCredential
from application_sdk.app import App, task

class MyConnector(App):
    @task
    async def fetch_data(self, input: FetchInput) -> FetchOutput:
        ref = basic_ref("my-db-creds")
        cred: BasicCredential = await self.context.resolve_credential(ref)
        conn = await connect(host=input.host, user=cred.username, password=cred.password)
        ...

self.context.resolve_credential(ref) reads from the injected SecretStore (Dapr in production, MockSecretStore in tests) and returns the typed object.

docs.title: Dapr Component Configuration
docs.text: In production, Dapr components map component names to external secret backends. The SDK reads from a component named secretstore by default (SECRET_STORE_NAME env var).

docs.title: Kubernetes Secrets (default for local / CI)
docs.text:
# components/secretstore.yaml
apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: secretstore
spec:
  type: secretstores.kubernetes
  version: v1

docs.title: AWS Secrets Manager
docs.text:
apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: secretstore
spec:
  type: secretstores.aws.secretsmanager
  version: v1
  metadata:
    - name: region
      value: "us-east-1"
    - name: accessKey
      secretKeyRef:
        name: aws-creds
        key: access_key_id
    - name: secretKey
      secretKeyRef:
        name: aws-creds
        key: secret_access_key

docs.title: HashiCorp Vault
docs.text:
apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: secretstore
spec:
  type: secretstores.hashicorp.vault
  version: v1
  metadata:
    - name: vaultAddr
      value: "https://vault.internal:8200"
    - name: vaultToken
      secretKeyRef:
        name: vault-token
        key: token

See the Dapr secret store documentation for the full list of supported backends.

docs.title: Deployment Secrets
docs.text:
A second secret store, deployment-secret-store (DEPLOYMENT_SECRET_STORE_NAME), holds environment-specific secrets such as Temporal auth credentials. The SDK reads from it automatically when ATLAN_AUTH_ENABLED=true.

The key names within the deployment secret are configurable:

ATLAN_AUTH_CLIENT_ID_KEY=ATLAN_AUTH_CLIENT_ID      # default
ATLAN_AUTH_CLIENT_SECRET_KEY=ATLAN_AUTH_CLIENT_SECRET

docs.title: Secrets inside an objectstore binding
docs.text:
An objectstore component can take its credentials from a secret store rather than from plain value entries:

apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: atlan-objectstore
spec:
  type: bindings.aws.s3
  version: v1
  metadata:
    - name: accessKey
      secretKeyRef:
        name: atlan-auth-secret
        key: ATLAN_AUTH_CLIENT_ID
auth:
  secretStore: deployment-secret-store

The SDK builds its own obstore store from this YAML, in parallel with the Dapr sidecar, and resolves each secretKeyRef in this order:

  1. The secret store named by auth.secretStore, read at worker startup once the sidecar is ready.
  2. An environment variable named after the ref's key — the fallback, and what secretstores.local.env amounts to in Docker Compose and SDR-local runs.

A ref that neither source holds makes the component broken. A broken optional binding degrades to "absent"; a broken required binding (the upstream store when ENABLE_ATLAN_UPLOAD=true) fails at startup and names the unresolved fields, rather than routing writes to the wrong bucket.

docs.title: Testing Without Dapr
docs.text:
Inject a MockSecretStore in tests to avoid needing a Dapr sidecar:

import pytest
from application_sdk.testing import MockSecretStore
from application_sdk.infrastructure import InfrastructureContext, set_infrastructure, clear_infrastructure

@pytest.fixture
def infra():
    ctx = InfrastructureContext(
        secret_store=MockSecretStore({
            "my-db-creds": '{"type":"basic","username":"admin","password":"secret"}',
        }),
    )
    set_infrastructure(ctx)
    yield ctx
    clear_infrastructure()

async def test_connect(infra):
    connector = MyConnector()
    output = await connector.fetch_data(FetchInput(host="localhost"))
    assert output.rows > 0

For richer credential test data, use MockCredentialStore:

from application_sdk.testing import MockCredentialStore
from application_sdk.infrastructure import InfrastructureContext, set_infrastructure

store = MockCredentialStore()
ref = store.add_basic("my-db-creds", username="admin", password="secret")
ctx = InfrastructureContext(secret_store=store.secret_store)
set_infrastructure(ctx)
# Always pair set_infrastructure with clear_infrastructure() in teardown,
# or use a yield fixture to avoid test pollution:
#   @pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
#   def infra():
#       set_infrastructure(ctx)
#       yield
#       clear_infrastructure()

docs.title: End-User Guide: AWS Secrets Manager
docs.text: If your app supports AWS Secrets Manager as an external credential source through the Atlan UI, users can set it up as follows.

docs.title: Creating a secret
docs.text:
1. Open AWS Secrets Manager in the AWS Console.
  2. Click Store a new secret → Other type of secret.
  3. Add key-value pairs matching the credential fields your connector expects:
  4. Basic auth: username, password
  5. IAM User: username, access-key-id, secret-access-key
  6. IAM Role: username, role-arn, external-id
  7. Give the secret a descriptive name and save.
  8. Copy the Secret ARN (format: arn:aws:secretsmanager:region:account-id:secret:name).

docs.title: Configuring in the Atlan UI
docs.text:
In your connector's configuration form: 1. Select AWS Secrets Manager as the credential source. 2. Enter the Secret ARN and AWS Region. 3. Map form fields to key names within the secret (e.g. password → db_password if your secret uses that key).

The platform will retrieve and inject the credential values at workflow start time.

docs.title: Troubleshooting AWS credential failures
docs.text:
• Access denied: The IAM role used by the Dapr sidecar must have secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permission for the secret ARN.
  • Wrong region: The region in the Dapr component config must match the secret's region.
  • Key name mismatch: Form field key names must exactly match the keys inside the AWS secret.
  • Stale cache: Dapr caches secrets for a configurable TTL. Rotate secrets and wait for the cache to expire, or restart the Dapr sidecar.

Check AWS CloudTrail for access-denied audit events.

docs.title: Building SQL Applications with Application SDK v3
docs.text:
This guide walks through building a SQL metadata extraction connector using the v3 Application SDK. By the end, you will have a working connector that extracts databases, schemas, tables, and columns, transforms them using an asset mapper, and publishes the results.

v3 replaces the v2 BaseSQLMetadataExtractionWorkflow + BaseSQLMetadataExtractionActivities split with a single SqlApp subclass. (SqlMetadataExtractor, the first v3 template, is deprecated and removed in v4.0.0; do not start on it.) If you are upgrading an existing v2 connector, see the Upgrade Guide for a step-by-step checklist.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A v3 SQL connector has five parts:

  1. App (extractor) --- a SqlApp subclass that declares the SQL to run and the map_* method for each entity.
  2. Handler --- a Handler subclass that implements HTTP endpoints for authentication, preflight checks, and metadata discovery.
  3. Client --- a client class (e.g., BaseSQLClient subclass or custom ClientInterface implementation) that manages the database connection.
  4. Asset mapper --- map_* methods that turn each raw SQL row into a pyatlan_v9 asset (replaces YAML transformers).
  5. Contracts --- typed Pydantic models for credentials, configuration, and task inputs.

The SDK orchestrates everything through Temporal workflows. You never import from temporalio directly --- the @task decorator handles activity registration, heartbeating, and retry configuration.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11+
  • uv package manager
  • Temporal server (local or remote)
  • Dapr runtime (for state and secret stores in production)

Install the SDK:

uv add atlan-application-sdk

You do not need to start any infrastructure: run_dev_combined() starts an embedded Dapr runtime and an in-process Temporal server (see Getting Started). To run against a standalone Temporal server and Dapr sidecar instead, see the Setup Overview.

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text:
A v3 SQL connector follows this layout:

my-connector/
  app/
    __init__.py
    clients.py          # Client class (BaseSQLClient or ClientInterface)
    contracts.py        # Typed Pydantic models (credentials, config, task inputs)
    handler.py          # Handler subclass
    connector.py        # SqlApp subclass (SQL templates + map_* methods)
    constants.py        # Connector-specific constants
    sql/                # SQL query files (*.sql)
    transformers/       # Additional transformation logic (optional)
    generated/          # Pkl-generated contract JSON files
      ...
  tests/
    test_connector.py
    test_handler.py
  main.py              # Local dev entry point (run_dev_combined)
  Dockerfile
  pyproject.toml
  atlan.yaml           # App manifest (app_id, execution_mode, Dapr config)

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
Define typed Pydantic models for your connector's credentials and configuration. This replaces the v2 pattern of passing Dict[str, Any] everywhere.

# app/contracts.py
from pydantic import BaseModel
from application_sdk.templates.contracts import ExtractionTaskInput


class MyCredential(BaseModel):
    """Normalize credentials from both handler (list of key-value pairs) and
    workflow (dict) formats into a single typed model."""
    host: str
    port: int = 5432
    username: str
    password: str
    database: str

    @classmethod
    def from_list(cls, credentials: list) -> "MyCredential":
        """Parse from handler's AuthInput.credentials (list of {key, value} dicts)."""
        creds = {c.key: c.value for c in credentials}
        return cls(**creds)

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, credentials: dict) -> "MyCredential":
        """Parse from workflow credential dict."""
        return cls(**credentials)

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        return self.model_dump()


class MetadataConfig(BaseModel):
    """Connector-specific configuration parsed from the workflow input."""
    exclude_views: bool = False


class MyFetchInput(ExtractionTaskInput):
    """Extended task input with connector-specific config."""
    metadata_config: MetadataConfig = MetadataConfig()

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
Extend BaseSQLClient to define the connection string template for your database. The SDK uses this template to build a SQLAlchemy connection URL.

# app/clients.py
from application_sdk.clients import BaseSQLClient, DatabaseConfig


class PostgresClient(BaseSQLClient):
    DB_CONFIG = DatabaseConfig(
        template="postgresql+psycopg://{username}:{password}@{host}:{port}/{database}",
        required=["username", "password", "host", "port", "database"],
    )

The required list declares which credential keys must be present. The SDK validates these at connection time and raises a clear error if any are missing.

Each value is made URL-safe before it fills the template, so a connection-form value cannot add a driver parameter or override one in defaults (such as sslmode):

  • host must be a hostname, an IPv4 address, or an IPv6 address in square brackets ([::1]). A value with a scheme, port, path or query raises SqlCredentialsParseError.
  • port must be a whole number from 1 to 65535, as an int or a string of digits. Anything else raises SqlCredentialsParseError.
  • Every other field, password included, is percent-encoded, wherever it sits in the template. SQLAlchemy decodes it, so the driver receives the original value. Store raw values, not pre-encoded ones.

host and port are only validated when the template contains {host} or {port}.

docs.title: Handler
docs.text:
The Handler ABC defines three HTTP endpoints that the Atlan platform calls during connector setup and operation. Each method receives a typed input and returns a typed output. Use your typed credential model to normalize the raw credential payload.

# app/handler.py
from application_sdk.handler import Handler
from application_sdk.handler.contracts import (
    AuthInput,
    AuthOutput,
    AuthStatus,
    PreflightInput,
    PreflightOutput,
    PreflightStatus,
    MetadataInput,
    MetadataOutput,
    SqlMetadataObject,
    SqlMetadataOutput,
)
from app.clients import PostgresClient
from app.contracts import MyCredential


class PostgresHandler(Handler):
    async def test_auth(self, input: AuthInput) -> AuthOutput:
        """Verify that the provided credentials can connect to the database."""
        try:
            cred = MyCredential.from_list(input.credentials)
            client = PostgresClient()
            await client.load(credentials=cred.to_dict())
            return AuthOutput(status=AuthStatus.SUCCESS, message="Connected")
        except Exception as e:
            return AuthOutput(status=AuthStatus.FAILED, message=str(e))

    async def preflight_check(self, input: PreflightInput) -> PreflightOutput:
        """Run pre-extraction checks (connectivity, permissions, table counts)."""
        return PreflightOutput(status=PreflightStatus.READY, message="All checks passed")

    async def fetch_metadata(self, input: MetadataInput) -> SqlMetadataOutput:
        """Return catalog/schema pairs for the Atlan UI filter tree."""
        cred = MyCredential.from_list(input.credentials)
        client = PostgresClient()
        await client.load(credentials=cred.to_dict())

        rows = []
        async for batch in client.run_query(
            "SELECT catalog_name AS table_catalog, schema_name AS table_schema "
            "FROM information_schema.schemata "
            "WHERE schema_name NOT LIKE 'pg_%' "
            "AND schema_name != 'information_schema'"
        ):
            rows.extend(batch)
        # BaseSQLClient.run_query lowercases column names, so dict keys are lowercase.
        # SqlMetadataObject keeps the uppercase field names from the wire schema.
        objects = [
            SqlMetadataObject(TABLE_CATALOG=r["table_catalog"], TABLE_SCHEMA=r["table_schema"])
            for r in rows
        ]
        return SqlMetadataOutput(objects=objects)

docs.title: Handler contracts
docs.text:
Method Input Output Purpose test_auth AuthInput AuthOutput Verify credentials work preflight_check PreflightInput PreflightOutput Check connectivity, permissions, table counts fetch_metadata MetadataInput SqlMetadataOutput Return catalog/schema tree for UI filters

AuthOutput.status uses AuthStatus (SUCCESS, FAILED, EXPIRED, INVALID_CREDENTIALS). A handler sets PreflightOutput.status to PreflightStatus.READY when extraction can proceed (advisory check failures included) or NOT_READY when it cannot. PARTIAL is deprecated (removal anchored at v3.40.0); return READY with the failed advisory checks listed instead.

docs.title: App (Extractor)
docs.text:
The core of your connector is a SqlApp subclass. You declare three things and the template does the rest:

  • sql_client_class --- the client from Client.
  • fetch_database_sql, fetch_schema_sql, fetch_table_sql, fetch_column_sql --- one query per entity. Each must stand alone: the default run() issues all four at once, so each query applies its own filters (here, the same system-schema exclusions in all three).
  • map_database, map_schema, map_table, map_column --- one asset mapper per entity. Each takes one raw row and the connection's qualified name and returns a pyatlan_v9 asset. All four are required for the default run(): the base ones raise Map*UnimplementedError.
# app/connector.py
from pyatlan_v9.model.assets import Column, Database, Schema, Table

from application_sdk.templates import SqlApp

from app.clients import PostgresClient


class PostgresApp(SqlApp):
    sql_client_class = PostgresClient

    fetch_database_sql = (
        "SELECT datname AS database_name FROM pg_database "
        "WHERE datname = current_database()"
    )
    fetch_schema_sql = """
        SELECT s.catalog_name AS database_name, s.schema_name
        FROM information_schema.schemata s
        WHERE s.schema_name NOT LIKE 'pg_%'
          AND s.schema_name != 'information_schema'
    """
    fetch_table_sql = """
        SELECT t.table_catalog AS database_name, t.table_schema AS schema_name,
               t.table_name
        FROM information_schema.tables t
        WHERE t.table_type = 'BASE TABLE'
          AND t.table_schema NOT LIKE 'pg_%'
          AND t.table_schema != 'information_schema'
    """
    fetch_column_sql = """
        SELECT c.table_catalog AS database_name, c.table_schema AS schema_name,
               c.table_name, c.column_name, c.data_type, c.ordinal_position
        FROM information_schema.columns c
        WHERE c.table_schema NOT LIKE 'pg_%'
          AND c.table_schema != 'information_schema'
    """

    def map_database(self, record, connection_qn):
        return Database.creator(
            name=record["database_name"],
            connection_qualified_name=connection_qn,
        )

    def map_schema(self, record, connection_qn):
        database = self.map_database(record, connection_qn)
        return Schema.creator(
            name=record["schema_name"],
            database_qualified_name=database.qualified_name,
        )

    def map_table(self, record, connection_qn):
        schema = self.map_schema(record, connection_qn)
        return Table.creator(
            name=record["table_name"],
            schema_qualified_name=schema.qualified_name,
        )

    def map_column(self, record, connection_qn):
        table = self.map_table(record, connection_qn)
        column = Column.creator(
            name=record["column_name"],
            parent_qualified_name=table.qualified_name,
            parent_type=Table,
            order=record["ordinal_position"],
        )
        column.data_type = record["data_type"]
        return column

Build every asset with its pyatlan_v9 .creator() factory. Each one computes its own qualified name from its parent's, so the naming grammar lives in pyatlan rather than in a hand-written f"{connection_qn}/..." string per connector (conformance rule P028 flags those). A mapper is a plain method of one row: unit test it by calling it with a dict.

Note: New connectors must use pyatlan_v9. The deprecated AtlasTransformer / QueryBasedTransformer YAML transformers, which still use pyatlan internally, are not part of a SqlApp connector.

Return the asset, not a dict. The SDK serialises whatever the mapper returns through application_sdk.common.asset_serialization.entity_bytes(), which encodes a pyatlan_v9 asset natively and stamps the framework-injected attributes on it — connectionName, and the three lastSync* attributes that make an asset clickable back to the run that last touched it. Do not stamp last_sync_* in the mapper: the only workflow id a mapper can reach is the child workflow's Temporal id, which is not the AE-dispatched run (see Asset Serialisation). Hand-rolling a serialize_entity() helper to convert the asset to a dict first costs two extra JSON passes per record and gives up the type checking that is the point of the asset mapper — asset.column_cont = 7 is a pyright error, payload["columnCont"] = 7 is not. A return value the seam does not recognise raises UnserializableMapperResultError rather than falling back to anything.

Declare envelope overrides, don't post-process. If your connector needs the finished line to differ — a sqlDialect on definition-bearing assets, or a root-level field a downstream app reads — set entity_envelope on the app class or override decorate_entity(), rather than reaching past entity_bytes() to mutate the serialised dict. See Entity envelope. Four connectors hand-rolled that pass and produced four incompatible wire shapes; a declared override is the same change with the fleet able to see it.

docs.title: What happens under the hood
docs.text:
Each @task method on SqlApp becomes a Temporal activity. The default run():

  1. Prime auth --- one serial connection before the parallel burst, so a source that caches authentication (MySQL 8's caching_sha2_password) does not lock the account out. A failure here raises its typed error and nothing else runs.
  2. Extract --- extract_databases, extract_schemas, extract_tables and extract_columns run in parallel, each streaming its query's rows verbatim into raw/<entity>/records.json.
  3. Transform --- the matching transform_* tasks run in parallel, each reading its raw file and running every row through its map_* method into transformed/<entity>/entities.json.
  4. Finalize --- finalize_extraction verifies the transformed tree is whole and returns the ExtractionOutput publish reads.

Every non-empty extract and transform task output is a FileReference with a canonical storage_path, which the task's persist step uploads to the deployment store. Do not add self.upload() calls or an upload task for that.

Publish reads Atlan's store, which in an SDR deployment is a different store from the deployment store (ADR-0014). So hand the transformed tree on with upload_refs(), by reference, and return the prefix it delivered to. atlan-mysql-app does this on every run; in a single-store deployment the same call writes to the one store:

from application_sdk.contracts.base import Output
from application_sdk.contracts.storage import DeclaredFile, UploadRefsInput
from application_sdk.templates.contracts.sql_metadata import ExtractionInput


class PostgresExtractionOutput(Output):
    connection_qualified_name: str = ""
    transformed_data_prefix: str = ""
    publish_state_prefix: str = ""
    current_state_prefix: str = ""


class PostgresApp(SqlApp):
    ...  # SQL templates and map_* methods as above

    async def run(self, input: ExtractionInput) -> PostgresExtractionOutput:
        out = await super().run(input)
        delivered = await self.upload_refs(
            UploadRefsInput(
                files=[DeclaredFile(ref=ref) for ref in out.transformed_files],
                source_prefix=out.transformed_data_prefix,
                prefix=out.transformed_data_prefix,
            )
        )
        return PostgresExtractionOutput(
            connection_qualified_name=out.connection_qualified_name,
            transformed_data_prefix=delivered.prefix,
            publish_state_prefix=out.publish_state_prefix,
            current_state_prefix=out.current_state_prefix,
        )

delivered.prefix is "" when there was nothing to deliver, which tells publish not to diff the tenant against an empty tree. Return your own output model, not ExtractionOutput: its validator back-fills an empty transformed_data_prefix from output_path, which undoes that signal.

docs.title: Available task methods
docs.text:
Method Input Output Default behavior extract_databases / extract_schemas / extract_tables / extract_columns ExtractionTaskInput ExtractionTaskOutput Runs the matching fetch_*_sql through sql_client_class extract_views / extract_procedures ExtractionTaskInput ExtractionTaskOutput Optional: not driven by the default run(); set fetch_view_sql / fetch_procedure_sql and call them from a run() override transform_databases / transform_schemas / transform_tables / transform_columns TransformInput TransformOutput Runs each raw row through the matching map_* method transform_views / transform_procedures TransformInput TransformOutput Optional, as for the extract pair

Override an extract_* or transform_* task to change one entity's SQL or mapper; call extract_entity / transform_entity from the override rather than writing the files yourself.

docs.title: Excluding tables and views by name
docs.text:
The connector form's "Exclude regex for tables & views" field arrives as the workflow arg exclude_table_regex (form key exclude-table-regex, flat or nested under metadata). ExtractionInput copies it into temp_table_regex, the SDK's name for the same filter, before validation, so it goes through the same pattern and SQL-injection checks. An explicit temp_table_regex wins.

SqlApp substitutes the value into extract_temp_table_regex_table_sql at {exclude_table_regex} and injects the result at {temp_table_regex_sql}. The column query uses extract_temp_table_regex_column_sql instead when you declare one (for example AND C.TABLE_NAME NOT REGEXP '{exclude_table_regex}'). Otherwise it gets the table fragment too, which then needs a T alias in the column query. Wrap {exclude_table_regex} in single quotes in the fragment. Block comments in the fragment are stripped before substitution, so a documented fragment is safe to inject into a template that mentions {temp_table_regex_sql} in its own header comment.

-- app/sql/extract_temp_table_regex_table.sql
AND T.TABLE_NAME NOT REGEXP '{exclude_table_regex}'

Read input.temp_table_regex in custom code, not exclude_table_regex.

docs.title: Adding custom tasks
docs.text:
A custom entity (SDK ≥ 3.60.0) is an extract_* / transform_* task pair whose bodies call extract_entity and transform_entity. Those two own the streaming, the event-loop offload and the canonical FileReference keys publish reads, so call them rather than writing the files yourself. A run() that drives the extra pair folds its output in with finalize_extraction, which verifies the whole transformed tree:

from application_sdk.app import task
from application_sdk.templates import SqlApp
from application_sdk.templates.contracts.sql_metadata import (
    ExtractionInput,
    ExtractionOutput,
    ExtractionTaskInput,
    ExtractionTaskOutput,
    TransformInput,
    TransformOutput,
)


class PostgresApp(SqlApp):
    fetch_function_sql = "SELECT ..."

    def map_function(self, record, connection_qn):
        ...  # build and return a pyatlan_v9 Function asset

    @task()
    async def extract_functions(
        self, input: ExtractionTaskInput
    ) -> ExtractionTaskOutput:
        return await self.extract_entity(
            entity_type="function",
            sql_template=self.fetch_function_sql,
            input=input,
        )

    @task()
    async def transform_functions(self, input: TransformInput) -> TransformOutput:
        return await self.transform_entity(
            entity_type="function", mapper_fn=self.map_function, input=input
        )

    async def run(self, input: ExtractionInput) -> ExtractionOutput:
        base = await super().run(input)
        task_input = self.build_task_input(
            ExtractionTaskInput, input, cred_ref=self.resolve_credential_ref(input)
        )
        raw = await self.extract_functions(task_input)
        out = await self.transform_functions(
            self.build_transform_input(task_input, raw.raw_file)
        )
        return await self.finalize_extraction(base, [out])

A run() that replaces SqlApp.run() instead of calling super().run() must still end in finalize_extraction; conformance rule P068 flags one that does not. _extract_entity, _transform_entity and _resolve_output_path are the names these methods had before 3.60.0; they are deprecated and removed in v4.0.0.

docs.title: Typed Contracts
docs.text:
v3 replaces Dict[str, Any] with Pydantic models for all task inputs and outputs. This provides:

  • Type safety --- errors caught at import time, not at runtime
  • Payload validation --- Temporal has a 2 MB payload limit; contracts forbid unbounded types (Any, bare bytes, unbounded list)
  • Self-documenting APIs --- contract fields visible in Temporal UI and IDE autocompletion

docs.title: Contract hierarchy
docs.text:
All SQL metadata extraction contracts live in application_sdk.templates.contracts.sql_metadata:

ExtractionInput          -- top-level input to run()
ExtractionOutput         -- top-level output from run(); what publish reads
ExtractionTaskInput      -- shared fields for every extract_* task; build it with build_task_input()
  TransformInput         -- passed to every transform_* task; build it with build_transform_input()
ExtractionTaskOutput     -- raw_file: FileReference | None (None for no SQL or zero rows), total_record_count
TransformOutput          -- transformed_file: FileReference | None (None for an empty input), total_record_count

docs.title: Bounded collections
docs.text:
Unbounded list and dict are forbidden in contracts. Use MaxItems to declare an upper bound:

from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import Field
from application_sdk.contracts import MaxItems

class FetchDatabasesOutput(Output):
    databases: Annotated[list[str], MaxItems(10000)] = Field(default_factory=list)
    chunk_count: int = 0
    total_record_count: int = 0

docs.title: FileReference for large data
docs.text:
When a task produces data too large for a Temporal payload, use FileReference. The SDK uploads it to the customer-owned deployment store (objectstore) automatically when the task returns:

from application_sdk.contracts import FileReference

class FetchOutput(Output):
    results: FileReference  # automatically uploaded on task output (to infra.storage)

class ProcessInput(Input):
    results: FileReference  # automatically downloaded on task input

FileReference is for task-to-task transfer within a run. To hand off artifacts to Atlan system apps (publish, QI, lineage), call App.upload() explicitly from run() — the interceptor's auto-upload only writes to the customer-owned store and is not visible to Atlan. See file-reference.md and ADR-0014.

docs.title: Entry Point
docs.text: v3 uses the application-sdk CLI to start your app. The ATLAN_APP_MODULE environment variable tells the CLI which class to load.

docs.title: For local development
docs.text:
# main.py
import asyncio
from application_sdk.main import run_dev_combined
from app.connector import PostgresApp

asyncio.run(run_dev_combined(PostgresApp))

run_dev_combined starts both the Temporal worker and the HTTP handler in a single process.

docs.title: CLI modes
docs.text:
The application-sdk CLI supports three modes:

Mode What it runs Use case worker Temporal worker only Production worker pods handler HTTP handler only Production handler pods combined Worker + handler Local dev, SDR (single-deploy runtime) 
# Local development
application-sdk --mode combined --app app.connector:PostgresApp

# Production (separate pods)
application-sdk --mode worker
application-sdk --mode handler

In production, the --app flag is optional --- ATLAN_APP_MODULE is the recommended approach (see Dockerfile section).

docs.title: Dockerfile
docs.text:
The base image handles the entrypoint, Dapr, and the application-sdk CLI. You only set your app module and copy your code. No ENTRYPOINT, custom entrypoint.sh, or CMD is needed. The base image handles mode selection at runtime.

# Application-sdk v3 base image (Chainguard-based)
FROM registry.atlan.com/public/app-runtime-base:3

WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies first (better caching)
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser pyproject.toml uv.lock README.md ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/home/appuser/.cache/uv,uid=1000,gid=1000 \
    uv venv .venv && \
    uv sync --locked --no-install-project

# Copy application code
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser . .

# App-specific environment variables
ENV ATLAN_HANDLER_PORT=8000
ENV ATLAN_APP_MODULE=app.connector:PostgresApp
ENV ATLAN_CONTRACT_GENERATED_DIR=app/generated

Key points:

  • Base image: registry.atlan.com/public/app-runtime-base:3 --- includes Dapr, the application-sdk CLI, and the entrypoint.
  • No CMD needed: The base image handles mode selection at runtime.
  • COPY . .: Copies the entire project (including app/, main.py, SQL files, etc.). The .dockerignore should exclude .git, tests/, etc.
  • --no-install-project: Installs only dependencies, not the project itself (the app code is copied separately).
  • ATLAN_CONTRACT_GENERATED_DIR: Relative path --- the base image WORKDIR is /app.
Variable Required Description ATLAN_APP_MODULE Yes Python import path to your App subclass (e.g., app.connector:PostgresApp) ATLAN_HANDLER_PORT Recommended HTTP port for the handler service (default: 8000). Fallback: ATLAN_APP_HTTP_PORT. ATLAN_CONTRACT_GENERATED_DIR Recommended Path to Pkl-generated contract JSON files (default: app/generated)

The base image entrypoint hard-fails at startup if ATLAN_APP_MODULE is not set.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
v3 provides in-memory mock implementations of infrastructure services so you can test without running Dapr or Temporal sidecars.

# tests/test_extractor.py
from app.connector import PostgresApp


def test_map_table_builds_qualified_name():
    """A mapper is a plain method of one row: no Temporal, no SQL client."""
    table = PostgresApp().map_table(
        {"database_name": "sales", "schema_name": "public", "table_name": "orders"},
        "default/postgres/1700000000",
    )

    assert table.name == "orders"
    assert table.qualified_name == "default/postgres/1700000000/sales/public/orders"

docs.title: Mock infrastructure
docs.text:
Mock Replaces Purpose MockStateStore Dapr state store In-memory key-value store with call tracking MockSecretStore Dapr secret store In-memory secret store with call tracking

Both mocks record every call for assertions:

async def test_state_store_tracking():
    store = MockStateStore()
    await store.save("key", {"value": "data"})

    assert store.get_save_calls() == [("key", {"value": "data"})]
    result = await store.load("key")
    assert result == {"value": "data"}

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
Here is a complete, minimal connector using v3 patterns.

# main.py
import asyncio
from application_sdk.main import run_dev_combined
from app.connector import PostgresApp

async def main():
    await run_dev_combined(PostgresApp)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

# Dockerfile
FROM registry.atlan.com/public/app-runtime-base:3

WORKDIR /app

COPY --chown=appuser:appuser pyproject.toml uv.lock README.md ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/home/appuser/.cache/uv,uid=1000,gid=1000 \
    uv venv .venv && \
    uv sync --locked --no-install-project

COPY --chown=appuser:appuser . .

ENV ATLAN_HANDLER_PORT=8000
ENV ATLAN_APP_MODULE=app.connector:PostgresApp
ENV ATLAN_CONTRACT_GENERATED_DIR=app/generated

# atlan.yaml
app_id: postgres
execution_mode: native
splitDeploymentEnabled: true
dapr:
  objectstore:
    enabled: true
  secretstore:
    enabled: true

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use typed contracts. Never pass Dict[str, Any] between tasks. Define Pydantic models for credentials, config, and task inputs (see contracts.py).
  2. Use asset mappers for transformation. Write pure Python mapper functions (raw rows → pyatlan entities) instead of YAML transformers. They are testable and explicit.
  3. Keep tasks focused. Each @task method should do one thing --- fetch databases, fetch schemas, transform, etc. The run() method handles orchestration.
  4. Use FileReference for large data. If a task produces output larger than ~1 MB, store it in object storage via FileReference rather than passing it through Temporal.
  5. Load credentials via credential_ref. Use input.credential_ref (the typed CredentialRef) in @task methods. In handlers, use typed credential models to normalize input.credentials.
  6. Log with the SDK logger. Use get_logger from application_sdk.observability for structured logging that integrates with Temporal.
  7. Test without sidecars. Use MockStateStore and MockSecretStore from application_sdk.testing to test your connector and handler without Dapr or Temporal running.
  8. Set ATLAN_APP_MODULE in the Dockerfile. This locks the app module to the image and avoids runtime misconfiguration.
  9. Use on_complete for cleanup. Override on_complete() for post-run cleanup (see Upgrade Guide Step 12).
